articles.title: Is buying a second property within a year too aggressive?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old working abroad wants a RM500,000 furnished Cheras subsale a year after buying her first unit, and worries falling birth rates will hurt property. Sean walks through the subsale steps and his long-term view.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is a second purchase this soon too aggressive, what happens in a subsale after she says yes, and will falling birth rates leave Malaysia with China-style oversupply?
articles.answer: Not too aggressive for her income and finances, and the building rents well. But as a member of a bulk-purchase club she should also weigh completed unsold units, which offer a subsale's certainty with a developer's discounts. Demographics will hurt outlying areas and big houses, not city units with job-driven demand.
points: A subsale takes about 18% in cash
One lawyer is cheaper and faster
Completed unsold units combine both
Fewer families means smaller city units

articles.title: Should I buy a second property, or keep it simple?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old government officer already owns a Klang Valley unit and invests in global equities. He asks whether two new projects with rebates are really good deals, or just sales tactics.
articles.viewerQuestion: Are these genuinely good investments or do the rebates make the numbers look better than they are, and with equities already in place, is another leveraged property worthwhile?
articles.answer: The rebates are retail-price sales tactics that everybody gets, and a newer project only wins when the entry price makes sense. Let the existing unit run, use your second 90% loan slot only when you can afford it, and keep the capital a third property would need in global equities.
points: Newer wins only if the price makes sense
Rebates are given to everybody
The exit depends on rent, not age
Cash in property is the worst deal
questions: Are property rebates and discounts from developers genuine savings or just sales tactics?
How do I know if a new launch is worth buying compared to an older unit?
What rental yield should I aim for so the rent covers my monthly instalment?
Should I buy a second property or put the money into global equities instead?
How much cash should I set aside for renovation and instalments before collecting my keys?

articles.title: How do we get the best price for the family home we must sell?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old plans to sell his overspending father's JB corner semi-D for RM2.2 million within two years to fund his parents' retirement. Sean explains how pricing, valuation and agents decide how fast it sells.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is two years long enough to sell at RM2.2 million, how does he get the best price, how does he pick an agent, and are there tax issues in the transfer?
articles.answer: Two years is plenty, and JB's market is strong, but price sets the speed. Get bank valuations first: asking well above what a bank will lend means buyers must find a large cash gap, so it will sit unsold. Pick one committed agent, and expect no RPGT on a home held this long.
points: Valuation decides what a buyer can borrow
Test the price, then lower it
One committed agent beats five
Protect the family first

articles.title: I own 10 fully paid condos at 59. Should I sell before I retire?
articles.excerpt: A viewer about to retire owns ten debt-free condos in Penang and Singapore. Sean agrees with selling the Penang units, but warns that selling too many too fast can be taxed as a business.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should KB sell some or all of the properties before retiring, move the money into fixed deposits and other assets, and stop dealing with tenants?
articles.answer: Selling the Penang units makes sense, perhaps keeping one, but slowly, so the sales aren't taxed as a property business. The three Singapore units are worth keeping for income.
points: Selling fast can be taxed as business
Singapore rent alone can fund retirement
Penang's LRT decides what to sell first
Refinancing is no longer the easy exit
questions: Should I sell my Penang condos before retiring?
How can I avoid being taxed as a business when selling multiple properties?
What is the RPGT rate for selling property in Malaysia?
Can rental income from Singapore properties fund retirement in Penang?
How does the Penang LRT affect property values and selling decisions?

articles.title: Should You Settle Your Housing Loan Early?
articles.excerpt: A reader with three mortgages dreams of being debt-free. Sean explains why he would keep the loans running, and what to do with the spare cash instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she pay the loans off as fast as possible to save on interest, or let them run the full term?
articles.answer: Keep the loans running. At around 4%, a housing loan is the cheapest money you can get, below the rate of inflation, so spare cash should go where it earns more than the loan costs.
points: Settling early can raise your tax bill
Your cash can earn more elsewhere
Her loans already pay for themselves
Her age favours more borrowing, not less
questions: Should I pay off my housing loan early or keep it?
Is it better to invest spare cash or settle my mortgage?
How does rental income tax affect early loan settlement?
Can EPF dividends beat housing loan interest?
What buffer should I keep for rental properties?

articles.title: I work in Singapore. Can I get a housing loan in Malaysia?
articles.excerpt: Singapore income converts well, so qualifying is rarely the problem. Rena Choong explains what Malaysian banks check for Malaysians working in Singapore, and what changes if you take up citizenship.
articles.viewerQuestion: How do Malaysian banks treat Singapore income, and what should Malaysians working in Singapore prepare before applying?
articles.answer: Converted to ringgit, Singapore income usually qualifies easily; paperwork is what trips people up. Have at least a year of steady employment, clear savings records and your Singapore documents ready, and decide first whether you plan to settle there.
points: Income converts generously
Malaysians keep Malaysian margins
Citizenship changes the terms
Savings and history reassure the bank
questions: How do Malaysian banks assess income earned in Singapore for a housing loan?
What documents do I need to prepare for a Malaysian housing loan if I work in Singapore?
Does holding a Singapore PR affect my housing loan margin in Malaysia?
What happens to my Malaysian housing loan eligibility if I become a Singapore citizen?
Can I buy a property in Malaysia while owning an HDB flat in Singapore?

articles.title: Now settled in Singapore, what should I do with my new KL unit?
articles.excerpt: A young engineer bought a Bukit Jalil unit, then got Singapore PR. Sean explains why he would rent out the whole unit, how to furnish it for the right tenant, and why there is no rush to come home.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he rent out the whole unit, rent it room by room and keep one room for visits, or let family stay, and how much should he spend getting it ready for tenants?
articles.answer: Rent out the whole unit and run it like a business, furnished for the tenants most likely to live there. Keeping a room for monthly visits or lending it to family wastes it, and there is no hurry to move back.
points: A spare room costs more than a hotel
The tenant decides the fit-out
Have more than one way to cover the loan
RM12,000 won't furnish a rental
questions: Should I rent out my whole unit or by room?
How much should I spend to furnish my rental unit?
What furniture do tenants look for?
Can I rent out my condo on Airbnb?
How does owning a Malaysian property affect Singapore PR?

articles.title: We own six properties that pay for themselves. Hold or start selling?
articles.excerpt: A couple in their 40s own a home and five rented units, all with positive cash flow. Sean explains how to decide whether to sell, hold or keep buying, starting with what the cash is for.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they sell one property and keep the cash, and if so which one, or hold everything?
articles.answer: Decide what the money is for before selling anything. If they do sell, Sean would start with the small, low-yielding Shah Alam unit; otherwise they can hold, since every unit pays its way, and agree as a couple on how much is enough.
points: Their buffer is already solid
Cash loses value faster than it seems
Leasehold renewal has precedents
The smallest unit uses a full loan slot
questions: How do I decide whether to sell or hold my rental properties?
What should I do with the cash from selling an investment property?
How much cash buffer should I keep for my property portfolio?
Will my leasehold property lose value over time?
Should I sell my lowest-yielding property first?

articles.title: I lost my booking fee on a SOHO. Should I give up on property?
articles.excerpt: A young investor expected an 85% loan on a SOHO unit, got 70% and walked away from the booking. Sean explains the title mix-up and how he buys a third property and beyond.
articles.viewerQuestion: How should he book a subsale unit without risking the booking fee, how does Sean buy a third property and beyond, and is property even worth it when 30% upfront cash makes the returns worse than EPF?
articles.answer: Don't give up over a misunderstanding of the title: anything called SOHO is financed as a home, so a third one gets 70%. Beyond two properties, Sean buys through developer deals that need little cash, finances them on credit and keeps his own capital for stocks and other assets.
points: 'Home' in the name means a home loan
Subsale and auction need the most cash
Use credit for property, cash for the rest
Declared rent works for you
questions: How is a SOHO unit financed in Malaysia?
What is the loan margin for a third residential property?
How much cash is needed upfront for a subsale property?
Why are auctions risky for first-time buyers?
How can I buy a third property with little cash?

articles.title: Should I buy a Cheras condo on a staff loan before starting a family?
articles.excerpt: A 31-year-old who commutes three hours a day has booked a condo near an MRT station on a cheap staff loan. Sean's advice takes a turn: keep the cash and sort out the commute and family plans first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is she doing the right thing for a first home bought to rent out now and live in later, should she look at subsale investments instead, and what else should she consider before starting a family?
articles.answer: Sean would hold off. The RM64,000 is worth more as a buffer while she starts a family, and the real problem, a three-hour daily commute, may be better solved by a job or a rental closer to home. If she does buy, it should be a pure investment that works on rent, which a subsale nearby may do better.
points: Mixed intentions need the 85% rule
The cash may be worth more than the cheap rate
With cash, a subsale may beat a new launch
A buffer buys choices
questions: Should I buy a condo to rent out first and live in later?
Is a staff loan worth using if it requires a large cash downpayment?
How do I compare a new launch condo with a subsale unit?
What should I consider before starting a family and buying a property?
Is a long commute a good reason to buy a property closer to work?

articles.title: My project has stalled. Will it be abandoned?
articles.excerpt: A buyer sees construction slowing and fears the project will be abandoned. Sean, a buyer in the same project, explains the difference between ailing and abandoned, and the real options for getting out or staying in.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is the project in trouble, and what can a buyer actually do if it ends up abandoned?
articles.answer: An ailing project is not an abandoned one. Check its official status, then choose between staying in for delay compensation or walking away at a cost. A full refund is very hard to get.
points: Ailing is not the same as abandoned
The developer is selling assets to fix it
Walking away costs money; a full refund is rare
Staying in can still pay off
questions: How do I check if my property project is officially ailing or abandoned?
What happens to my deposit if I cancel the sale and purchase agreement?
Can I get a full refund if my project is abandoned?
What compensation do I get if my property is delayed?
Should I continue paying my loan if the project is stalled?

articles.title: Strata landed or individual title: which kind of landed home to buy?
articles.excerpt: At a talk in Batu Kawan, Sean explains the difference between gated landed strata homes and traditional individual-title houses, from security and maintenance to who will buy at RM1.8 million.
articles.viewerQuestion: What is the difference between landed strata and individual-title homes, and which holds its value better?
articles.answer: Landed strata costs more up front and comes with rules and maintenance fees, but gives security, planned infrastructure and a say over the neighbourhood. Sean expects most future landed homes to be strata, and individual-title prices to hit a ceiling because buyers at that level expect security.
points: You pay for planning
Rules limit renovation
Individual titles hide their upkeep
Who buys at RM1.8 million?

articles.title: Is a student-rental unit near Sunway a good investment?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old is eyeing a USJ 1 project built for room-by-room student rentals, linked by BRT to the Sunway universities. Sean thinks it can work, but warns that only another investor will ever buy it from you.
articles.viewerQuestion: Are student investment properties around Sunway sound, what are the risks, does furnishing matter, and should he pay a company to manage the rooms?
articles.answer: It can work. Sunway's universities and schools aren't likely to move, which removes the biggest risk, and the agent's figures aren't unrealistic. The real risk is the exit: a unit built only for students can be sold only to investors, and only while its numbers still add up.
points: A campus moving out is the main risk
Only investors will buy it from you
Students wear buildings out
Furnishing is expected, and costs more

articles.title: I'm 20 and earn RM3,500. How should I prepare for property?
articles.excerpt: A 20-year-old accounting student running his own social media agency wants to start investing after graduating. Sean says to hold off and build the business first.
articles.viewerQuestion: What should he do over the next few years to prepare for his first property?
articles.answer: Don't make property the priority yet. While the business is young, flexibility and active income come first; property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich, so scale the agency and diversify once it earns well.
points: The business will out-earn any investment
Property ties up money
RM10,000 is not enough
Expecting fast money is the classic mistake

articles.title: I own two properties at 25. How do I reach RM10 million?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old second-generation business owner holds two KL properties bought below market and wants RM10 million in property within ten years. Sean says to pause and grow elsewhere.
articles.viewerQuestion: How should he grow towards RM10 million in property in ten years: commercial property, a purchase using his wife's foreigner quota, or more residential?
articles.answer: For now, don't grow it. He already has the two or three properties Sean encourages over a lifetime, so the next step is to settle the second unit, put his own money into other, uncorrelated assets, and grow his income and business knowledge, because property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich.
points: A third property is expensive
Commercial property is playing with fire
Diversify into uncorrelated assets
Judge success by cash flow, not asset value

articles.title: I want 10 properties in 10 years on RM5,500 a month. Too aggressive?
articles.excerpt: A 29-year-old with RM50,000 saved wants positive cash flow and ten properties within 15 years. Sean explains cash back against cash flow, how rent drives a high-rise's value, and why to go slowly.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should YK take high cash back with negative cash flow, how is capital growth judged, is buying three units in quick succession overcommitting, and should spare cash go into a flexi loan?
articles.answer: Take positive cash flow over cash back where possible, buy one unit at a time and get each one rented before the next, and build up salary first. Ten properties in ten years on RM5,500 a month is a target nobody else has set.
points: Cash back is borrowed money
Rent sets a high-rise's value
Studios suit only expensive land
Active income drives the portfolio

articles.title: My tenant has stopped paying rent. What can I legally do?
articles.excerpt: A tenant who stops paying but won't leave is every landlord's nightmare. Lawyer Tea explains the legal route Sean's viewers can take: a letter of demand, then a court distress order.
articles.viewerQuestion: When a tenant stops paying rent and won't leave, what is the legal way to get your money and your property back?
articles.answer: Act on the first missed month: send a letter of demand, and if the tenant hasn't paid within 14 days, apply to court for a distress order. The order lets you seize and auction the tenant's belongings and take the unit back, in two to three months at best.
points: Start while the deposit still covers you
A distress order moves quickly
Doing it yourself can backfire
Paperwork decides what you recover
questions: What is the legal process to evict a tenant who hasn't paid rent?
How long does a distress order take to recover possession?
Can I cut off utilities or change locks if my tenant stops paying?
What documents do I need to prove a tenancy in court?
How much does it cost to get a letter of demand and distress order?

articles.title: My tenant wants to pay six months upfront. Will it hurt my next loan?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old in Kota Kinabalu bought a subsale condo below market value and rented it out the day renovation finished. Sean explains what he did right, and why rent paid six months at a time can cost him his next loan.
articles.viewerQuestion: Will rent paid every six months, rather than monthly, affect his income assessment when he applies for a second property?
articles.answer: Yes, it will. Banks look at rental income month by month in your bank statements, so lump sums or uneven amounts may not be counted, and that can cost him the next property. Ask the tenant to pay the same amount every month instead.
points: Banks want steady monthly credits
Keep repairs separate from rent
Subsale lets you negotiate
Stay ready for the deal

articles.title: Should my third property be subsale, auction, new or bulk purchase?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old with two landed homes and RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash weighs subsale, auction, new and bulk purchase for her third. Sean says to keep her cash and let the deal decide.
articles.viewerQuestion: For her third property, should she use cash on a subsale or auction unit with 10% down, or buy new or through bulk purchase, and save her cash?
articles.answer: Keep the cash and use credit. Sean has no favourite channel; he buys wherever the best deal is, but with her aim of letting the property pay for itself, new launches and bulk purchases fit better than subsale or auction, and her savings are worth more as runway for her business.
points: Less cash in means more options later
A bigger discount beats a standard one
Auctions carry hidden problems
Her business may out-earn her job

articles.title: Three transit-linked condos, same cash flow. How do I choose?
articles.excerpt: A 40-year-old civil servant in Johor Bahru has shortlisted three new transit-linked serviced apartments in the Klang Valley for cash flow. Sean explains what to compare after cash flow, and why she must visit in person.
articles.viewerQuestion: If all three give similar cash flow, what should decide it, how much does walkable convenience matter, why are some Mont Kiara subsales so cheap, and how should she judge bulk-purchase units near KLCC with cash back?
articles.answer: After cash flow, compare each project's price with the median of past transactions around it, and the cash each needs up front. Walkable shops and transit genuinely justify higher rent. And living in Johor is no reason to buy new: visit the sites, and consider subsales and bulk-purchase deals too.
points: Below-median prices leave room to grow
Upfront cash differs by deal
Older units are cheap for a reason
Prime location is not enough

articles.title: Is a condo linked to a train station a better buy?
articles.excerpt: Every new project near an MRT or LRT station now calls itself a TOD. Sean explains what transit-oriented development means, who it suits, and the trade-off between convenience and security.
articles.viewerQuestion: What is a transit-oriented development, and is a home in one a better buy?
articles.answer: A TOD is built around public transport, so residents can live, work and shop without relying on a car. That makes it strong for rental to young workers, but the same accessibility brings crowds, noise and weaker security, so it suits investors and singles better than families who want privacy.
points: Young tenants want the link
Easy access cuts both ways
Someone pays for the walkways
Compartmentalisation matters

articles.title: Unsold units near completion: warning sign or better deal?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor sees plenty of units still for sale in a project close to handover. Sean explains why developers end up with unsold stock, and when that works in a buyer's favour.
articles.viewerQuestion: Do the unsold units signal a problem, does the delay matter to a buyer like him, and are dual-key and tri-key units worth it?
articles.answer: Not in this case. Few Malaysians can borrow for a unit above RM1 million, so slow sales near completion are expected, and a developer that keeps building through a delay is a financially strong one. Judge the unit on location, rent and long-term value, and treat any discount as a bonus.
points: Developers clear stock quietly
Price limits who can buy
Delay hurts families more than investors
Dual-key units stretch one loan slot
questions: Do unsold units near completion mean the project is in trouble?
Are dual-key or tri-key units worth buying?
Does a late delivery matter if I buy close to completion?
How do I compare expected rent with my instalment?
Should I buy a completed unsold unit instead of one under construction?

articles.title: How do I know a location suits me before buying a home?
articles.excerpt: Viewers often ask Sean whether a home is worth buying. He can't know their lives, so he offers two tests to run first: affordability, then a weekday and a weekend in the new location.
articles.viewerQuestion: How can you tell whether a home and its location will suit your life before you commit?
articles.answer: Run two tests. First, can you carry the instalment for 30 to 35 years? Only then picture an ordinary weekday and weekend from that address, from the commute to school runs and errands, and see whether it still works.
points: The instalment shapes your whole life
Weekdays are most of your life
Don't buy for a once-a-month view
Bigger isn't always better

articles.title: What should I actually check in my sale and purchase agreement?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers initial every page of their SPA without reading it. Sean goes through his own landed strata agreement and points out the clauses that protect a buyer of a new property.
articles.viewerQuestion: Which parts of a sale and purchase agreement should a buyer actually read and understand?
articles.answer: Read the whole agreement, and know the clauses that give you leverage: the stated price, the payment schedule, the schedule of finishes, the conditions for vacant possession, area adjustments and the defect liability period.
points: Taxes follow the stated price and date
The payment schedule is fixed for homes
Finishes are described, not branded
Keys need a certificate, and facilities too

articles.title: Is it a good time to buy? What ten years of data says
articles.excerpt: Why did some Malaysians lose money on property over the past decade? Sean reads ten years of official data and swaps timing for a test you can actually apply.
articles.viewerQuestion: Why did some buyers lose money over the last decade, and how do you tell whether it is a good time to buy?
articles.answer: Nobody can time the market, so stop trying. If your finances are ready, buy only below the location's past transacted median, with rent that gives a healthy yield. That limits the damage even if you happen to buy at a peak.
points: When you bought decided who lost
Property does not double every ten years
Nobody can call the bottom
The outlook is positive, but supply is rising
questions: Why did some people lose money buying property in Malaysia over the past ten years?
Is now a good time to buy property in Malaysia?
How much do house prices actually rise in Malaysia each year?
What rental yield should I look for before buying a property?
Should I buy below the median transacted price in an area?

articles.title: What happens to my properties when I die?
articles.excerpt: Property owners spend decades building a portfolio but rarely plan how it passes on. Two succession lawyers explain what happens with and without a will, and how to prepare one.
articles.viewerQuestion: What happens to your properties if you die, with or without a will, and how should a property owner prepare?
articles.answer: Without a will, the Distribution Act decides who inherits, and your family must go to court before anyone can act. A will lets you name an executor and decide who gets what, and the lawyers treat it as a plan for your family, not just a list of assets.
points: Without a will, the law picks your heirs
Your family needs a court order first
Loans don't fall due at once
Executors must trace assets and debts first
questions: What happens to my properties if I die without a will?
How do I prepare a will for my property in Malaysia?
Who inherits my house if I pass away without a will?
What does an executor do when distributing properties?
How are outstanding housing loans handled when the owner dies?

articles.title: What mistakes do young buyers make in a slow market?
articles.excerpt: In 2019, with sales slow and developers offering ever more rebates, Sean's inbox filled with young buyers in trouble. He lists four: abandoned projects, signing before the loan, buying with a partner, and overgearing.
articles.viewerQuestion: What are the most common mistakes young buyers make, and how can they be avoided?
articles.answer: Four keep recurring: buying from developers who may abandon the project, signing the SPA before the loan is approved, buying with a boyfriend or girlfriend, and spending the cash back from heavily discounted deals. Be patient, check your loan eligibility first, and buy only what you can afford.
points: Abandoned projects still cost you
Never sign the SPA before the loan
Don't buy with a partner
Cash back tempts overspending

articles.title: We're 26 and earn RM20,000 together. Is an RM800,000 home too much?
articles.excerpt: A debt-free couple of 26 with RM300,000 in savings want a new launch of RM700,000 to RM900,000 to start a family in. Sean says they can afford it, with two conditions, and how to judge a building before it exists.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is that price too high for their income, can he borrow in his name alone, should they buy new now or subsale later, and how can they judge a building's common areas before it is built?
articles.answer: They can afford it, and his RM10,000 income alone roughly qualifies at three times the instalment. Two conditions: don't pay much above the area's median price, and check that rent for similar units nearby covers about 85% of the instalment, so the home can be rented out when the family outgrows it.
points: The 85% rule protects the upgrade
Don't overpay for romance
Banks judge today's income
Learn to read a floor plate

articles.title: Should I buy a Rumawip or other affordable housing unit?
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of affordable homes sit unsold while city prices hit records. Sean explains who these schemes really serve, and how they change the price of the homes around them.

question.context: A May 2026 news report found tens of thousands of completed homes priced below RM300,000 still unsold in Malaysia. Developers must build a share of affordable homes such as Rumawip, often 30% of a project's units at a ceiling price of RM300,000, while prices in prime areas keep rising.
question.text: Is an affordable housing unit a good buy, and how do these schemes affect other buyers?

answer.quote: People want affordable houses in the location that they want.
answer.summary: If you qualify and the location suits you, it can be very good value, because these homes are heavily subsidised. But Sean says the schemes have produced unsold homes while their cost is passed on to the open-market homes around them.

reasons.title: A good location makes it a bargain
reasons.body: Land and other costs are subsidised, so a RM300,000 Rumawip stands out in an area where open-market units cost about RM900 per sq ft. Market rent there usually covers the instalment, and one Rumawip unit in Bangsar South was auctioned at RM370,000.

reasons.title: The income limit is high
reasons.body: A married couple can qualify for Rumawip on a household income of up to RM15,000 a month and a single buyer on RM10,000, well above the median. If you qualify, Sean sees renting the unit out as your right, though he doesn't encourage it.

reasons.title: Open-market buyers pay for it
reasons.body: If each affordable unit costs RM450,000 to build and sells at RM300,000, a developer building 300 of them loses RM45 million and spreads it over the other 700 units. Some buyers now pay more for a project without affordable housing.

reasons.title: Compare it with open-market homes
reasons.body: A developer Sean interviewed points out that many lower-income buyers struggle to get a loan or find 10% down, while an open-market unit at RM350,000 may need no down payment and carries no restriction on renting or selling later.

actions: Check whether you qualify, and what restrictions apply to renting or reselling the unit.
Judge the location first: a subsidised home is good value only where people want to live.
Before buying to rent out, compare the rent nearby with your instalment.
When buying an open-market unit, ask whether the project includes affordable housing.
Compare against open-market units at a similar price, which may come with discounts and fewer restrictions.
articles.caveat: This is Sean's view of the market in May 2026, not advice on a particular scheme, and criteria differ between federal and state schemes. For the hardcore poor, he argues, government rental housing near the city would help more than ownership.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2026 episode, which includes clips from his earlier interviews with developers. The quoted line is Sean's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Income limits and price ceilings are as stated in May 2026 and differ between schemes.

video.title: DILEMMA OF MALAYSIA PROPERTY MARKET | OVERSUPPLY OF AFFORDABLE HOUSING

articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.

question.asker: From Lau, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Lau believes that because land is limited, a landed home in KL is almost guaranteed to appreciate over 20 to 30 years. Condos, on the other hand, age: however well managed, the building and facilities start to look old.
question.text: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?

answer.quote: The moral of the story is it's very easy to look back.
answer.summary: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.

reasons.title: Landed wins on growth, condos win on rent
reasons.body: Official statistics rank landed terrace houses first for capital appreciation, with apartments close behind; corner lots do best of all. But a two- to three-bedroom condo in PJ rents for about RM2,500 to RM2,800, a rate tenants will not pay for a terrace, because condos offer security, facilities and less space to clean and maintain.

reasons.title: Yesterday's safe bet was once the fringe
reasons.body: Subang Jaya, PJ and Damansara Utama were on the edge of development 20 to 30 years ago, and people who bought early apartments in Mont Kiara, Hartamas or Puchong made money too. Townships launch terraces first because they sell easily; condos come later, once land is scarce.

reasons.title: Open landed homes hit a price ceiling
reasons.body: Individual-title terraces sit on public roads that often become shortcuts, and guarding them depends on a residents' association. A household paying RM1.2 to 1.5 million earns around RM18,000 to RM20,000 a month and expects security. Sean believes unguarded landed homes will hit a price cap, and notes many older owners downsize into 1,500 to 1,800 sq ft condos.

reasons.title: Big landed homes are hard to sell
reasons.body: Luxury homes bought for RM800,000 years ago are now listed at RM3 to 4 million and struggling to sell. On a RM3 million home, a buyer needs about RM300,000 down plus RM300,000 to RM400,000 for renovation before moving in, which only the top 5% or so of Malaysians can afford.

actions: Decide first whether you want capital growth or rental income; they point to different property types.
If you buy landed, favour guarded or strata projects and avoid lots facing a main road or a likely shortcut.
Look at today's early-stage townships, rather than chasing locations that have already made their money.
Before buying a large landed home, ask who could afford to buy it from you in 20 years.
Consider renting the dream home and putting your capital into rental apartments instead, as Sean suggests.
articles.caveat: With unlimited capital, Sean says he would happily buy landed and commercial property in prime city areas; these trade-offs bite hardest for buyers stretching to afford. He also warns against copying US house-flipping advice, since Malaysian financing works very differently.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #241. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rents and prices are as Sean stated them in February 2024.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #241 | APARTMENT VS LANDED

articles.title: Should I buy from a big branded developer or a smaller newcomer?
articles.excerpt: Big listed developers sell a lifestyle; smaller ones compete on facilities, price and discounts. Sean compares two brochures and lists the questions to ask at any sales gallery.

question.context: Viewers shopping for new launches ask whether to stick with big, publicly listed developers or consider smaller and newer ones. Sean compares brochures from one of each: a two-room unit from a big name in Petaling Jaya and a three-room unit from a smaller developer in Kuala Lumpur, both at about RM750,000.
question.text: Does the developer's brand matter, and how should a buyer compare projects from big and small developers?

answer.quote: investors only look at numbers
answer.summary: For an investment, the brand matters less than the numbers: tenure, price per sq ft against the neighbours, the net price after rebates, and the rent it can earn. Big developers sell a lifestyle and command a premium; smaller ones often offer more space and discounts for the money. For your own home, buy what feels right within your budget.

reasons.title: Big names sell a lifestyle
reasons.body: Branded developers market the surroundings, lakes and landscaping, and their brand reassures buyers. Smaller developers tend to compete on facilities, price and discounts.

reasons.title: Brochures leave things out
reasons.body: Developers don't advertise what works against them, such as leasehold tenure or how many car parks come with a unit. Ask directly.

reasons.title: Built-up may include extras
reasons.body: Some developers count air-conditioner ledges or balconies in the built-up area, which lowers the apparent price per sq ft. It is marketing, not cheating, but compare like with like.

reasons.title: Construction time changes the deal
reasons.body: Whether a project takes three, four or five years matters: you are paying today for a unit completed years later, and rebates often vary with the construction stage.

actions: Ask whether the land is freehold or leasehold, and how many car parks are included.
Check the price per sq ft of neighbouring projects on property portals.
Ask what the built-up area includes, and the construction period.
Work out the net price after every discount and rebate.
Visit the site to see what is next door, such as a school, market or busy junction.
articles.caveat: This 2017 comparison predates the wave of stalled projects during COVID, after which Sean has stressed a developer's financial strength more.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this September 2017 video, which he says is not sponsored. The projects compared are not named here. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: My building now allows only one Airbnb operator. What can I do?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer got the keys to a city-centre unit meant for Airbnb, then the building demanded a RM100,000 deposit from operators and let only one operate. Sean explains why, and how to get the unit earning.

question.asker: From Mr Kong, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Kong bought his first property, a new unit in central Kuala Lumpur, to run as a short-term rental and lined up an Airbnb operator. Soon after he got the keys, building management required a RM100,000 deposit from short-stay operators and restricted their access. His operator pulled out, and he hears only one operator is now allowed in the building.
question.text: Is it fair for management to allow only one operator, and what should he do now?

answer.quote: focus on the problem just move on as quickly as possible
answer.summary: A large deposit for operators is reasonable and keeps a building manageable, and he cannot challenge the arrangement until a joint management body is formed. Meanwhile his unit earns nothing, so sign with the approved operator or furnish it and rent it out long-term.

reasons.title: Short-stay should be plan D
reasons.body: Sean rates a project by whether long-term, medium-term or room rental can cover the instalment, with Airbnb only as a last option. A unit that relies on Airbnb alone has nothing to fall back on.

reasons.title: Short-stay can be banned
reasons.body: Penang has limited it to commercial-title projects, Singapore bans it nationwide, and a building's owners can vote it out. Any of these can end the strategy overnight.

reasons.title: Why a big deposit helps
reasons.body: With seven or eight operators, residents and managers cannot tell whose guests caused damage. A RM100,000 deposit filters for operators with the money to pay for repairs, and fewer of them is easier to manage.

reasons.title: Airbnb buildings need a quick exit
reasons.body: Heavily used buildings can deteriorate like student housing, families won't buy into them, and about 10,000 similar units are coming around Bukit Bintang and KLCC. The time to sell is while rates are high, which is when owners least want to.

actions: Talk to the approved operator, even if its terms are less generous.
If you have no budget to furnish, buy simple furniture online and rent the unit long-term for now.
Use zero-interest instalment plans to furnish if your credit is good.
Raise the operator question at the AGM once the joint management body is formed.
Keep short-stay units for later in your portfolio, after projects whose long-term rent covers the loan.
articles.caveat: If another operator paid the same deposit and was still refused, that would be worth questioning. Sean had heard of the building but had not seen evidence of falling rents there.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #271. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in January 2025. The episode is sponsored by Versa, a savings app, and Sean mentions the instalment plans of The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he works with.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #271 | DILEMMA FOR AIRBNB FOCUSED PROJECTS

articles.title: Could a bulk purchase get me my second property sooner?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old spent his savings on a compact terrace house in Subang Jaya and wants an investment unit next. Sean explains why developers have unsold units, and why entry price decides who wins on rent.

question.asker: From Mr N, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr N is 27, earns RM6,500 a month and expects about 20% a year in raises. Last year he bought a compact terrace house in SS19, Subang Jaya, for RM415,000, below the area's median of about RM450,000, spending RM50,000 on the down payment and fees and RM60,000 on renovation, including his EPF Account 2. He has about RM10,000 in cash and RM20,000 in shares left.
question.text: Will a non-gated terrace house keep rising in value, how can he buy a second property with little cash, and if a bulk-purchase group buys many units in one project, won't they all compete for the same tenants?

answer.quote: Entry price determines the success of your investment for property.
answer.summary: The house is a good buy, though open, non-gated terraces will rise more slowly as security matters more to buyers. With his cash used up, his next unit has to be bought on credit: a discounted unit whose rent covers the instalment, completing in a few years while he saves for the furnishing.

reasons.title: Open terraces have a price ceiling
reasons.body: Easy access makes non-gated houses targets when crime rises, and their roads are public, so residents cannot seal them off. As prices approach RM1 million, which needs about RM15,000 a month in income, buyers expect security and facilities, so growth slows.

reasons.title: Unsold units come from ambitious pricing
reasons.body: Developers raise prices as a project sells, and the last 10% can stay unsold. They cannot cut prices openly without upsetting earlier buyers, so they sell the rest at a discount through investment clubs instead.

reasons.title: A lower entry price wins the rental race
reasons.body: In a project of hundreds of identical units, the owner who paid less has a smaller instalment and cash back to furnish properly, so a fully furnished unit beats a bare one at the same rent.

reasons.title: Cash back belongs to the property
reasons.body: Sean warns that cash back is not spending money for a car or a holiday. It should go into furnishing the unit or reducing the loan, or the rent will not perform.

actions: Add CCTV, alarms and better locks to a non-gated home.
Agree with your spouse on how many properties you want and when, before buying more.
Look for a discounted unit whose rent covers the instalment, due to complete in four to five years.
Save for furnishing while it is being built; a three-bedroom fit-out can cost RM50,000 to RM60,000.
Look for completed projects launched before COVID, which often have better materials than new launches.
articles.caveat: If he only wants two or three properties in his lifetime, Sean says taking it slowly and building cash first is fine. Not every developer works with bulk-purchase clubs, so the choice of units is limited.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #286. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2025. Sean is a member of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club discussed in this episode, not its owner; his recent purchases came through it, and the episode links to it.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #286 | WHY SO MANY UNSOLD UNIT?

articles.title: Should I buy now the condo I'll downsize to in 20 years?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old father of three wants a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out now and retire into later, but it needs RM150,000 down. Sean says no: sell the old apartment, regain two 90% loans and buy for cash flow.

question.asker: From RC, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: RC is 36 with three children. He and his wife earn about RM20,000 a month together, and his side business brings in about RM25,000 more. They own a Shah Alam apartment bought for RM345,000 in 2014, rented at about RM1,600, and a RM1.3 million semi-D bought in 2023, both in joint names, so any further loan is capped at 70%. He is thinking of a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out until they downsize in 20 to 25 years, which would need about RM150,000 down and RM2,200 a month.
question.text: Does it make sense to buy now, rent it out even at a small loss, and move in at retirement? Or should he sell the Shah Alam apartment?

answer.quote: Invest in properties using credit. Invest in everything else using cash.
answer.summary: Don't buy it. Nobody knows what he will need, earn or be able to do at 56, and putting RM150,000 into a 70% loan for an own-stay project is the wrong tool. Sell the apartment, which frees a 90% loan for each of them, and buy for cash flow instead.

reasons.title: Twenty years is too far to plan a home
reasons.body: By 56 his income, health and family will all be different; if his side business grows, he may prefer somewhere quite different. A building also needs good management to stay in shape for decades, and the Urban Renewal Act uses 30 years as a checkpoint. Sean expects oversupply in parts of Bukit Jalil.

reasons.title: Joint names used up both 90% loans
reasons.body: Each Malaysian gets two 90% loans for residential property. A couple who buys every home jointly uses both people's slots each time, so their third purchase is capped at 70%. Selling the joint apartment frees a 90% slot for each of them.

reasons.title: At 70%, many units beat this one
reasons.body: With 30% down, which is the international norm, almost any KL project rents for more than its instalment. Putting RM150,000 down on an own-stay project only to break even is a poor use of that cash.

reasons.title: The apartment is ready to sell
reasons.body: Held for about ten years, it falls outside RPGT, which is counted from the SPA date. Sold at RM330,000 to RM350,000, it would roughly clear the loan, and a cut in interest rates would make it easier to sell as more buyers qualify.

actions: Prepare to sell the Shah Alam apartment, and ask agents to test the market now.
Keep the RM150,000 invested, or park it in the semi-D loan account to reduce interest if your bank allows it.
With your two freed 90% loans, buy units where the rent covers the instalment, comparing new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase.
If you want sole names later, ask the bank whether one spouse can refinance the other's share; that spouse's income must qualify for the whole loan.
Shop for a retirement home when you are near retirement; any time can be a good time to buy at the right price.
articles.caveat: If his wife has her own income, Sean encourages putting a property in her name alone. A joint name makes sense mainly for a spouse without income, who otherwise has no claim to the home.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #295. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and RPGT rules are as stated in September 2025. Sean owns a unit in Bukit Jalil himself and is a customer of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #295 | BUYING A HOUSE TO RETIRE IN 20 YEARS TIME?

articles.title: Is buying an auction property worth the risk?
articles.excerpt: Auction prices can be the market's most genuine, but your deposit is lost if financing fails. Sean explains how auctions work and what to check before you bid.

question.context: When an owner misses three consecutive monthly instalments, the bank can send the property to auction, a process that takes six to eight months. Auctions now run online, and many of the units on offer are newer ones from investors who bought more than they could carry.
question.text: How does buying at auction work, and should a first-time buyer try it?

answer.quote: This auction process requires a lot of capital.
answer.summary: It can be a genuine bargain, but only for buyers with capital and knowledge. You pay 10% to bid and must settle the rest within 90 to 120 days, on a loan based on your winning price, so first-time buyers without savings are better off with new properties.

reasons.title: The loan follows the price you pay
reasons.body: To bid on a unit with a RM360,000 reserve price you put up 10%, RM36,000. Win at RM380,000 and you can borrow 90% of that, RM342,000, not 90% of a RM500,000 market value. If the bank lends only 70%, you must find the difference.

reasons.title: Some deals can't be financed
reasons.body: A title under a private caveat can only be bought with cash, and some auctioned houses stand on land owned by someone else. Sean has seen bidders lose their 10% because no bank would lend.

reasons.title: You buy it as it is
reasons.body: Units are sold as is, often unseen inside. Unpaid maintenance fees can be large, up to RM160,000 on one unit left empty for years, so check whether the bank's terms say it will settle them. An occupant, especially an owner who has lost the home, can mean trouble.

reasons.title: Prices fall each round without bids
reasons.body: When nobody bids, the bank lowers the reserve, for example from RM500,000 to RM450,000, RM410,000 and then RM360,000. Genuine bidders can still push a unit back towards market value, so knowing which round to go in is a skill.

actions: Have 10% of the reserve price ready to bid, plus cash to cover any shortfall in financing.
Check how much a bank will lend on that particular unit before you bid.
Read the sale terms for caveats, who owns the land and who pays outstanding maintenance fees.
Use an agent experienced in auctions to arrange a viewing and find out who occupies the unit.
Set a maximum bid and stick to it; an agent can bid for you within your limit.
articles.caveat: If you have little more than an emergency fund, Sean says new properties are the better route. For buyers in their 30s to 50s with capital, auctions are worth comparing with subsale: they are no longer the shady, unregulated halls older buyers warn about, and many units are fairly new.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this March 2021 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean checked his notes with Jeff, an agent who specialises in auction properties and whom the video recommends. The process is as described in 2021.

video.title: AUCTION PROPERTY

articles.title: I own two properties. How would you buy four more?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old with RM700,000 in shares and funds and two properties wants four more. Sean lists the ways investors get around the 70% loan limit, and asks why four.

question.asker: From Vu, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Vu is 36, married and earns about RM12,000 a month. He has about RM700,000 in shares, ETFs and funds and about RM400,000 in EPF. He owns two properties: one rented out since handover three years ago, with rent covering about 90% of its instalment, and one under construction.
question.text: If he wanted to buy four more investment properties, how would Sean go about it?

answer.quote: The goal is never to buy cheap properties
answer.summary: Buy only units bought with little cash whose rent covers the instalment, and get around the 70% loan limit on a third residential loan in one of several ways. But replace 'four more' with a target value or rental income, keep building the share portfolio that is already working, and buy one when a good deal appears.

reasons.title: Leverage is the point of property
reasons.body: Banks fund 90% or more, a tenant pays the loan, and your own capital can be invested elsewhere or parked in the loan account to cut interest while staying withdrawable. Sean would not buy property outright in cash.

reasons.title: The third loan is capped at 70%
reasons.body: Each Malaysian gets two residential loans at up to 90%; from the third, it is 70% however high the income. On a RM500,000 unit that means RM150,000 in cash.

reasons.title: There are ways around the cap
reasons.body: Commercial-title suites can be financed at up to 85%; bulk-purchase discounts of 20% to 30% cover the gap; equity in older units can be refinanced after 10 to 15 years, though cash-out is now restricted; and refinancing existing loans with an insurer-linked lender can, Sean says, free the 90% slots again at a higher rate. Or pay the difference in cash.

reasons.title: Unit counts lead to bad buys
reasons.body: An arbitrary target, such as six properties by 40, pushes people to buy whatever is available. A target like RM20 million in value, or a monthly rental income, rewards buying fewer, better units.

actions: Set a target value or monthly rental income with your spouse instead of a number of units.
Only buy units needing little upfront cash, with about 6% yield or rent above the instalment.
Compare commercial-title financing, bulk purchase and refinancing before paying 30% down.
Keep growing the share portfolio that built your wealth.
Don't announce how many properties you own.
articles.caveat: Sean says he avoids low-cost and welfare housing as investments, though they would make four units cheap. The refinancing rules he describes are as of late 2024 and were tightening.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #269. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2024. Sean is a long-term customer of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner, and refers viewers to a contact for insurer-linked home loans; the episode is sponsored by Versa, a savings app. A subsale method he describes, financing at a bank valuation above the agreed price, is left out here.

articles.title: What should I check before buying in a mixed development or township?
articles.excerpt: Living above the office and the mall sounds convenient, but whether it works depends on who controls the shops. Sean explains, from his time on a township team, what makes a mixed development and township succeed.

question.context: Mixed developments put homes, offices and a mall on one site, and large townships add schools, landed homes and transport over many years. Sean filmed this in a Johor township where he had worked on the development team, as residents were collecting their keys.
question.text: What decides whether a mixed development or township is a good place to buy?

answer.quote: please ask who owns the retail units
answer.summary: Ask who owns the shops. A mall owned and managed by one party can control its tenant mix and marketing; one sold off unit by unit to hundreds of owners often can't, and declines. In townships, back a developer with a long-term master plan, and judge value rather than brand.

reasons.title: The retail mix makes or breaks it
reasons.body: Anchor tenants such as supermarkets and hardware chains draw their own crowds, and a good mix of grocers, bookshops and services is what makes living above a mall convenient.

reasons.title: Strata malls are hard to manage
reasons.body: When retail units are sold to individual owners, management has no say over who rents them, and rebranding or marketing needs hundreds of owners to agree. Several older strata malls struggled for this reason.

reasons.title: Townships grow in stages
reasons.body: A good master plan first builds a self-sustaining mixed core, then adds schools, transport links and landed phases to draw people in over ten years or more.

reasons.title: Brands cost more for a reason
reasons.body: Established township developers price higher because they look after the area for years. For a young investor unsure where to start, choosing a major brand is a safe default, but pay for value, not the name.

actions: Ask whether the retail component is owned by one party or sold as strata units.
Look at the anchor tenants and the mix of shops, not just the building.
Read the township's master plan and what the developer has already delivered.
Check transport links to the places residents work.
Compare prices with neighbouring projects to judge the brand premium.
articles.caveat: Sean's view of this township draws on his time working for its developer; other townships and developers may follow different models.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this February 2018 video. Sean previously worked on the development team for the township he films here, which is not named in this summary. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Should I buy a property with my boyfriend or girlfriend?
articles.excerpt: Couples who buy in joint names find a break-up leaves both of them on the loan. Sean explains why he discourages it, and the arrangement he prefers.

question.context: Sean has seen friends' break-ups turn a property they bought together into a long, sticky problem. Couples usually join names because neither can afford the home alone, and bankers often suggest adding a second name to get a loan approved.
question.text: Should an unmarried couple buy a property together in joint names?

answer.quote: I will not encourage couples to actually buy property by joining names.
answer.summary: No. Joint names use up both partners' 90% loans on one property, and nobody plans for a break-up. If you must, set the terms out in writing; better still, buy in one name with the other as guarantor.

reasons.title: It wastes your 90% loans
reasons.body: Each person can usually get up to 90% financing on their first two residential loans; from the third it is normally 70%. Buying jointly uses both partners' quota on one property, while buying separately lets a couple hold up to four at 90%.

reasons.title: Break-ups don't service loans
reasons.body: If a couple stops talking, the instalments can stop too. The bank sends warning letters to both of you, and both get arrears recorded in CCRIS.

reasons.title: Joining names often means overreaching
reasons.body: If one income qualifies for a RM300,000 home but together you buy a RM700,000 landed house, you take on about RM3,500 a month for 30 years. Lose one income and the home is at risk.

reasons.title: One name, one guarantor
reasons.body: Sean prefers the property in one partner's name, with the other acting as guarantor on the loan if the income falls short. The other partner keeps their own quota for later purchases.

actions: Don't buy a property as proof of your relationship.
If one income can't support the home, look at a cheaper one before adding a second name.
If you do buy jointly, agree in writing, ideally with a lawyer, what happens if either of you loses a job, stops paying or wants to sell.
Consider buying in one name with your partner as guarantor.
articles.caveat: Sean has no objection to joint names between family members who trust each other, though never with a stranger, and a couple with clear written terms can make it work.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this November 2018 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included. Loan margins are as described in 2018, so check current rules with a bank.

articles.title: I cancelled my booking. Was it FOMO, or the right call?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old booked a RM640,000 unit on a promised 15% return, then cancelled. Sean explains why that was right, and how to tell what you can actually afford.

question.asker: From Xiao Bai, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Xiao Bai is 25, takes home about RM4,600 a month after EPF, has a car loan, and saves RM1,000 to RM1,500 a month with about RM20,000 put aside. He booked a RM640,000 leasehold unit in Bandar Sunway with more than RM30,000 cash back and a 10% rebate. The instalment would be about RM2,700 plus RM370 maintenance, and the agent promised a 15% return. After a month of doubt, he cancelled.
question.text: Was walking away right, or too conservative? And how does he stop worrying that prices will run away before he is ready?

answer.quote: It's a good move that you cancel.
answer.summary: Cancelling was right. The numbers only worked if nothing went wrong, and on his income a property of around RM300,000 to RM400,000 is the safer place to start.

reasons.title: A 15% return is a red flag
reasons.body: A good rental yield in Malaysia is about 5 to 6%. Anything far higher usually comes from student or Airbnb-style room-by-room rental, so ask whether the figure is gross or net. If a developer could really deliver 15%, it would charge more for the unit.

reasons.title: Student-style buildings are hard to exit
reasons.body: Buildings full of students wear out fast, so the sinking fund rises. Only other investors will buy such units, since families do not want to live there, and when a campus moves away, rents fall.

reasons.title: He could not survive a bad year
reasons.body: After the car loan, roughly RM3,500 of his income counts toward borrowing, enough for about RM400,000 to RM500,000. A RM2,700 instalment with little savings leaves nothing to carry the unit through six empty months.

reasons.title: Time yourself, not the market
reasons.body: Sean says any time is a good time to buy if you are ready. The cure for fear of missing out is knowledge: agents earn when you sign, not when you are still paying through a vacancy.

actions: Do your research before paying a booking fee, not after.
Visit about 20 properties in your budget; the sales pitches start to sound alike, which makes you immune to them.
Before buying, have six months of emergency funds, insurance, and a clear career path.
Work out the real price after cash back and rebates; after handover, banks value the unit on that lower figure, so selling early loses money.
Compare price per sq ft across areas. Bandar Sunway near RM1,000 can cost more than Mont Kiara or Bangsar South.
articles.caveat: Buying would not necessarily have been wrong for someone confident of a fast-rising income, such as in sales. Sean went all in on his first property at a similar income and nearly crashed, and says he would tell his younger self to slow down.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #321. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices are as stated in September 2026.

articles.title: I own four cars and want a fifth. Should I buy property instead?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old in Kuching with RM500,000 in fixed deposits, four cars and a baby on the way asks about landed homes, his rented-out house and his uncle's. Sean says fix the spending first.

question.asker: From TK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: TK is 28, a project manager in Kuching earning RM8,000 a month and spending about RM6,800, much of it on four cars; he is eyeing a fifth for when his baby arrives. He has RM500,000 in fixed deposits and RM100,000 in EPF, and owns a double-storey house bought for RM418,000 with RM80,000 down, rented at RM900 against a RM1,450 instalment, though it could fetch RM1,200. He lives in his uncle's corner house and is weighing that house, a new RM700,000 to RM800,000 double-storey or a RM500,000 to RM600,000 apartment.
question.text: Should he keep his rented house, buy his uncle's, and choose landed or an apartment for his family home, and how much should he put down?

answer.quote: Why do you need four cars in the first place?
answer.summary: Keep the house he owns and, for a family with this many cars, a landed home makes sense. But on RM8,000 with RM6,800 spent each month, the real problem is spending: until he controls it and stops buying cars, the property questions don't matter.

reasons.title: His rented house is earning its keep
reasons.body: New double-storeys nearby sell for about RM620,000, so his RM418,000 house has likely gained. Early in a loan most of each instalment is interest; at RM1,200 rent, about 85% of the RM1,450 instalment, the tenant is effectively paying the bank's interest for him.

reasons.title: His uncle's house depends on the price
reasons.body: Bought for RM280,000 in 2015 with neighbours now at RM400,000, it has risen about 43% in ten years, and corner lots usually fetch 25% to 35% more. Compare his uncle's price plus renovation with RM800,000 for a new house in an area whose water and power supply he doesn't yet know.

reasons.title: Cars lose value; homes gain it
reasons.body: In ten years his cars will be worth half or less, while both houses he knows have risen. In Kuching renting is cheaper than owning, but the saving only helps if it is invested rather than spent on another car.

reasons.title: Count cash flow, not units
reasons.body: A better goal than owning many properties is positive monthly cash flow, such as RM10,000 a month across the portfolio. In Kuching, Sean would buy an apartment only if long-term rent, not Airbnb income, covers the instalment.

actions: Bring monthly spending down, ideally to about half your income, before buying more property, and don't buy the fifth car.
Raise the rent on your existing house to the market rate of about RM1,200 when the tenancy is renewed.
Ask your uncle his price, then compare it plus renovation with buying new.
Take a 90% full flexi loan and park spare cash in it to cut interest, after checking when your bank lets you withdraw it.
Move some of the RM500,000 fixed deposit into options that earn more, such as EPF, which pays about 6%.
articles.caveat: If the uncle would sell near his 2015 price, it is an easy yes. And Sean would buy an own-stay apartment only if nearby rents cover about 85% of its instalment, his rule for judging an own-stay purchase.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #293. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in August 2025.

articles.title: Cash back on a new launch, or a lower loan with positive cash flow?
articles.excerpt: Developers now offer free legal fees, furniture and even cash back, but the extras inflate the loan. Sean explains how rebates work and when cash in hand beats a unit whose rent covers its instalment.

question.context: A conventional purchase needs about 18% of the price in cash, around RM90,000 for a RM500,000 unit. Developers have responded with rebates that grow ever more generous: waived legal fees and stamp duty, free kitchen cabinets or full furnishing, and cash back, where the bank values a unit above the price you actually pay.
question.text: Is it better to take a new launch with big rebates and cash back, or pay a down payment to borrow less and have rent cover the instalment?

answer.quote: your rental is in accordance to market value
answer.summary: Rebates are built into a higher price and loan, so a new launch rarely has positive cash flow: rent follows the market, not your instalment. If you have cash, paying down to borrow less is safer. Cash back only helps if you use it to cover the monthly gap, not to spend.

reasons.title: Free extras raise the loan
reasons.body: A unit worth RM500,000 can carry an SPA price of RM600,000 to RM650,000 once rebates are included. Borrowing RM650,000 instead of RM450,000 makes a big difference to the instalment.

reasons.title: Rent doesn't care what you paid
reasons.body: Owners often set the asking rent from their instalment, but tenants pay what similar units fetch. A unit financed at an inflated price will struggle to break even.

reasons.title: Cash back can bridge the gap
reasons.body: If the instalment is RM3,000 and rent RM1,800, cash back can cover the RM1,200 difference for a few years while rents rise, leaving your own savings free to invest elsewhere.

reasons.title: Sudden cash changes habits
reasons.body: Buyers who receive RM30,000 to RM50,000 in cash back often feel richer and spend it. Without discipline, the buffer is gone before the shortfall begins.

actions: Compare the SPA price with the unit's likely market value after handover.
Check market rents for similar units, not your instalment, to estimate income.
If taking cash back, work out how many months of shortfall it will cover.
Keep cash back in a separate account reserved for the property.
Resist 'book today' offers until you have done the numbers.
articles.caveat: Sean put this to his audience as an open question in April 2020, when cash in hand mattered more. The best case is a unit with both cash back and positive cash flow.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this April 2020 'question of the week' video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Should I buy three condos mostly in cash and stop working at 35?
articles.excerpt: A Malaysian working in Singapore plans to come home, put RM200,000 down on each of three RM300,000 condos and live off the rent. Sean shows why fixed deposits beat that plan, and what to do instead.

question.asker: From Mr Lee, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Lee is 35 and has worked in Singapore for about eight years. Gains from shares during COVID went mostly into a Singapore condo whose rent covers all its costs with a little to spare. He also has several hundred thousand ringgit in cash and savings earning interest, and wants to move back to Malaysia and stop working.
question.text: Is it a good plan to buy three RM300,000 condos in Kuala Lumpur with RM200,000 down on each, borrowing only RM100,000 apiece, and live on the roughly RM500 a month each would leave?

answer.quote: Use credit to buy properties, not use capital.
answer.summary: No. Putting RM600,000 in cash into three condos for about RM1,500 a month is a poor return; the same cash in fixed deposits at about 3% earns that without tenants. Buy with loans while he still has a salary to qualify, keep his capital invested, and don't stop working altogether.

reasons.title: The cash would take decades to pay back
reasons.body: RM600,000 for RM1,500 a month takes 400 months to recover. At about 3% a year, the same RM600,000 in fixed deposits pays about RM1,500 a month with no vacancies or bad tenants.

reasons.title: RM300,000 condos are the wrong stock
reasons.body: At that price in Kuala Lumpur, Sean says, you are mostly looking at welfare-type apartments, which he would leave alone.

reasons.title: Loans need an income
reasons.body: Malaysia lets buyers borrow up to 90% and still find units whose rent covers the instalment. That needs a salary or declared income to qualify, so buy before quitting rather than after.

reasons.title: Interest is a cost against rent
reasons.body: Loan interest can be written off against declared rental income, which is one more reason not to pay down so much up front.

actions: Keep the cash in fixed deposits or the investments you already know well.
Buy one ready-built unit of around RM600,000 whose rent covers the instalment, and try it before buying more.
Sign for any properties while still employed, then leave the job once the loans are approved.
Take three to six months off before deciding what to do next, rather than retiring outright.
Find work you would do even unpaid; Sean argues life is only stressful when you do what you dislike.
articles.caveat: If he has no wish to borrow at all, Sean would still put the cash into safer non-property investments first, because they keep the flexibility a family emergency may need.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #280. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2025. Sean recommends buying through FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club he is a member of, not its owner, and the episode links to it. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

articles.title: Is a cheap unit with good rent worth buying?
articles.excerpt: A buyer is offered two old units in central KL at RM160,000 each, renting to foreign workers at a 6.33% yield. Sean explains why cheap is not the same as money-making.

question.asker: From Mrs. Y, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mrs. Y has bought a 1,750 sq ft own-stay unit from a large listed developer in KL East, still under construction. She is now offered two 425 sq ft units at RM160,000 each in an old building in Chow Kit, completed in 2000 and refurbished in 2020. They rent for RM1,000 a month, mostly to foreign workers, with a RM130 management fee, and she works out a 6.33% return before maintenance.
question.text: With steady rent but little prospect of the price rising, is it still a good investment?

answer.quote: Don't buy a property just because it's cheap.
answer.summary: No. The cash flow works, but with almost no capital appreciation, a loan slot used up and only about RM200 a month to show for it, Sean says better deals are available and this one is not worth the headspace.

reasons.title: The yield clears the bar, just
reasons.body: Sean's break-even is about 5.4%: a RM100,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM450 a month. At 6.33% the unit is roughly a point above that, and on a 90% loan of about RM145,000 the surplus comes to around RM200 a month.

reasons.title: There is almost nothing to sell later
reasons.body: Units like these compete on being the cheapest, for tenants who need them rather than want them, so the only buyers are other cash-flow investors and there is little resale activity. Even selling at 10% more in ten years, about RM176,000, the surplus of roughly RM2,400 a year barely returns the down payment. In the worst case it cannot be sold, and repairs after bad tenants eat the surplus.

reasons.title: It spends a 90% loan slot
reasons.body: Malaysians get two 90% loans for residential property. With her own-stay unit, this would use the second, so any better deal later could only be financed at 70%. Paying cash would be worse still: EPF pays about 6% with less risk.

reasons.title: Better deals are out there
reasons.body: She has not compared it against 20 other properties. Sean finds deals from branded developers with higher returns and no upfront deposit, so an old, cheap unit like this would need a double-digit return, 10% to 15%, before he considered it.

actions: Visit at least 20 other properties in your price range, across new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase, before deciding.
Ask a bank for its valuation first, to see whether it would value the unit at the asking price.
Don't pay cash for a property like this; compare its return against EPF at about 6%.
Keep your remaining 90% loan slot for a deal with both cash flow and room to grow.
For an old, low-priced building, look for a double-digit return of 10% to 15% before considering it.
articles.caveat: Sean's no rests on having better deals within reach. Cheap units in old buildings can make sense at a double-digit yield, though he discourages investors from low-cost housing meant for those who need it most. Separately, he says buying her own-stay unit from a large developer gives her more certainty of completion while building costs rise.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #311. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in May 2026. Sean buys through FAR Capital's bulk purchases as a client, not its owner.
