articles.title: When should you stop renting and buy a home?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old renter is tired of moving and wants a home of his own, but friends warn him off. Sean tests the decision with his 85% rule.

question.asker: From CY, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: CY is 34, single, earns about RM17,000 a month and lives frugally. He has RM180,000 in shares and cash and RM235,000 in EPF, and supports his mother. He rents a condo in Taman Desa for RM3,000 a month, and has had to move three times in six years when landlords took their units back. He is eyeing a RM850,000 project nearby with an instalment of about RM3,800, but friends say not to buy until he marries.
question.text: Should he buy a home in the area he already lives in, or keep renting and invest the money instead?

answer.quote: Go ahead bro, I really support that decision.
answer.summary: Buy it. He can afford it, he knows the area, and the unit would rent for most of its instalment if his plans ever change. That is what makes an own-stay purchase safe.

reasons.title: It passes the 85% rule
reasons.body: Sean's test for an own-stay home: local rent should cover about 85% of the instalment. In the early years most of each instalment is interest, so a tenant would cover that cost if you had to move out. Here, similar units rent for about RM3,000 against an instalment of about RM3,800, which Sean counts as meeting the rule.

reasons.title: He is buying where he already lives
reasons.body: The classic mistake is an emotional dream home far from work, such as a landed house in an outer suburb. The owner then faces hours of daily traffic or rents a second place in town. A home renovated for yourself is hard to let out, and a distant one is hard to sell. Taman Desa is central and CY has lived around it for six years.

reasons.title: His foundations are in place
reasons.body: Before buying a home, Sean wants three things settled: solid savings, a stable career and insurance protection. CY has all three, so the question becomes whether he wants to spend on housing, not whether he can afford to.

reasons.title: A home pays you in certainty
reasons.body: Some property is bought to make money; a home is bought to spend it. The instalment buys the security renting cannot: no landlord calling to reclaim the unit in your busiest month. Sean compares it to choosing a better car than the bare minimum, which is fine if you can afford it.

actions: Check what the unit would rent for, and aim for rent covering about 85% of your instalment.
Buy in an area you already know and that suits your daily commute, not a faraway dream location.
Confirm your savings, career and insurance are solid before committing.
Plan the exit now: if a better job comes up elsewhere, you can rent the unit out at market rate.
Treat renovation as spending on yourself. It makes the home yours but adds little to the resale price.
articles.caveat: If you want to build a property portfolio, Sean's own order is the reverse: buy investment units whose rent covers the instalment first, so your borrowing capacity stays intact, and buy your home later. His "just buy it" is for someone like CY, who invests elsewhere and wants a home for stability.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #282. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices and rents are as stated in the episode.

articles.title: A third of my condo is unsold. Will the developer cut prices on me?
articles.excerpt: A buyer's RM620,000 condo is about to be handed over with 270 of 770 units unsold, and rent nearby falls short of the instalment. Sean explains how developers clear stock, and why he would furnish, rent and hold.

question.asker: From CG, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: CG bought a 1,100 sq ft condo for RM620,000 four years ago, at 28, to live in, partly out of fear of missing out. Due for handover soon, it is low-density and far from public transport; 270 of its 770 units are still unsold, though the developer has raised the price twice. The instalment is about RM2,900, while smaller partly furnished units next door rent for RM2,500 to RM2,700. CG now wants to rent it out or sell.
question.text: Will the developer cut prices to clear unsold units, what does selling cost, and should CG rent below the instalment or sell at a loss?

answer.quote: entry price is everything
answer.summary: Don't sell at a loss. Fully furnish it at handover, rent it out to cover most of the instalment, and hold until the market recovers enough to sell without a loss. Developers rarely cut prices openly, but they do sell leftover units privately through bulk purchasers, which is the competition CG faces.

reasons.title: Price rises are not profit
reasons.body: Developers often raise prices to fund bigger discounts, because the marketing budget is a share of the price. A higher list price only means gains if units actually sell at it.

reasons.title: Leftovers are sold quietly
reasons.body: Cutting prices in public would anger existing buyers, so developers short of cash sell blocks of units under NDA to bulk purchasers. Those buyers get lower instalments and can rent for less than earlier owners.

reasons.title: Selling below the loan costs cash
reasons.body: Selling for less than you owe means paying the bank the difference, perhaps RM40,000 to RM50,000. Renting at a shortfall of about RM200 a month would take many years to cost as much.

reasons.title: A furnished unit stands out
reasons.body: Discouraged owners in a slow project tend not to furnish, so a well-furnished unit can win the tenants who like the area but cannot afford to buy, at a rent close to the instalment.

actions: Fully furnish the unit at handover and rent it out.
Compare your break-even rent, instalment plus maintenance, with what furnished units achieve.
Hold for two to three years and sell once a price covers your loan and costs.
Avoid paying down the loan with savings just to cut the interest, unless you have no better use for the cash.
For future purchases, compare the price with the area's median price per sq ft.
articles.caveat: Sean's expectation of a coming property upturn underpins the advice to hold. An own-stay buyer whose budget cannot carry the monthly shortfall may still need to sell.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #273. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2025. Sean is a member of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner, and says three of his last four purchases were stock-clearance deals of the kind described.

articles.title: What should you check when you get your keys?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers hunt for scratches and hollow tiles and miss what stops a home from working. Sean sets out what to check first in a defect inspection.

question.context: You have collected the keys to a new home, and the developer gives you a limited window to report defects. Most buyers walk in looking for stains and scratches, and miss the things that actually stop a home from working.
question.text: What should you check during a defect inspection, and in what order?

answer.quote: These are things that you cannot really live without.
answer.summary: Check function before looks. Test every power point, water point, door and window first, compare the unit against your sale agreement, then move on to cosmetic flaws, and report everything through the proper channel.

reasons.title: Utilities come first
reasons.body: Test every power point with a phone charger, plus the distribution board, doorbell and any water heater or appliances supplied. Doors and windows should open and close smoothly, and window seals should feel firm.

reasons.title: Water problems hide
reasons.body: Fill each sink and check the joints underneath. Pour water on bathroom floors, especially in the shower, to see that it runs to the drain. Look for stains on ceilings and around windows that point to leaks, particularly in landed homes.

reasons.title: Your sale agreement is the checklist
reasons.body: If the agreement promises laminated flooring in the bedrooms or full-height tiles in the kitchen, check that is what you got; a mismatch matters more than a stain. Some buyers even measure wall to wall, after stories of 900 sq ft units measuring 850.

reasons.title: Hollow tiles are more serious than they look
reasons.body: A hollow wall tile can eventually fall off; a hollow floor tile can crack under heavy furniture because there is no mortar beneath it. Straight walls and even floors are not a luxury at any price point.

actions: Bring a phone charger, your sale agreement and a measuring tape, and mark each defect with a sticker as you go.
Check the common facilities too: the building should have its certificate of completion, and the gym and pool should be working, not "under maintenance".
Submit defects through the developer's official channel; the staff follow process, so be thorough rather than confrontational.
Note the defect liability period, usually 24 months; leaks or cracks in that time are the developer's to fix. Structural renovation in a landed home can void claims for related cracks.
For a rental unit, prioritise whatever stops a tenant moving in; each round of repairs can cost two to three months of instalments.
articles.caveat: The quality of supplied furniture and finishes is usually not a claimable defect, because it cannot be measured. For a rental, cosmetic flaws rarely matter to tenants; for your own home, ones that bother you every day are worth pursuing.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this January 2020 walk-through. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Parts of the older automatic captions are unclear, so only clearly stated points are included.

video.title: CHECK FOR DEFECTS IN YOUR PROPERTY

articles.title: After an earthquake and a gas fire, how protected is your property?
articles.excerpt: After the Myanmar earthquake, the Putra Heights gas pipeline fire and a market sell-off, viewers asked whether property is still safe. Sean goes through the protections every owner should have in place.

question.context: In one week, an earthquake damaged buildings in Myanmar and Bangkok, a gas pipeline fire destroyed homes in Putra Heights, Selangor, and new US tariffs hit share and crypto prices. Sean's inbox filled with questions about whether high-rises are safe and whether owning property is too risky.
question.text: What should a property owner have in place before disaster strikes, and do events like these change what to buy?

answer.quote: the key question for all of us to answer is, how covered are you?
answer.summary: Disasters cannot be predicted, but their damage to your finances can be limited. Keep an emergency fund, insure your life, your loans and the building, keep a cash buffer for each property, and check what is around a home before you buy it.

reasons.title: Heirs inherit the debt too
reasons.body: If an owner dies, their family must keep paying any outstanding housing loans. Without enough life insurance, MLTA or MRTA, which the bank offers with the loan, is the cheaper way to cover that. Sean warns against cancelling it to save money unless the property is worth well more than the loan.

reasons.title: Check what your fire policy covers
reasons.body: Some policies cover only the structure, others also cover belongings, and not all cover floods. Earthquake cover is unlikely to be available from Malaysian insurers at a sensible cost.

reasons.title: A buffer gives you time
reasons.body: Sean keeps enough cash to pay six months of instalments on every property, so a unit can stand empty for six months without affecting him. An emergency fund of three to six months' expenses can pay a rental deposit while an insurance claim is processed.

reasons.title: Know what is next to the house
reasons.body: Rivers, pylons and pipelines have setback zones. Township developments make sense because buyers can see what surrounds them. Sean expects high-rises with proper piling and shear walls to withstand tremors better than older landed houses.

actions: Build an emergency fund of three to six months' expenses before investing.
Get at least a medical card, and life cover or MLTA or MRTA for every property loan.
Read your fire policy to see whether it covers floods and contents as well as the structure.
Keep six months of instalments in cash for each property you own.
Check for pipelines, pylons and rivers near a home before you buy.
articles.caveat: Sean notes that the cause of the fire was still under investigation when he recorded this. He also sees sell-offs after such events as buying opportunities, which only suits investors who have done their own research.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #279, recorded in the week after these events rather than in answer to a single viewer. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean mentions a recent purchase through FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club he is a member of, not its owner, and that The Makeover Guys, a renovation company, furnishes his units; neither bears on the protections summarised here.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #279 | LESSONS FROM THE EARTHQUAKE, FIRE, AND TARIFFS

articles.title: I bought at a discount. Why am I still losing money?
articles.excerpt: A homeowner who bought "at a good rate" during COVID now struggles with the instalment and cannot find tenants. Sean explains why a discount is not a bargain, and how to decide whether to hold, rent or sell.

question.asker: From Mr A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr A bought a 1,500 sq ft condo at Subang Park Homes in SS19 during COVID, because the price looked like a good deal. He lives there with his wife and child, but the loan and maintenance now cost about RM4,000 a month, and similar units listed for rent at RM3,000 to RM3,500 find no takers.
question.text: Did he buy into a money-losing development, and what should he do now?

answer.quote: Is it cheaper? Yes. Is it still expensive? Yes.
answer.summary: A discount only helps if the price ends up below the area's median, not just below the project's old price. For a home already bought, the question now is whether to hold, rent or sell, and that depends on valuation, recent sales and the loan balance.

reasons.title: The discount was measured against the wrong number
reasons.body: "20% below market value" usually means below a bank valuation or the developer's old asking price. The real market price is what similar units actually sold for. If the area median is RM900 per sq ft and a project drops from RM1,300 to RM1,100, it is cheaper and still expensive.

reasons.title: A quiet address does not draw tenants
reasons.body: High rents come from temporary demand: jobs, universities and tourism. A hidden residential corner suits a family, but most renters will pay more to live near a train station or highway.

reasons.title: The 85% test was never done
reasons.body: For an own-stay home, Sean checks that local rent covers about 85% of the instalment, so you have an exit if plans change. On a RM3,500 instalment that means rent of about RM3,000. Checking demand first would have shown the risk.

reasons.title: Who loses depends on when they bought
reasons.body: The developer profited at launch, and early buyers likely gained, but later buyers at peak prices often have not. Across the market, people who bought at the 2015 to 2016 peak are still underwater, while those who bought in the 2019 to 2021 dip gained equity.

actions: Ask your bank for a current valuation; it sets what your buyer can borrow.
Check the latest transacted prices in your project. If the last sale was a year ago, demand is thin.
Compare your outstanding loan with a realistic sale price. If selling leaves you owing the bank, decide whether to pay the gap now or keep paying monthly.
If you rent it out, check the competition: unfurnished listings with no takers leave room to win; furnished ones with no takers signal real trouble.
Next time, decide own stay or investment first, and check local rent before you buy.
articles.caveat: As a family home, the property is doing its job, so it is not automatically a failure; the pain is the instalment. On smart-home features, which Mr A also asked about, Sean thinks they add little to rent or resale and suit owners furnishing a home for themselves.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #309. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #309 | BOUGHT AT DISCOUNT PRICE STILL LOSE MONEY

articles.title: I'm between jobs with savings. Should I buy my first property now?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old who left medicine for a master's degree has about RM380,000 saved and wants a RM400,000 investment unit in the Klang Valley, which he barely knows. Sean says research now, buy after six months in a new job.

question.asker: From Mr J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr J is 27 and lives in Melaka. He resigned as a government doctor to study a one-year master's in health tech, finishing in late 2026, and earns occasional income as a part-time property agent. Counting money market funds, cash, stocks and an insurance savings plan, he has about RM380,000, and he spends about RM2,000 a month. He is a client of a property investment club, can borrow RM600,000 to RM700,000, and wants a unit of about RM400,000 for cash flow, though he doesn't know KL or Selangor.
question.text: How should he choose between projects in unfamiliar areas, do view and floor level matter, and what should he do with his cash?

answer.quote: Don't buy any properties before 6 months income from your new job.
answer.summary: Wait. Without a payslip he can't qualify for a loan anyway, and a 35-year commitment needs a steady income first. Use the time to get to know the Klang Valley, then buy once he has six months of income from his new job.

reasons.title: Invest where people move for work
reasons.body: Sean always recommends main city centres such as KL, JB, Penang and Kuching, because fresh graduates head to the capital for jobs and rooms there are in short supply: about RM700 for a small room and RM1,200 for a master bedroom around Cheras. JB prices near the RTS link have already run up.

reasons.title: View matters only at the extremes
reasons.body: A KLCC or KL skyline view earns a premium for luxury and short-stay units, and a unit facing another tower 30 m away loses out. For a unit bought on rent versus instalment, view hardly matters, but floor level does in dense areas like Mont Kiara or Bangsar South, where low floors sit in the shadow of the next tower.

reasons.title: Completed units let you roll faster
reasons.body: A new launch can take four years before it earns rent you can show the bank. A completed or nearly completed unit can be let within months, and six months of declared rent helps you qualify for the next loan; developers also negotiate harder near completion.

reasons.title: His cash is well placed
reasons.body: Money market funds and savings keep him liquid while he has no steady income. With RM2,000 a month in spending, RM110,000 in the bank covers about four years, more than he needs as a buffer.

actions: Watch videos of KL and Selangor areas, then visit them: ride the LRT, walk the malls and get a feel for each address.
Join site tours if your investment club runs them, and view about 20 properties within your budget.
Stay within the RM400,000 range you are comfortable with, below the most you can borrow.
Plan who will manage the unit for you if you buy far from where you live.
Leave room in your savings for a wedding if marriage is likely in the next few years.
articles.caveat: Property investment beyond two or three units suits people who enjoy driving around, viewing buildings and dealing with strangers; if that drains you, stopping after using your two 90% loans is enough. Sean's thoughts on stocks in the episode are, in his words, not financial advice.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #298. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2025. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, the club Mr J belongs to, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #298 | DOCTOR TURNED AGENT HUSTLING FOR A KL PROPERTY

articles.title: My big house is suddenly empty. Hold, rent it out or sell?
articles.excerpt: A 40-year-old bought a corner terrace house for his family, and now lives in it alone. Rent covers less than the instalment, so he wonders whether to sell. Sean says hold and rent it out.

question.asker: From Happy Dragon, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: He is 40, takes home RM13,500 a month and bought a corner terrace house near Elmina, Shah Alam, in 2020 for about RM750,000, with an instalment of about RM2,800 at 4.2%. He spent about RM170,000 in cash renovating and furnishing it so his grandfather and a caretaker could live with him; his grandfather has since died and he now lives there alone. Nearby rents to university students and lecturers are about RM2,000. Selling would recover the price but not the renovation. He has about RM150,000 in ASB, RM20,000 in fixed deposits and a car loan of RM1,100 a month.
question.text: Should he keep the house empty until a property upturn, rent it out at a monthly shortfall, or sell?

answer.quote: So I think you should hold.
answer.summary: Hold it and rent it out. The rent covers most of the interest, so the gap he pays each month is mostly principal, and the house has already risen in value since he bought it.

reasons.title: The shortfall is mostly principal
reasons.body: About 80 to 85% of an instalment is interest, so roughly RM2,380 of his RM2,800. A RM2,000 rent covers most of that, leaving about RM800 a month that mainly pays down the loan, which on a RM13,500 income Sean calls a kind of forced saving rather than a loss.

reasons.title: Landed homes rarely rent for the full instalment
reasons.body: Rent covering the whole instalment usually happens only with high-rise, where yields are higher. Landed owners give up some yield for more room for capital growth.

reasons.title: The renovation is not a property loss
reasons.body: Sean reckons he bought at a discount of about 10%, so selling at the same price already returns his deposit. The house is now worth about RM850,000, roughly 13% above the price he paid; the RM170,000 he spent on furnishing for his family does not make the property itself a losing one.

reasons.title: A corner lot is its own market
reasons.body: The gap between a corner lot and an intermediate unit is very large, with different demand and supply, which is another reason to keep it.

actions: Rent the house out at RM2,000 or more rather than leaving it empty.
Consider furnishing it fully to rent room by room, or to attract better tenants for the whole house.
Judge the monthly gap against how much of the instalment is interest, not against the full instalment.
Before buying an investment, work out the expected rent and furnishing cost first.
Review idle savings: money earning about 3.2% may not keep up with inflation.
articles.caveat: This holds because his income is high and he has no other big commitments; someone stretched by an RM800 monthly gap would weigh it differently. Sean is openly bullish on prices, and says he cannot judge this exact street without its past transactions.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #288. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2025. Sean also spends part of the episode encouraging the viewer to stop comparing himself with others, which is left out here.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #288 | HOLD ON UNTIL PROPERTY BULLRUN

articles.title: Who will buy my condo in 30 years? What's the exit strategy?
articles.excerpt: A returning Malaysian asks how condo investors ever cash out when buildings age, lifts break and few owners pay maintenance. Sean explains how condos make money, why he plans to hold for good, and what to avoid.

question.asker: From Double O, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: After nearly two decades abroad, Double O is relocating to Kuala Lumpur and plans to invest a sum just under seven figures in property, and worries that a condo held for 30 to 40 years will suffer shabby lifts, cracks, run-down facilities and high maintenance fees with few owners paying, and that unlike a landed house it cannot simply be rebuilt.
question.text: How are investors with many ageing condos supposed to exit, and who will buy them?

answer.quote: my very simplified low-level thinking strategy is to hold it forever
answer.summary: Sean buys condos expecting to hold them for good: if rent covers the instalment, the tenant pays off the loan and the unit is his in 30 years, so any price growth is a bonus. Ageing is manageable when owners live in or rent long-term and pay maintenance; buildings full of short-stay investors are the ones to exit early or avoid.

reasons.title: Condos pay three ways
reasons.body: Capital appreciation, rent, and equity built as the tenant's payments reduce the loan. Early on, about 88% of each instalment is interest, so equity builds slowly at first.

reasons.title: Rent sets the resale price
reasons.body: A RM500,000 unit renting for RM2,750 can be sold at RM600,000 and still give the next investor a 5.5% yield, about break-even with the loan. Every RM500 a month of surplus rent supports roughly RM100,000 more in price.

reasons.title: Everything but the structure can be replaced
reasons.body: Lifts, pipes and pools can be renewed if the management collects enough. Buildings where most owners live in or rent long-term stay well kept, as in many 15- to 20-year-old blocks in Mont Kiara.

reasons.title: Short-stay buildings need a fast exit
reasons.body: Only investors will buy a unit in a short-stay building, and only while the yield holds. Once rates fall, everyone sells together and maintenance collection collapses.

actions: Buy below the median price per sq ft of nearby transactions.
Aim for a yield of about 6%, at which rent roughly covers the instalment and costs.
Favour buildings where most units are owner-occupied or rented long-term.
Join the management body or AGM to keep maintenance collection healthy.
If you buy a short-stay unit, plan to sell while its returns are still high.
articles.caveat: Double-storey landed terraces have the highest capital growth in Malaysia, but rarely rent for their instalment, so they suit investors with cash to cover the gap. Sean prefers to live in rented landed homes away from the city and invest in city condos.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #268. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2024. Sean says he follows FAR Capital's seven investment criteria; he is a member of the bulk-purchase club, not its owner. The episode is sponsored by Versa, a savings app.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #268 | EXIT STRATEGY

articles.title: My Airbnb studios are bleeding cash. Did I fail as an investor?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old bought two city-centre studios in 2017 for Airbnb, then COVID hit and both lose money every month. Sean explains what went wrong, why it was not a total failure, and why he would sell.

question.asker: From Mr Core, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Core is 34 and owns a landed home and two 411 sq ft leasehold studios with commercial title in central Kuala Lumpur, bought in 2017 for about RM578,000 each to run as Airbnb. Each instalment is about RM3,500. The project completed in 2020, during COVID; one unit now rents long-term for about RM2,300, and the other, run by a management company on an 80:20 split, nets him about RM25,000 a year. Banks value each unit at RM600,000 to RM650,000, and there are auction listings in the project.
question.text: Is this a failed investment, should he sell one unit, and how does he still reach his goal of five income-generating properties?

answer.quote: I would suggest to sell this and start working for the next deal
answer.summary: Not a failed investment: he bought near the top of the cycle, was hit by COVID, and still held on with about a 10% gain. But Sean would sell both units, because thousands of new studios nearby will compete for tenants and he is paying about RM3,000 a month for nothing but a target number of units.

reasons.title: A good project has several ways to rent
reasons.body: Sean only rates a project if long-term rent alone can cover the instalment, with medium-term, room-by-room or Airbnb as extra options. When a launch leads with Airbnb returns, it usually means long-term rent cannot cover the loan.

reasons.title: Airbnb can be taken away
reasons.body: Singapore bans it, Penang has banned it in residential-title projects, and a building's owners can vote it out at an AGM. Short-stay income also has to be shared with an operator, or it becomes a second job.

reasons.title: Rent sets the price
reasons.body: A buyer works out the instalment against the rent, which is why the valuation is stuck around RM600,000. About 10,000 to 12,000 new units of a similar size and price are coming nearby, and tenants prefer new, so rents and prices are more likely to fall than rise.

reasons.title: Aim for cash flow, not a unit count
reasons.body: Five properties is an arbitrary number. Set a monthly positive cash flow instead: first enough for rent to cover where you live, then the amount the lifestyle you want needs.

actions: Before buying, check that long-term rent alone covers the instalment.
Keep cash to cover about six months of a fully furnished unit standing empty.
Find out what you still owe the bank, what units actually sell for at auction and the asking prices, then set your exit price.
Sell both studios and put the money into the next deal while you are young.
Replace a target number of units with a monthly cash-flow target.
articles.caveat: Sean's call to sell rests on the new supply he expects near this project. A short-stay unit in a stronger location, or one whose long-term rent already covers the loan, may be worth keeping.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #287. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2025; the viewer's rent figures are taken from his email as read out, and some of Sean's spoken figures in the episode were unclear in the captions, so they are left out.

articles.title: My father will give me RM300,000 for a property. What should I buy?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old earning RM3,500 has been offered up to RM300,000 by her father towards a property, and finds agents pushy. Sean suggests asking him to hold it until her income and knowledge catch up.

question.asker: From Miss P, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss P is 25, earns RM3,500 a month and rents a cheap room in Subang Jaya near work. Her father has offered up to RM300,000 towards a property, as he has done for her siblings, so she has something to fall back on. Her fiancé's family has bought him an apartment in cash, ready well before their wedding in two years. She has been viewing new launches near Subang and PJ, finds the agents pushy, and wonders whether a completed subsale is better.
question.text: Should she buy a new launch or a completed subsale with the money, and how does she make the most of it?

answer.quote: hold on this money for me first until I am ready
answer.summary: Not yet. On RM3,500 a month she would be stretched by any loan, so ask her father to hold the money while she researches and raises her income to about RM5,000. Then use it on a subsale or bulk-purchase unit whose rent covers the instalment, and live in the fiancé's apartment.

reasons.title: New launches price in the future
reasons.body: Developers know local rents, price a unit you get in three or four years at tomorrow's prices, and since COVID add bigger safety margins. That is why few new launches have rent covering the instalment.

reasons.title: Subsale needs the cash she has
reasons.body: A RM500,000 subsale needs about RM90,000 up front plus RM35,000 to RM40,000 to furnish, which is what stops most young buyers. Her father's money removes that barrier.

reasons.title: Keep the gift for investment
reasons.body: Sean would not spend it renovating the marital home, where a simple renovation can cost RM100,000. Her father's purpose is a safe haven for her, so it belongs in a property that pays its own way.

reasons.title: Twenty viewings make you immune
reasons.body: After visiting about 20 properties across types and areas, you learn what you like and can see sales tactics coming, such as 'only two units left'.

actions: Ask your father whether the money must buy a home, and whether there is a deadline.
Live in your fiancé's apartment after the wedding and budget for its renovation separately.
Visit about 20 properties, new and old, high-rise and landed, before deciding.
Check your loan eligibility, and work to raise your income towards RM5,000.
Then buy a subsale or bulk-purchase unit whose rent covers the instalment, putting spare cash in the loan account.
articles.caveat: If her father wants the money used now, Sean would still choose a subsale over the new launches she shortlisted. Auctions are best left until after several purchases.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #261. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in September 2024. Sean is a client of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club he recommends joining, not its owner. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #261 | DADDY GIVING RM300K TO BUY PROPERTY!!

articles.title: Should I spend most of my cash on a fifth property before I marry?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old commission earner with four properties wants to put RM214,000 of his RM300,000 savings into a dual-key unit yielding 7.3%, a year before his wedding. Sean says the deal is fine; the timing isn't.

question.asker: From YG, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: YG is 27, earns about RM300,000 a year in commission and has RM300,000 in cash. He owns his landed home, an apartment and a low-cost flat, and helps pay for his father's flat; together his commitments come to about RM5,600 a month after rent. He is getting married next year and, unsure his income will last, wants to buy a dual-key unit near a mall for RM520,000, valued at RM480,000, with a 70% loan and about RM214,000 upfront, yielding about 7.3%.
question.text: Is this purchase a good move given his commitments and wedding plans, and is spending RM214,000 the smartest route to passive income?

answer.quote: I don't agree. Why put yourself in such a situation?
answer.summary: No, not now. The property itself is a solid buy, but with renovation it would take about RM260,000 of his RM300,000, leaving a few months of spending on a commission income just before a wedding. Rushing because he doubts next year's income shows he isn't ready.

reasons.title: Cash flow is what sinks investors
reasons.body: With about RM40,000 left and about RM8,000 a month in spending, he could last roughly six months if sales dried up. A property can't be turned into cash quickly: refinancing takes months and a sale seven to nine months before the money arrives.

reasons.title: Paying more cash isn't smarter
reasons.body: Every RM100,000 borrowed over 35 years at 4% costs about RM450 a month, so a yield of about 5.4% breaks even and about 6% covers maintenance and other costs. Sean would rather borrow the most he can, keep a year of expenses and six months of instalments per property in cash, and invest the rest.

reasons.title: Doubting your income means you're not ready
reasons.body: Sean learned in sales that income stays high when the work stays consistent. Buying now because the bank will lend on this year's income is a sign the plan rests on fear, not readiness.

reasons.title: Low valuations are normal in new projects
reasons.body: A newly completed project has few transactions, and banks know developers' prices include discounts, so a valuation below the price is common. Subsale units in good locations bought with 20% to 30% down often give positive cash flow.

actions: Park the RM200,000 in a fixed deposit, EPF or another stable investment, and treat it as gone so you keep working hard.
Rebuild a cash buffer that covers your commitments for at least six months before buying again.
Budget the wedding before committing savings to another property.
Get MLTA, MRTA or life insurance to cover your loans.
Look at what you spend each month; about RM8,000 is high for your stage.
articles.caveat: With about RM1 million in the bank, Sean says spending RM260,000 on this unit would be fine. And a buyer with no properties yet, and so a 90% loan available, should simply go ahead.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #301. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Some of the viewer's figures are unclear in the captions, so only totals Sean confirms are used. Figures are as stated in November 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #301 | IS THAT PROPERTY WORTH THE ANXIETY?

articles.title: Where do I find the money for my first property?
articles.excerpt: Many buyers find a good deal and are just short of the 10% down payment. Sean goes through the four Fs of funding, and why raising income beats blaming property prices.

question.context: Young buyers often spot a promising deal and find themselves short of the 10% down payment, or unable to qualify for a loan because of card debts and instalment plans. Many complain that salaries no longer keep up with prices.
question.text: Where can a first-time buyer find the money for a property, and what should come first?

answer.quote: you should ask yourself how can you afford this
answer.summary: First save six months of expenses. Then the money comes from the four Fs: family, friends, financial institutions and fools. Borrow from family or friends only if you repay on time, keep your credit clean for the bank, and steer clear of being anyone's 'fool'. Above all, work out the income you need and how to reach it.

reasons.title: Six months of savings comes first
reasons.body: If you spend RM3,000 a month, have RM18,000 in the bank before you look at property. Paying the minimum on cards all year and clearing them with the bonus leaves nothing to invest.

reasons.title: Partners split the bad times too
reasons.body: Buying with a friend halves the down payment, but both names are liable. When the unit is empty, each of you pays half the instalment every month.

reasons.title: Beware anyone who wants your name
reasons.body: 'Fools' are people who lend their name and credit to someone else's scheme for a promised share. If a deal were certain to make money, nobody would need to share it.

reasons.title: Work back from the price
reasons.body: Banks lend roughly where the instalment is a third of income. A RM500,000 property costs about RM2,500 a month, needing about RM7,500 of income; ask what would raise yours from where it is.

actions: Save six months of expenses before you start viewing.
Clear card debts and instalment plans so they don't block your loan.
If family or friends help, agree repayment terms in writing and keep to them.
Never lend your name or credit for someone else's purchase.
Calculate the income your target property needs, and plan side work or skills to reach it.
articles.caveat: Sean notes that loan rates were around 4.5% to 4.8% in 2019, far below the 12% of earlier decades, and that first-home schemes and developer packages may reduce the cash needed for a new launch.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this June 2019 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: Sourcing Money for Property Investment

articles.title: Do I need my own fire insurance for a landed house?
articles.excerpt: Many owners assume MRTA or MLTA is the only insurance they need. Sean explains what fire insurance covers for an individual-title house, how to set the sum insured, and that the bank's bundled policy is optional.

question.context: Home buyers usually think of mortgage insurance, MRTA or MLTA, but a house also needs cover against fire and other damage. Banks typically bundle a fire policy with the loan, and many owners don't know what it covers or that they can choose another.
question.text: What does home or fire insurance cover, who needs to buy it, and how much cover is enough?

answer.quote: there's one more thing which is called fire insurance
answer.summary: If you own an individual-title house, you need your own cover; in a strata building, the joint management body insures the building. Insure the cost of rebuilding, not the market price, and compare policies, since you don't have to take the one bundled with your loan.

reasons.title: It covers more than fire
reasons.body: Policies now cover the building, its contents and add-ons: flood, landslide, burglary damage, burst pipes and gas explosions, and for landlords, lost rent if a tenant leaves early and malicious damage.

reasons.title: Strata owners are covered differently
reasons.body: For condos and other strata titles, insuring the building is the joint management body's responsibility, so this matters most for individual-title terrace houses.

reasons.title: Insure the rebuilding cost
reasons.body: A house worth RM2 million may cost far less to rebuild, since the land is not destroyed. The sum insured should cover materials, contractors and consultants to rebuild it.

reasons.title: The loan keeps running
reasons.body: If the house becomes uninhabitable, the bank still expects instalments. Some policies add cover for instalments in that case, and for common landed problems such as roof leaks and termites.

actions: Check whether your current policy, often bundled with your loan, covers flood and contents.
Work out the rebuilding cost of your house, not its market value.
Compare quotes from other insurers before renewing the bank's package.
Add landlord cover if the house is rented out.
Remind parents in older landed homes to check their cover.
articles.caveat: Switching away from a bank-bundled policy can mean paperwork for a saving of a few hundred ringgit a year. Earthquake cover was not discussed.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this 2021 video, which he made after being approached by someone at Tune Protect and which features Tune Protect's home insurance and promotions. The general points are kept and the product details and prices are left out. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: PROPERTY INSURANCE, HOME CARE, CHEAPEST FIRE INSURANCE

articles.title: Subsale or new, freehold or leasehold: what matters for unit one?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old saving more than half their pay asks four questions before a first investment unit. Sean explains why new launches are priced up, why tenure and feng shui come second, and why location tier matters most.

question.asker: From L, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: L is 28, earns RM7,000 a month and saves RM3,000 to RM4,500 of it, with about RM50,000 in shares and ETFs, RM50,000 in crypto, a RM20,000 emergency fund and no loans. Agents say L can afford RM400,000 to RM800,000; L's instinct is a RM400,000 to RM500,000 unit whose rent covers the instalment.
question.text: Why do most first-time buyers buy new rather than subsale or bulk purchase, does leasehold matter, does feng shui matter, and what price range should a first investment be?

answer.quote: I will go for tier one location instead of a local market focused location
answer.summary: First-time buyers buy new because they have no cash, and developers price that convenience in, so new units are often worth less than their price at handover. For an investment, tenure and feng shui matter less than paying below the area's median price, and with about RM700,000 Sean would buy in a tier one location.

reasons.title: New launches price in the free extras
reasons.body: Discounts, free legal fees and other perks are built into the price of a unit you get in four or five years. That is why owners find at handover that banks value a RM500,000 unit at about RM480,000: they paid the real price, and borrowed the rest.

reasons.title: A subsale shows you what you are buying
reasons.body: You can see the view, build quality, defects, neighbours' rents and recent sale prices before you commit. The catch is cash: about 18% of the price, so about RM90,000 for a RM500,000 unit, before renovation.

reasons.title: Tenure and feng shui come after price
reasons.body: Freehold matters more for landed homes, but a leasehold unit near work beats a freehold one two hours away. A unit next to a cemetery at 30% below market can be a good investment; one with perfect feng shui at 30% above it will still lose money.

reasons.title: Tier one locations have no rent ceiling
reasons.body: Areas such as Mont Kiara, popular with expatriates, command rents locals would never pay; Sean rents a one-bedroom there for about RM5,000. At RM700,000 he would choose Dutamas over Petaling Jaya for the higher yield.

actions: Compare a subsale's instalment with the rents its neighbours get before buying.
Reserve about 18% of the price in cash for a subsale, plus renovation.
Judge any unit against the median price of its location, not against its perks.
Aim for the cheapest project in a tier one location.
Check you could carry the instalment if the unit stayed empty for six months.
articles.caveat: Freehold matters more for a landed home you plan to live in for good. Sean's preference for completed unsold units through a bulk-purchase club applies only while developers have overhang stock to clear.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #285. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2025. Sean says in the episode that he is a VIP member of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club he recommends for completed unsold units, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #285 | NEW PROPERTY PRICES ARE MOSTLY INFLATED

articles.title: No property at 49. Should I spend my inheritance on a walk-up flat?
articles.excerpt: A single 49-year-old teacher in Penang earning RM3,800 inherited RM170,000 and plans to buy a cheap walk-up flat in cash to rent out. Sean suggests an affordable home bought partly on a loan, to live in and let rooms.

question.asker: From CL, a viewer from Penang who wrote in by email
question.context: CL is 49, single and a private school teacher earning RM3,800 a month net. CL owns no property and has no loans, holds one credit card with five months of history, and was refused two more. CL has recently inherited RM170,000, and also has RM100,000 in fixed deposits and RM50,000 in EPF Account 2.
question.text: Is it sound to buy a cheap walk-up flat in cash with the inheritance to rent out, then buy a second flat to live in?

answer.quote: I would suggest to not go for a walk up apartment
answer.summary: Rather than paying cash for a walk-up to rent out, buy an affordable state-scheme home of about RM280,000 to RM350,000 with as large a loan as CL qualifies for, live in it and rent out the other two bedrooms. Keep most of the cash in reserve, and work on earning more.

reasons.title: Age shortens the loan
reasons.body: Most banks lend only until 65 to 70. On a RM300,000 loan at 4%, 35 years means about RM1,328 a month; 15 years means about RM2,219, which needs roughly RM7,000 of net income to qualify.

reasons.title: Owning solves two worries
reasons.body: Landlords are often reluctant to rent to older tenants, and an own home removes that risk. Renting out two rooms covers part of the instalment, and the rent becomes income once the loan is paid.

reasons.title: Walk-ups make poor rentals later
reasons.body: Stairs are hard work in retirement and for families with strollers, so tenants are always the lowest-budget group and rents compete on price. Older walk-ups also bring repair levies and other hidden costs.

reasons.title: Keep cash, borrow cheaply
reasons.body: Spending it all on property leaves nothing for emergencies, and banks won't lend for repairs as readily as for a purchase. In later life, a government reverse mortgage scheme can turn a paid-off home into monthly income.

actions: Ask a bank now how much you can borrow on your current income.
Look at Penang's affordable housing and apply for first-home incentives such as stamp duty waivers.
Pay the difference between the loan and the price from the inheritance, and keep the rest in fixed deposits or EPF.
Rent out the spare bedrooms once you move in.
Add income through tutoring or other side work.
articles.caveat: Sean expects CL's loan eligibility to be about RM120,000 to RM200,000 on a RM3,800 income, which limits the choice of home. Resale values of affordable homes after their moratorium are untested.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #264. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in November 2024. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #264 | 50 YEARS OLD WITHOUT ANY PROPERTY

articles.title: Must your first property also be your home?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old bought an investment condo before a family home, and his future in-laws disapprove. Sean explains why investing first can be the smarter order.

question.asker: From Nick, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Nick is 26, a dentist earning about RM20,000 a month, with RM100,000 in cash and RM100,000 in stocks. He has just bought a subsale three-bedroom condo in Shah Alam near his clinic for RM490,000, with his parents helping on the deposit. The instalment is RM2,000, maintenance RM330, and similar units rent for about RM2,200. He plans to rent a landed house nearby for RM1,600. His future in-laws think the couple should have bought their own home first.
question.text: Is it better to buy a home first and invest later? And how should he explain his plan to in-laws who think he is being too aggressive?

answer.quote: I support your move.
answer.summary: Invest first and keep renting your home. Use your strongest borrowing years and your cheapest loans on property that tenants help pay for, and buy the family home later.

reasons.title: The 90% loans are worth using early
reasons.body: Buyers get two residential loans at a 90% margin; from the third, it drops to 70%. Nick's unit needed about 17% upfront including stamp duty and legal fees, roughly RM85,000. As a third property it would need at least RM150,000. Spending a 90% loan on a home uses up one of the two cheap slots and much of his borrowing capacity.

reasons.title: A home tends to become a big commitment
reasons.body: On RM20,000 a month, the bank would happily lend Nick enough for a RM1 million landed house at around RM4,000 a month. After that come children, a bigger car and insurance. Buying the home first often leaves nothing for investing.

reasons.title: Judge it over 20 years, not in month one
reasons.body: Property is a long game. The aim of the first years is simply for the rent to roughly cover the instalment while the loan is paid down and the property gains value. A small monthly shortfall is the cost of holding, not a sign of failure. Compare who is wealthier in 15 to 30 years, not after the first year.

reasons.title: Renting keeps the couple flexible
reasons.body: A landed house renting at RM1,600 might cost RM800,000 to RM1 million to buy, at roughly RM4,000 a month. Renting costs far less, lets the couple move as their careers change, and spares them maintaining rooms they do not use yet.

actions: Once the first tenancy has run smoothly for about six months, start looking for the next investment.
Buy the family home later. Sean suggests putting it in the spouse's name, as he did, with extra life insurance so the loan is covered if anything happens to the main earner.
Hand the day-to-day work to a property management company so investing does not eat into your career.
Keep lifestyle spending low; spend on watches, cars and gadgets only from investment returns, not salary.
With family, listen for the worry behind the objection, but take investment advice from people already living the outcome you want.
articles.caveat: Sean's backing rests on Nick's unusually strong position: high income, solid savings and help with the deposit. With a thinner buffer, a monthly shortfall or a long vacancy hurts far more. Sean also says Shah Alam would not have been his own pick, but supports buying where you know the area well.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #254. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Loan margins and prices are as Sean stated them in June 2024.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #254 | FIRST PROPERTY MUST BE A HOME?

articles.title: What kind of property investor am I, and which strategy suits me?
articles.excerpt: Property makes money through rent or capital growth, and investors lean one way or the other. Sean describes four types, from cash-flow buyers to people who analyse forever and never buy.

question.context: Property makes money in two ways: rent, which in Malaysia usually comes from condos and serviced apartments whose rent nears the instalment, and capital growth, which usually comes from landed homes bought early in a new township. Rarely does one property do both well.
question.text: What types of property investors are there, and which approach should a new buyer take?

answer.quote: the higher the risk the higher the return
answer.summary: Sean sees four types: cash-flow investors, high-leverage buyers of new launches, cash-rich owners storing wealth, and those who only analyse. None is right or wrong, but doing nothing is the worst. A conservative buyer can mix the first two: a condo whose rent nearly covers the loan, and a landed home for growth.

reasons.title: Cash-flow investors build steadily
reasons.body: They buy older, cheaper high-rises of about RM200,000 to RM400,000 near schools, markets or colleges, where rent exceeds the instalment. Banks treat each such unit as an asset and keep lending, though capital growth is modest.

reasons.title: High-leverage buyers bet on recovery
reasons.body: They buy several new launches at once using discounts of up to 30% to 40% as cash back to cover instalments until the market recovers. It can pay well, or go badly wrong.

reasons.title: Wealth-storers don't need rent
reasons.body: Business owners with surplus cash buy landed property as a hedge against inflation and may not even rent it out.

reasons.title: Analysis without action costs years
reasons.body: Some attend every course and talk the market through but never buy. Sean saw 2018, with developers desperate and first-home schemes everywhere, as a good time for those with stable finances to act.

actions: Decide whether you are buying for rent, for growth, or for both.
Before buying, check that local rent covers 80% to 90% of the instalment, depending on your risk appetite.
Visit about 20 properties to understand the market.
Take your time if your finances are still being sorted out.
Match the strategy to your income's stability.
articles.caveat: Sean was describing the market at the end of 2018. Some leverage-heavy approaches he describes, such as relying on mortgage insurance in place of repayment, carry serious risk if the market does not recover.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this December 2018 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: 4 TYPES OF PROPERTY INVESTORS

articles.title: Is it worth paying to furnish a unit before renting it out?
articles.excerpt: Spending RM30,000 to furnish a unit for RM500 more rent looks like a five-year payback. Sean explains how he weighs the cost, and why higher rent can add to a property's value.

question.context: Malaysian homes are usually handed over bare, like a car without an engine. Many owners ask how spending about RM30,000 to have an investment unit designer-furnished can be justified, when it may raise the rent by only RM400 to RM500 a month.
question.text: How do you decide whether furnishing a rental unit is worth the cost?

answer.quote: Using the lowest amount of investment to get the highest rental returns.
answer.summary: Furnish to let the unit faster or at a higher rent, but compare the right numbers. Against the roughly RM12,000 a unit needs anyway to be livable, a RM30,000 package costs about RM18,000 more, which buys time and design sense, and higher rent can lift what the property is worth.

reasons.title: Compare against the bare minimum
reasons.body: RM30,000 divided by RM500 suggests five years to break even. But a unit needs a kitchen cabinet, lights, fans, curtains, a water heater and other basics before anyone can live in it, about RM12,000 if you do it yourself, so the real extra is closer to RM18,000.

reasons.title: You are paying for time and design sense
reasons.body: Doing it yourself means managing contractors, taking leave for deliveries and having the eye for it. If you live nearby and enjoy that, you save money; Sean, who values time most, would rather pay. Furnishing companies typically finish in about 30 working days.

reasons.title: Rent can lift the property's value
reasons.body: RM400 to RM500 more rent a month is roughly the instalment on another RM100,000 of loan over 30 years. Where buyers value a property on its rental return, that extra rent can make it worth about RM100,000 more.

reasons.title: First impressions win tenants
reasons.body: Like a show unit in a sales gallery, a dressed-up unit wins on the first viewing. At the same rent, a tenant will pick the designed unit over an empty or semi-furnished one.

actions: Check the rents for bare, semi-furnished and fully furnished units in your project before deciding.
Spend only on what raises the rent or shortens the time the unit sits empty.
Skip personal touches like plaster ceilings and marble tops in an investment unit; save them for your own home.
Choose your contractor or furnishing company before you collect the keys, not after.
Do it yourself only if you have the time, the design sense and live close to the unit.
articles.caveat: For your own home the rule doesn't apply: there your budget is the limit. And whether the extra rent justifies the cost depends on your project's rental market.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this January 2021 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company the video promotes, so he has a stake in this advice. Figures are as stated in 2021.

video.title: WHY SHOULD I FULLY FURNISH MY PROPERTY?

articles.title: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
articles.excerpt: A reader has booked a hotel unit with a guaranteed 7% return. Sean explains where the guarantee really comes from, and why the exit is the bigger problem.

question.asker: From JH, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JH has booked a 360 sq ft unit for RM700,000 in a hotel-run project near Genting Highlands. The developer guarantees a 7% return for three years, enough to cover the instalment and management fees with about RM1,000 a month to spare. After that, investors share 70% of the hotel profit for six years, and the operator handles utilities, furnishing and a refurbishment every three years.
question.text: He worries about the narrow access road, the operator choosing not to renew after nine years, and another pandemic. Is this kind of investment worth it?

answer.quote: I'm not a huge fan of GRR investment property.
answer.summary: Stay away unless it is a third or fourth property you can afford to lose. The guaranteed return is your own borrowed money paid back to you, the price is inflated, and the hotel operator is your only way out.

reasons.title: The guarantee is built into the price
reasons.body: A guaranteed rental return (GRR) is usually loaded into the sale price. A unit worth RM500,000 might be sold at RM700,000; you borrow the extra RM200,000 from the bank, and the developer hands it back to you as "returns" over three to five years.

reasons.title: You are paying city-centre prices for Genting
reasons.body: RM700,000 for 360 sq ft is about RM1,944 per sq ft, around what KLCC and TRX projects cost and more than Bukit Bintang. For short-stay rentals, the city centre also draws far more visitors than a tourist spot.

reasons.title: There is only one way out
reasons.body: A good investment property can be let long-term to families, short-term to expats, room by room or on Airbnb. This one only works as a hotel. If the operator walks away, as several did during the pandemic, you cannot live in it, rent it to locals or easily sell it, because buyers only want it for income it no longer makes.

reasons.title: The real return is thinner than 7%
reasons.body: Take off about 4% loan interest and roughly 1% in operating costs, and the margin is closer to 2%. Hotel use wears a building fast, so maintenance only rises. The operator is on a service contract it can leave after five years while your loan runs for 35, and business terms outside the sale agreement are not government-regulated.

actions: Work out the price per sq ft and compare it with prime city projects before trusting a guaranteed yield.
Ask what you would do if the operator left: could you live in it, rent it to locals, or sell it?
If you fear not finding tenants, buy below your limit instead. Sean suggests that someone approved for RM600,000 buy around RM480,000, so six empty months are survivable.
Keep your first two properties conventional; treat a scheme like this only as a third or fourth you can afford to lose.
Compare it with simpler options: fixed deposits, an index fund, or KL rentals yielding 5 to 6%.
articles.caveat: Sean stresses this is his general view of guaranteed-return schemes, not a judgement on this operator, and having a licensed hotel operator is a point in its favour. For an experienced investor with four or five properties, it is a risk you can choose to take.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #259. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Scheme terms vary by developer, so read the actual agreement before relying on any guarantee.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #259 | THE REALITY OF GRR (GUARANTEED RENTAL RETURN) SCHEMES

articles.title: What does buying a property really cost beyond the 10%?
articles.excerpt: Most first-time buyers budget the deposit and nothing else. Sean lists the costs that kept surprising him on his first purchase.

question.context: Ask what you need to buy a property in Malaysia and most people say 10%. Sean had exactly that for his first purchase, and the bills he had not budgeted for kept arriving one after another.
question.text: What else do you actually have to pay when you buy a property?

answer.quote: It's never 10%.
answer.summary: Budget well beyond the deposit. Legal fees on both the purchase and the loan, transfer stamp duty, valuation, handover deposits, compulsory insurance and yearly taxes all fall on the buyer, and a subsale costs the most upfront.

reasons.title: Legal fees come with more than one agreement
reasons.body: Developers often advertise a "free SPA", but that covers only the sale agreement. You also pay legal fees on the loan agreement with your bank, and owners of older blocks later pay again when the strata title is issued.

reasons.title: The transfer duty is the big one
reasons.body: Stamp duty on the memorandum of transfer (MOT) is due when ownership passes to you. Sean puts it at up to about 2% of the price, around RM14,000 on a RM700,000 home, and says few developers cover it.

reasons.title: Handover comes with deposits
reasons.body: Before you get the keys, a strata property usually needs about three months of maintenance fees as deposit, plus deposits for water, electricity and telecoms. A subsale also needs an independent valuation, paid by the buyer, before the bank will lend.

reasons.title: Some costs never stop
reasons.body: Banks effectively require mortgage insurance (MRTA or MLTA) before lending, and many require fire insurance too. Every year you also pay quit rent to the state and assessment tax to the local council; in strata buildings these often appear as a jump in the January or February maintenance bill.

actions: Plan for upfront cash well above 10% of the price, and more for a subsale.
Ask the developer in writing exactly which legal fees, and whether the MOT duty, are covered.
Set aside handover money: about three months of maintenance plus utility deposits.
Add mortgage and fire insurance to your loan costs, and quit rent and assessment tax to your yearly budget.
Estimate the legal fees and stamp duty for your price with the purchase cost calculator on this site.
articles.caveat: This is a 2019 episode. Fee scales have been revised since, and first-home stamp duty exemptions come and go with each Budget, so use these costs as a checklist and get current figures from your lawyer.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this April 2019 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Fee levels are as Sean described them at the time and have since changed.

video.title: HIDDEN COST WHEN YOU BUY PROPERTY IN MALAYSIA

articles.title: I earn well but fear losing my savings. Should I invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old in Melaka earning RM24,000 a month, with RM450,000 in cash, fears one wrong move. Sean says buy a rental unit well within her means, and leave renovate-and-flip alone.

question.asker: From Miss J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss J is 30, lives in Melaka and works in sales, averaging about RM24,000 a month. She has about RM450,000 in cash, RM80,000 in stocks and a RM160,000 car loan, and spends about RM10,000 a month. Coming from an ordinary family with no backup, she worries that one failure would be hard to recover from, and wonders whether to flip a renovated landed house, buy for rental, keep her money in fixed deposits or start a business.
question.text: Is she ready to invest in property, what should she buy, and should she flip houses or start a business instead?

answer.quote: Don't even think about flipping.
answer.summary: Yes, she is ready, but should play well within her means: a rental unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million in a proven KL location, where the rent covers the instalment. Buying an old house to renovate and sell is where people without construction experience lose money.

reasons.title: A rental unit has few unknowns
reasons.body: In an established area you can see the selling prices, rents and neighbours before you buy, and work out the instalment and furnishing costs. If you can carry six months of vacancy, the worst case is lowering the rent a little until a tenant signs.

reasons.title: She can absorb a bad month
reasons.body: She could borrow RM2.5 million or more, but a RM1 million loan costs about RM4,500 a month, which her RM14,000 monthly surplus covers even if the unit sits empty. Sean prefers one RM1 million unit in a top KL location to two RM500,000 units elsewhere.

reasons.title: The contractor wins most flips
reasons.body: Without contacts or experience, contractors will exceed any budget: a RM200,000 gap between a run-down and a renovated terrace vanishes once wiring, pipes or the roof need replacing. Sean has never seen anyone outside the trade make money flipping.

reasons.title: Melaka's high-rise market is weak
reasons.body: Melaka has a population limit, abandoned projects and too many units built for short-term stays, which Penang and some building managements now restrict. Landed homes for own use still do well there, but for high-rise investment Sean points her to KL.

actions: Learn how each kind of loan charges interest, so you can tell a fair return from a scam.
Follow Sean's four steps: set your intent, check your loan eligibility, view 20 properties in your budget, then buy.
Start with a unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million whose market rent covers the instalment.
Have RM50,000 for furnishing plus six months of instalments ready at key collection, and skip auctions for a first purchase.
Keep your job; if you want a business, test the idea cheaply before putting savings into it.
articles.caveat: Buying a landed house in Melaka to renovate and live in for ten years or more is a different matter: bought at the median price, Sean is confident it wouldn't lose money. It is the quick two-year flip he disagrees with.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #304. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #304 | PROPERTY INVESTMENT NEED NOT TO BE RISKY

articles.title: Why hold a property for 35 years instead of selling it?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer plans to sell after five years for a RM100,000 gain and asks why anyone would hold for 35. Sean explains the long equity game and why cash loses to inflation.

question.asker: From Mr. C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr. C is planning his first purchase, a two-bedroom unit in a new Subang Jaya project with strong rent. His plan was to buy where rent covers the instalment and maintenance, then sell after about five years for a gain of perhaps RM100,000. He doubts the long game: older apartments decline, newer projects keep coming, and a RM500 to RM1,000 monthly surplus could turn negative during vacancies or repairs.
question.text: What is the point of holding several properties for 30 to 35 years if they may be hard to rent or sell by then?

answer.quote: Don't be too concerned of cash. Build the asset first.
answer.summary: Flipping is hard now because developers already price in the gains, so Sean holds properties whose rent covers the instalment on zero down payment and lets tenants pay them off. Cash from a sale loses value to inflation while the property keeps pace, though there is no rule that you must hold to the end.

reasons.title: Each RM500 surplus is about RM100,000 of value
reasons.body: A buyer can pay about RM100,000 more and still have rent cover the instalment. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM1 million three years ago with a RM4,000 instalment, should rent for RM5,500 to RM6,000, so he could sell at RM1.2 million to RM1.3 million, but would then have to find somewhere to put the cash.

reasons.title: Cash loses to inflation
reasons.body: Sean puts real inflation at around 10% to 12%, against about 6% from EPF, so cash shrinks every year. Property hedges inflation: rising building costs, higher wages and lower interest rates all lift the value of what existing owners hold.

reasons.title: Older units still rent
reasons.body: Older Mont Kiara units first sold at around RM380,000 to RM420,000 still yield about 5% to 5.5% at today's prices, because not everyone can afford new. Whether new beats old still comes down to location and management.

reasons.title: Tenants and the bank do the work
reasons.body: A break-even portfolio costs Sean about one and a half to two months of instalments a year in agent fees and repairs, roughly five years' worth over a 30-year loan. Five RM300,000 units renting at RM1,500 each would then pay him RM7,500 a month, for working on each unit once or twice a year.

actions: Buy only where rent covers the instalment and maintenance with zero down payment, Sean's strict rule.
Compare the price with the area's median so you never overpay.
Look at 20 different properties across the buying channels before settling on this one.
Use credit for property and put your own capital into other investments.
Judge any gain as a percentage of what you put in, not as a lump sum.
articles.caveat: The plan fails if the unit bleeds, with rent covering only half the instalment. Nor must you hold to the end: if life changes, such as moving overseas, Sean would sell. And if RM100,000 is large against your savings, taking the gain may be the right call for you.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #303. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2025.

articles.title: Our hotel-scheme unit has paid nothing and won't sell. What now?
articles.excerpt: Two siblings bought a serviced apartment leased back to a hotel operator with a guaranteed return. It completed four years late and has paid nothing since. Sean lists the red flags and their few ways out.

question.asker: From Mr K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr K and his sister jointly bought a serviced apartment as an investment, leased back to a hotel operator under a guaranteed rental return. It completed more than four years late; they sued for late delivery and won. The operator, which shared an office with the developer, never paid them; they won judgment against it, but it is a RM2 company. There is still no strata title and no AGM, and unknown companies bill them for utilities and maintenance. They could not find a buyer even at RM210,000 below their purchase price.
question.text: What can they do with a unit that pays nothing and cannot be sold?

answer.quote: not all properties make money
answer.summary: There is no good way out. They can sell at a deeper loss and pay the bank the difference now, or keep paying the loan and wait on a rescue by a bigger developer that may never come. The real lessons are for buyers who have not yet signed for a scheme like this.

reasons.title: Guaranteed returns are priced in
reasons.body: A guaranteed 6% for five years is usually added to the price up front, so a unit worth RM500,000 is sold at about RM650,000 with a large discount. It only works if the operator and developer stay solvent and honest.

reasons.title: If it's so good, why share it?
reasons.body: A developer with a profitable hotel would run it or partner with another developer. Selling rooms to hundreds of buyers is a way to raise cash from people who want an investment with no effort.

reasons.title: You may not control your own unit
reasons.body: In a hotel-run building the key cards are held centrally, so owners often cannot rent their unit out themselves.

reasons.title: Selling below the loan costs cash
reasons.body: If the loan is about RM800,000 and the unit sells for less, the owners must pay the bank the difference in cash. The alternative is to keep paying for years while the unit earns nothing.

actions: Before buying, check that current rents nearby already cover the instalment you will pay at completion.
Avoid guaranteed-rental-return and hotel-leaseback schemes.
Avoid buying jointly with a relative unless each of you can carry the loss alone.
If stuck, work out whether you can afford to sell below the loan before cutting your losses.
Take complaints about a missing joint management body or strata title to the Commissioner of Buildings, and keep legal advice on disputed bills.
articles.caveat: Sean notes the worst case is the developer winding up altogether; while it is still operating, a takeover by a bigger developer remains a slim chance. For other buyers, distressed sellers in such buildings can be an opportunity if the price falls below replacement cost.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #275. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2025. The developer and project are not named here. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.
