articles.title: Can I really buy a property with no money down?
articles.excerpt: Discounts, rebates and cash backs promise a property with no capital. Sean explains how these deals work, and why you still need cash and a strong loan profile to use them.

question.context: Buyers used to need 10% down, and Sean needed nearly RM50,000 to buy his first RM300,000 property. Today developers offer discounts of at least 10%, cash backs and RM500 booking fees, and many young buyers take that to mean property needs no money at all.
question.text: Is a no money down deal really free of money, and who can use one?

answer.quote: You still need money even though it's a zero money down deal.
answer.summary: Only by the end of the deal. You still need cash to get it started and the income to qualify for a loan at the right margin; the "zero" appears only once the bank releases the loan and refunds what you paid.

reasons.title: Subsale deals still need 10% upfront
reasons.body: In a subsale, the deal rests on the gap between the bank's valuation and the price, so that a 90% loan covers the whole purchase. You still pay a 2% earnest deposit and the rest of the 10% at the SPA, refunded only after the loan is released, and you usually cover any extra RPGT the seller pays.

reasons.title: Developers want more than RM500
reasons.body: Established developers usually ask 1% to 3% upfront, often RM5,000 to RM15,000. It is refunded once construction reaches a stage the bank pays for, such as when the foundation is done.

reasons.title: It all depends on a 90% loan
reasons.body: These deals work only if your age, income and record get you a 90% loan. From the third property the margin drops to 70%, which is why discounts of 25% to 30% and cash backs appeared: they fill that gap.

reasons.title: Infinite returns didn't save the old deals
reasons.body: About 11 or 12 years earlier, Sean saw investment clubs sell bulk-purchase units on "infinite returns", since any return divided by zero capital is infinite. None of those properties succeeded.

actions: Keep cash for the booking fee, earnest deposit and balance of the 10%, even when a deal is billed as zero down.
Check that you qualify for a 90% loan before relying on a discount or cash back.
Decide in advance what the capital you keep will do, such as investing it, rather than letting it fund your lifestyle.
Be wary of anyone promising several properties on a fresh graduate's salary.
articles.caveat: Some wealthier buyers, often business owners, prefer to pay 30% to 50% down and borrow less, to save interest or park their cash; Sean sees no right or wrong in that. Using as little of your own money as possible suits someone building several properties, not someone stretching to buy one.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this July 2021 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Loan margins and developer practices are as described in 2021.

articles.title: Is an older Bukit Jalil apartment a good first investment?
articles.excerpt: A 33-year-old with savings and no debts wants a well-kept 1990s subsale unit in Bukit Jalil whose rent already covers the loan. Sean calls it safe, but would look for better options first.

question.asker: From Miss L, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss L is 33, earns RM10,000 to RM13,000 a month, has about RM60,000 in savings, RM50,000 invested and no debts besides RM700 a month in insurance. She once lived as a student in an apartment block built in the late 1990s in Bukit Jalil, and an owner is selling a well-kept 1,200 sq ft unit there for RM455,000, about RM371 per sq ft. Similar units rent for about RM2,200 a month.
question.text: Is this subsale unit a good first investment property?

answer.quote: I will not get it mainly because I have better options.
answer.summary: It is a very safe deal she can afford, and she wouldn't lose money. But Sean wouldn't buy it himself, because the same budget can buy newer units with more room to grow. With no rush, she should negotiate harder and compare all four buying channels first.

reasons.title: The rent already covers the loan
reasons.body: A RM400,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM1,800 to RM1,900 a month, around RM2,000 with maintenance, so today's RM2,200 rent breaks even. It could also let to families, medium-term tenants or students room by room, and Sean's rule is that the more ways a unit can cover its instalment, the better.

reasons.title: Old buildings protect the bottom, not the upside
reasons.body: Across the road, newer Bukit Jalil projects transact at RM900 to RM1,000 per sq ft and some rent for far more. A new building next door underpins an old one's value, but the old one rarely doubles. Sean treats buildings over ten years old as their own category, with their own median price.

reasons.title: Subsale takes real cash
reasons.body: She would need about RM45,500 down and about RM36,000 more for legal and other costs. Sean's own test is to have RM50,000 for renovation plus six months of instalments left over after buying.

reasons.title: The location is strong
reasons.body: Bukit Jalil has a KL address, quick roads to the city, rail links and private universities, which Sean believes keep students living nearby after they graduate. Families from older wealthy areas nearby also help their children buy apartments there.

actions: Before any investment, have six months of expenses as an emergency fund, medical insurance and a clear career path.
Negotiate: offer the price you would be happy with, such as RM400,000, and walk away if the owner refuses.
Compare what the same budget buys through new launch, subsale, auction and bulk purchase.
Compare an older unit's price with the median for older buildings, and a new one's with the median for new buildings.
If you buy, fully furnish the unit so it can be let in every way, from families to room by room.
articles.caveat: If she values certainty and knows the building well, buying it is not wrong: Sean calls it an awesome deal and a very safe route. The only regret would be watching newer projects nearby grow faster over ten to 15 years.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #308. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in March 2026. Sean mentions that he buys bulk-purchase units as a customer of FAR Capital; he does not own the company.

articles.title: Cheap old house or new house with no down payment?
articles.excerpt: An unmarried couple must choose between a cheap 30-year-old house needing renovation and a new one with a bigger instalment. Sean says the real question is whose income the loan depends on.

question.asker: From Winston, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Winston, 34, works in Seremban; his girlfriend, 31, works in KL and does not want to give up her KL salary. They are not yet married, have RM400,000 in savings and earn about RM9,000 a month between them. After viewing more than 12 houses they have two options: a 30-year-old house in a convenient spot for RM338,000 at about RM1,500 a month, needing around RM200,000 for deposit, renovation and furniture; or a new house with zero down payment at about RM3,000 a month.
question.text: Should they spend most of their savings on the old house with the easy instalment, or take the new house with little cash upfront but double the monthly commitment?

answer.quote: You clearly cannot afford the bigger house.
answer.summary: Take the old house, and buy it in one name. On one income, a RM3,000 instalment is out of reach, and counting on a partner who has not committed to living in Seremban is the real risk.

reasons.title: Do not borrow on income you cannot count on
reasons.body: Sean discourages unmarried couples from buying in joint names; some split up before construction even finishes. Split evenly, each earns about RM4,500. That carries RM1,500 a month easily, but RM3,000 only works if she stays in, and she is not yet sure she will.

reasons.title: Compare with the area median, not the new house
reasons.body: RM338,000 against RM700,000 is the wrong comparison. What matters is recent prices in the same taman: if similar houses sold for around RM400,000, RM338,000 is a good buy; at market price it is fine. Just never pay above market without a clear reason.

reasons.title: Renovation does not add its cost to the value
reasons.body: A RM338,000 house plus RM200,000 of renovation is not a RM538,000 house. Valuers look at approved built-up area, such as extended kitchens and bedrooms with approved plans, not at marble or premium finishes. Unapproved extensions can even stop a future buyer getting a loan.

reasons.title: An old house is as good as how it was lived in
reasons.body: A house lived in continuously is usually fine, because problems get fixed as they appear. One left empty for five to ten years needs far more work, as seals and pipes crack once used again. Older layouts, with a staircase in the middle, also feel tighter than new designs.

actions: Agree on the life plan first: where you will both live, and how the household will work after marriage.
Buy in your own name, on your own income; your partner can contribute if she chooses.
Check recent transacted prices in the same taman before making an offer.
Bring a contractor to a second viewing, ask how long the house was empty, and get two or three quotations itemised space by space.
Do the necessities first: structure, wiring, plumbing, roof and toilets. Leave the nice-to-haves until your finances allow.
articles.caveat: If you are married, both committed to Seremban and investing together, the question changes. It becomes whether the RM200,000 would earn more invested elsewhere than the extra RM1,500 a month the new house costs, which Sean leaves for another episode.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #242. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices are as stated in February 2024.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #242 | OLD VERSUS NEW PROPERTY

articles.title: RM700,000: a terrace house in the outskirts or a condo in the city?
articles.excerpt: The same RM700,000 buys a 1,000 sq ft condo in PJ or a double-storey terrace in Seremban or Nilai. Sean weighs commuting time, rental returns, growth, security and family life.

question.context: Seremban, Nilai and other towns outside Kuala Lumpur have become popular with buyers escaping city prices, and many commute daily. With about RM700,000, a buyer can choose a 1,000 sq ft condo in Petaling Jaya or a double-storey terrace of 1,600 to 2,800 sq ft in a gated township further out.
question.text: Which is the better buy: a high-rise in the city or a landed house in the outskirts?

answer.quote: I fancy time and convenience way more than space currently
answer.summary: For Sean at that stage, the city condo, because time and convenience mattered more than space and it rents far better. A landed house in the outskirts suits families who value space and gardens and whose work hours are flexible enough to avoid the daily commute.

reasons.title: Commuting costs hours
reasons.body: From outlying towns, rush-hour commutes take about an hour each way; a friend in Kota Kemuning leaves at six to reach the city. Flexible hours and working from home make the outskirts more workable.

reasons.title: City condos rent far better
reasons.body: A RM700,000 condo in PJ or Mont Kiara rents well when fully furnished. Landed houses outside the city fetch lower rents and cost more to furnish, so owners usually top up the instalment every month.

reasons.title: Doubling landed prices are history
reasons.body: With more developers building landed homes, a terrace bought at RM700,000 rarely doubles any more. For a condo, 10% to 15% over five years is a good result.

reasons.title: Each suits a different family
reasons.body: Landed homes are easier with young children and groceries, with fewer trips between car and door. Condos offer layered security and shared facilities, which some families move into landed-to-high-rise for.

actions: Time the commute from each option at rush hour before deciding.
Decide whether the purchase is to live in, for rent, or for capital growth.
Compare realistic rents for each option against the instalment.
Weigh maintenance fees and how often your family would use the facilities.
Treat claims that landed houses always double with caution.
articles.caveat: Sean's own preference reflects a city-based job in 2019. A family with flexible work, or a well-located gated landed project, may do better in the outskirts.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this October 2019 video, recorded in Seremban. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rental figures in the captions were unclear and are left out.

video.title: LANDED HOUSE OUTSKIRT VS HIGHRISE IN THE CITY

articles.title: My kids are grown. At 44, should I finally buy a home of my own?
articles.excerpt: A 44-year-old whose parents bought property in his name has found an apartment he loves, but worries about savings and a short loan tenure. Sean sets out when to buy and when to rent, using the 85% rule.

question.asker: From JR, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JR married young and is 44; his children are in their 20s and now financially independent. He and his wife each earn about RM140,000 a year. His parents bought several properties in his name and keep the rent, so his finances look odd on paper. He lives in a landed house, has found an apartment he loves, and feels a void at not owning a home himself, but has little savings and a shorter loan tenure ahead.
question.text: Is buying a home at this stage sound, or would renting make more sense?

answer.quote: There is no rush.
answer.summary: Buy if the rent for that apartment covers at least 85% of his instalment and his loan eligibility passes; rent if the rent is well below the instalment. Either way there is no rush: his children are independent and his biggest responsibilities are done.

reasons.title: The 85% rule protects the exit
reasons.body: If current rent for similar units covers about 85% of the instalment, he can rent it out or sell without a loss if his needs change in five years. At his age a loan may run only 25 to 28 more years, depending on the bank's age limit.

reasons.title: Rent in your name counts for loans
reasons.body: Banks recognise rental income with a stamped tenancy agreement, six months of bank statements showing the deposits and the SPA, and the names must match. Rent from units in his name but paid to his parents does nothing for his eligibility.

reasons.title: Renting is cheaper when rent is far below the instalment
reasons.body: If a RM1 million to RM1.2 million unit rents for about RM2,800 but costs RM4,000 to RM5,000 a month to finance, renting is the practical choice; the owner may later offer to sell it to him.

reasons.title: Owning buys certainty
reasons.body: A landlord can sell and ask you to leave, so money spent customising a rented home is lost. Sean found that owning his home brought a peace of mind and pride that renting does not.

actions: Compare rent for similar units in that building with your likely instalment.
Check your loan eligibility, and whether the landed house is in your name and what it is worth.
Have tenants of the units in your name pay into your account, so the rent counts as your income.
Ask your parents to sort out a will or trust for the properties in your name.
Consider charging your working children a modest rent at home, saved towards their own deposit.
articles.caveat: If the apartment's rent already covers the instalment, Sean would simply buy it and treat it as a future investment unit. The advice assumes the purchase leaves comfortable room in the monthly budget.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #276. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in March 2025. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company that furnishes Sean's units.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #276 | IS HOME OWNERSHIP JUST A ROMANTIC FEELING?

articles.title: Should I buy my own place, or wait until I can afford it?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old in oil and gas earns RM11,000 but has only months of savings and likes a new PJ project costing RM3,000 a month. Sean says it is that unit she cannot afford, not property.

question.asker: From Miss L, a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: Miss L is 34 and works in oil and gas, where restructuring is common. She lives in her brother's condo and pays about RM1,500 a month towards its costs; he is now jobless, with a wife and young child. She earns about RM11,000, or RM8,500 net, but after her car, her parents' allowance and her credit card has RM1,500 to RM2,000 left, three to four months of savings and no investments. A new PJ project she likes would cost about RM3,000 a month including maintenance.
question.text: Should she buy that unit for own stay or investment, keep renting, or do something else?

answer.quote: It's not because the market is not ready. You are not ready.
answer.summary: Not now. Her income qualifies for a loan, but what is left each month cannot carry a RM3,000 commitment. Stay put, build savings and income, and when ready, buy a cheaper unit for investment first while she still values flexibility.

reasons.title: It's that unit she can't afford
reasons.body: Banks see RM11,000; they don't see that only about RM2,000 is left after expenses. At RM3,000 a month before renovation and insurance, the PJ unit is out of reach, but a RM300,000 to RM400,000 unit at about RM1,350 to RM1,800 a month would not be.

reasons.title: Savings are the real issue
reasons.body: Losing a job is out of her control; her savings are not. Sean's test is RM50,000 to RM60,000 for the makeover plus six months of costs: about RM68,000 in hand at key collection for a RM3,000-a-month unit.

reasons.title: The RM1,500 is cheap rent
reasons.body: What she pays her brother is cheap rent, and while he is jobless it means far more to him than it would to a landlord. Unless living together is straining things, staying helps him, and she shouldn't ask for the money back.

reasons.title: Single means flexible
reasons.body: Without children she does not need the certainty of her own home, and renting from owners whose units lose money is her best arrangement for now. Sean does encourage women to own an investment unit of their own, rented out until it is needed.

actions: Ask a bank how much you can borrow, using your payslip and EPF statement.
Visit 20 properties within that range, without booking anything.
Build your emergency fund before committing to any purchase.
Work out how to earn RM500 to RM1,000 more a month from your professional skills, not a second job.
When ready, buy for investment first, in a price range where the rent can cover the instalment.
articles.caveat: If she is set on that unit, Sean says it can work if she grows her income and has the savings in place by the time the keys are handed over. And once marriage and children come, the certainty of an own-stay home matters more.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #299. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #299 | TOO BAD YOU JUST CANNOT AFFORD THAT PROPERTY

articles.title: I'm in my 70s. What should my daughter do with our paid-off house?
articles.excerpt: A mother in her 70s has mapped out what her daughter should do with their landed home after she passes. Sean explains why cash and careful plans may not serve the next generation.

question.asker: From Madam X, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Madam X is in her 70s and still teaches private tuition. She and her daughter, in her late 20s, own a freehold landed home in an upmarket area worth about RM1.3 million, bought with a 95% down payment, and keep a flexi loan and some cash for emergencies. The daughter earns about RM3,000 a month plus RM500 from a part-time job, and should clear the remaining loan in about eight years.
question.text: Is it sensible for the daughter, after her mother has passed away, to rent out the house for about RM3,000, buy a RM300,000 to RM350,000 condo near work, and do her own repairs to save money?

answer.quote: Simple life does not come cheap.
answer.summary: Sean wouldn't lock the daughter into a plan. She could simply keep living in the house, and should first work out what she wants; if she does invest, a loan works better than cash, and she should buy as soon as a unit's rent covers its instalment rather than wait.

reasons.title: Cash loses value faster than it seems
reasons.body: Official inflation is about 2.3%, but Sean puts his own at 10 to 11% a year, and fixed deposits pay only around 2%. He suggests keeping three to six months of expenses as an emergency fund and putting the rest into assets you understand.

reasons.title: Property bought in cash is a weak investment
reasons.body: NAPIC data shows landed homes across Malaysia rising about 2 to 3% a year on average, less than EPF or blue chips have returned. Property is also slow to turn into cash: even after you agree a sale, the money takes about six months to arrive.

reasons.title: Property pays when you borrow
reasons.body: It is one of the few assets you can buy with up to 90% financing. The daughter could refinance the paid-off house, or take a loan on a RM300,000 condo now if its rent covers the instalment, and use her savings elsewhere. Sean counts insurance as part of the cost, so loans don't become a burden on the family.

reasons.title: Let the next generation choose
reasons.body: A carefully planned portfolio can become a burden if a child's life goes elsewhere. Sean would rather parents act as the safety net while children find their own goals, and says that time spent earning more is often better than saving on plumbers and electricians.

actions: Keep three to six months of expenses as an emergency fund, and invest the rest in assets you understand, such as index funds, EPF or ASB.
If you buy property to invest, use a loan rather than cash, and count insurance as part of the cost.
Buy an investment unit only if its rent covers the instalment; if it does, there is no need to wait.
Let your children decide what they want before handing them a plan or a property portfolio.
Pay professionals for repairs if your time can earn more than their fee.
articles.caveat: If the daughter has no wish to invest, Sean says she needn't sell or rent out the house at all: she can stay on and avoid new commitments while she builds her career.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #314. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #314 | LEAVING MORE THAN JUST PROPERTY BEHIND

articles.title: Should I sell my paid-off leasehold flat and rent near work instead?
articles.excerpt: A 41-year-old paid off a PJ leasehold apartment now worth less than she paid, and has RM600,000 in cash. Sean says keep it and rent it out, rent near work, and buy only with an investor's eye.

question.asker: From Peggy, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Peggy is 41 and has saved steadily for 20 years. She has fully paid off a leasehold apartment in Petaling Jaya, bought for RM620,000 and now worth about RM600,000, and finds the nearby MRT noisy. She has about RM600,000 in cash, spends RM500 to RM600 a month on commuting and parking, and could rent near work for RM3,000 to RM4,000. Her child may go to university in five to eight years, and her partner lives 30 km away.
question.text: Should she sell the leasehold flat or rent it out, and rent near work or buy another property, new or subsale?

answer.quote: I don't want to fix a temporary problem with a permanent solution
answer.summary: Keep the flat and rent it out rather than sell before an expected upturn. Rent a place near work rather than tie a long loan to a job that may change; if she buys, buy a subsale near work as an investment, with a yield of 6% or more.

reasons.title: Leasehold matters less for high-rise
reasons.body: Owners have converted leasehold blocks to freehold or renewed leases for RM1,000 to RM2,000 each, and Sean doubts any state government will take back occupied land. The real limit is financing, since banks restrict loans on short remaining leases.

reasons.title: Paying off early has trade-offs
reasons.body: It saves interest for someone who would not invest the cash, but rent from a paid-off unit is taxed in full, with no loan interest to deduct. A flexi loan with savings parked in it cuts interest while keeping the cash available.

reasons.title: Refinancing releases less now
reasons.body: A paid-off RM600,000 flat could once release about RM480,000. With cash-out now assessed over 10 years, it is closer to a third of that.

reasons.title: Rent where you work, buy where tenants would
reasons.body: Living near work saves hours and money. The same reason others would rent near offices makes a well-priced unit there a good investment, rented out if she changes job.

actions: Rent out the PJ flat and hold it rather than selling now.
Rent close to your workplace for a year before deciding whether to buy.
Shortlist five to eight properties near your office and work out each yield: monthly rent times 12, divided by price.
Buy only if the yield is 6% or more, and prefer a subsale you can negotiate.
Keep property in your own name so you have security of your own.
articles.caveat: At 41, a loan may run only until 65 or 70, which raises the instalment; this is why Sean judges the purchase by yield rather than by whether rent covers a 35-year instalment.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #263. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2024. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean says he works at.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #263 | RENT WITH THE INTENT OF INVESTMENT

articles.title: Should parents buy property for their children?
articles.excerpt: Some parents pay the down payment on their children's homes; some children ask for their parents' EPF. Sean explains when help teaches responsibility, and when it breeds entitlement.

question.context: Parents who bought homes decades ago, such as a PJ terrace bought for RM120,000 and now worth about RM1.2 million, can afford to help their children buy at today's prices. Sean has heard from children who resent paying for a home their parents chose, and from one who wanted his parents to withdraw their EPF for his second home.
question.text: Should parents buy property for their children, and should children ask them to?

answer.quote: Be accountable for whatever decisions that you make.
answer.summary: Parents can help, but use it to teach: pay the down payment and let the child pay the instalments, as savings for the future. Children should stand on their own feet; borrowing a sum and repaying it is fine, but asking for parents' savings to invest is not.

reasons.title: Paying the instalment teaches responsibility
reasons.body: A friend earning RM4,000 to RM5,000 and living with his parents had a unit bought in his name, the parents paying the down payment. Already paying close to RM2,000 a month for a car, he resented the instalment, but it taught him that commitments must be paid.

reasons.title: Handouts breed entitlement
reasons.body: Sean knows a family where each of six children was given a home. They had no idea what their RM1.6 million semi-D costs, about RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month over 35 years, and came across as arrogant.

reasons.title: Parents' savings aren't yours to risk
reasons.body: If you want your parents' EPF, ask whether you can promise them the 5.5% to 6% a year it earns. Rates, bank rules and government policy can all change, and if the deal fails, the loss falls on their retirement.

reasons.title: Know what a home costs to carry
reasons.body: Sean's rule of thumb: every RM100,000 of loan costs about RM500 a month over 30 years, so a RM1 million condo means RM5,000 a month and an income near RM15,000. A peer on RM6,000 who owns one is most likely being helped.

actions: Parents: if you help, explain why, and present the property as long-term savings rather than a gift.
Children: if you borrow from your parents, borrow a fixed sum and repay it with interest once you can.
Don't ask parents to withdraw EPF or other retirement savings to fund your investment.
Buy within your own means, using the RM500-per-RM100,000 rule to check the instalment.
articles.caveat: For very wealthy families, Sean says it is a different conversation. And many young people now would rather have cash for a business or other ventures than a property bought for them.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this November 2019 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included.

video.title: Should parents buy property for their children?

articles.title: My parents will pay half. Must I buy a home to live in?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor's parents will pay half the price, but only for a home to live in. Sean explains how to protect a one-income household and handle the condition.

question.asker: From Lim, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Lim works in airline healthcare and takes home about RM4,500 a month. She is the household's breadwinner while her husband builds his business. She has RM37,000 in savings and RM19,000 in stocks, and her parents will give the couple RM50,000. She wants to invest in property for passive income, but her parents would rather she buy a home to live in, and have offered to pay half its price.
question.text: Is her money enough, or too risky while her husband's business is unstable? Should she buy new or subsale, and how should she handle her parents' condition?

answer.quote: Keep your money in your savings.
answer.summary: Protect your savings while the household runs on one income, and accept your parents' help graciously. Buy through a channel that needs little cash, and if the condition is a home, choose one that would still rent well.

reasons.title: Her savings are the household's safety net
reasons.body: With one income supporting the family, savings should cover about six months of expenses. Sean's principle is to own property using as little of your own money as possible. On RM4,500, an instalment of about RM1,500 supports a property of roughly RM300,000 to RM380,000.

reasons.title: Subsale and auction need too much cash
reasons.body: A subsale needs about 18% of the price upfront, around RM90,000 on RM500,000, before renovation, which itself costs RM38,000 to RM80,000 for a basic condo. Auction deposits of 5 to 10% are forfeited if the loan fails, and hidden problems such as unpaid fees or title issues make auctions unsuitable for first-timers.

reasons.title: New launches and bulk deals need the least cash
reasons.body: Developers clear leftover units by selling them in bulk to investor groups at 20 to 30% off, sometimes more, because open discounts would anger earlier buyers. Sean buys this way; two such units each pay him around RM1,200 to RM2,500 a month after costs, and the cash back can fund renovation.

reasons.title: Half the price is generous, with strings
reasons.body: Find out the limit (RM300,000? RM500,000?), the intent (most likely that their daughter always has a home of her own), whether they will want a say on location, and whether her husband is comfortable with it. Then judge the home as if you paid full price, because with half paid upfront almost anything looks cash-flow positive.

actions: Keep your savings as an emergency fund, and put the RM50,000 gift in fixed deposits or EPF until there is a plan.
Work out your loan limit, then visit about 20 properties in that range across buying channels.
As a first-timer, skip auction properties.
Ask your parents openly what their offer covers and whether conditions come with it, and discuss it with your spouse.
If you buy a home, choose one whose rent would cover about 85% of the full instalment, so you can rent it out when you move.
articles.caveat: Whether to accept help is personal; Sean says he would rather succeed without his parents' money, but there is no right or wrong. If you decline, the low-cash bulk purchase route still works. Note too that Malaysia's small down payments are unusual: many countries expect around 25%.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #318. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean buys bulk-purchase units through FAR Capital as a paying client, not as its owner. Figures are as stated in August 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #318 | MY PARENTS ARE PAYING HALF FOR MY HOUSE

articles.title: My sight may fail. Keep buying property, or slow down and live?
articles.excerpt: A 31-year-old with two properties has a genetic condition that may affect his sight. His parents urge him to slow down. Sean agrees: pause until the second unit is rented, build reserves, and spend time with family.

question.asker: From S, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: S is 31, single and lives with his parents in a small town, with a stable job and income of about RM7,000 including rent. He has a certified disability: a rare genetic condition that may lead to blindness. He owns a unit in Wangsa Maju whose rent covers its loan but for about RM100 a month, and a unit in Batu Kawan due in 2027 that he plans to rent out. He hopes property could one day fund gene or stem cell therapy.
question.text: Should he keep buying properties for financial security, or take his parents' advice to slow down and enjoy the present?

answer.quote: I am fully agreeable with your parents
answer.summary: Slow down, but don't stop. He can't qualify for another loan until the Batu Kawan unit is rented anyway, so spend the time building reserves and furnishing money, plan for the worst case with his sight, and make time with his family. Buy a third only once he has more than he needs.

reasons.title: Each unit needs a six-month reserve
reasons.body: Sean keeps enough to cover six months of a unit standing empty: about RM10,000 for the Wangsa Maju unit and about RM20,000 for Batu Kawan. With RM30,000 to RM40,000 to furnish the new unit, that is roughly RM80,000 to save.

reasons.title: Plan for the worst case
reasons.body: If his sight failed in two years, would his job still pay, is there support for people with disabilities, and who would care for him if his parents retired? Those answers matter more than a third unit.

reasons.title: A third loan is harder
reasons.body: A third residential loan is capped at 70%, so it needs at least 20% in cash; a commercial title gets 85%. Rent from the new unit counts as income only after six months with a tenancy agreement and SPA.

reasons.title: Time with family is scarce too
reasons.body: Sean missed trips with friends while building his portfolio and can't get those moments back. Parents are not getting younger, and few people regret one less property on their deathbed.

actions: Set aside six months of instalments for each property.
Save RM30,000 to RM40,000 to furnish the Batu Kawan unit before handover.
Work out your income and care needs if your sight deteriorates.
Put spare money into flexible investments such as EPF or fixed deposits rather than another property.
Consider a third property only after the second is rented and reserves are full.
articles.caveat: Sean notes that some people simply enjoy the process of investing and would keep at it regardless; the advice to slow down rests on S's health and family, not on the market.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #260. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in August 2024. The viewer's medical details are kept to what the answer needs. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #260 | TAKE SOME TIME AWAY FROM PROPERTY INVESTMENT

articles.title: Do I need to own a property before I propose?
articles.excerpt: Many young men feel they must buy a home before proposing, and stretch for a landed house to do it. Sean questions the norm, and warns against making a dream home the first property.

question.context: Many of the emails Sean receives come from young men planning to buy their first home before proposing, as many of his friends around 30 have done. The pressure falls hardest on those from other states who already pay rent in Kuala Lumpur, on top of the cost of a car, a ring and a wedding.
question.text: Is it necessary to own a property before proposing, and what kind of first home makes sense for a couple?

answer.quote: please do not have your dream home as your first property
answer.summary: No. It is fine to rent while saving, and if you do buy, buy within your budget rather than a dream home. An RM800,000 landed house needs about RM4,000 a month for 30 years, which can absorb one partner's entire salary and put the relationship under strain.

reasons.title: The norm creates a heavy burden
reasons.body: Car, ring, wedding and home all fall in the same few years. Outstation workers paying rent in Kuala Lumpur find it especially hard to save a deposit as well.

reasons.title: A dream home can take a whole salary
reasons.body: For a couple earning RM4,000 to RM6,000 each, a RM4,000 instalment leaves every other cost, from furnishing to utilities, on one salary.

reasons.title: Smaller first homes are fine
reasons.body: A terrace house has four bedrooms; many couples use one or two. A studio or a cheaper apartment can be a sensible start.

reasons.title: Don't buy jointly before marriage
reasons.body: Sean repeats his warning against buying with a boyfriend or girlfriend. Once engaged and sure of each other, a couple can consider a joint purchase.

actions: Set a budget together for the wedding and the home, and stick to it.
Consider renting, or living with family, while you save after marriage.
Size your first home to the rooms you actually need.
Keep the instalment well within one salary.
Ignore pressure from others about what a couple should own.
articles.caveat: If family support makes a good first home affordable, buying before marriage is a fine start. Sean admits he is no relationship expert and offered this as a discussion.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this November 2019 video, which he framed as an open discussion. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: MUST YOU HAVE A PROPERTY BEFORE YOU PROPOSE?

articles.title: Our family bought units through a property guru. How do we get out?
articles.excerpt: A viewer's parents bought several units through a property guru at the 2018 peak and now pay thousands a month to hold them. Sean explains how the scheme worked and how to decide what to sell.

question.asker: From Miss C, a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: Miss C is 34. In 2017 and 2018 her parents followed property gurus and bought several units at marked-up prices, through compressed loans and with cash back that has since disappeared. The loans are in her and her mother's names, and most carry no MRTA. Her mother, 65 and seriously ill, uses her EPF to cover about RM6,000 to RM7,000 a month after rent. Selling now means a loss, and her father refuses to sell the family's landed house. Miss C has fully paid one unit of her own.
question.text: How deep is the trouble, and what can the family do when selling most of the units means taking a loss?

answer.quote: You are in a bad situation, but not the worst.
answer.summary: Bad, but recoverable. Put every unit into one table to see which can be sold and which must be held, and ask her father to refinance the family house for a standby credit line instead of selling it.

reasons.title: The cash back was never spare money
reasons.body: Guru deals came with large cash back, meant to pay for renovation and to cover the negative cash flow until the next upturn. Sean says many buyers spent it instead and forgot it was borrowed money they still pay interest on.

reasons.title: Compressed loans hid the real risk
reasons.body: Buyers applied for several similar units with different banks at the same time, so the credit system read it as one buyer comparing rates, and all the loans went through. Sean says the system now records each property's address, so this no longer works, but the debt taken on then remains.

reasons.title: A table shows which units to release
reasons.body: Compare each unit's outstanding loan with its current selling price, and its rent with its instalment and maintenance. Where the loan is close to the selling price, sell to exit. Where the rent covers the instalment, hold. Where a sale would still need a top-up, hold unless you can afford the difference.

reasons.title: Without cover, debt passes to the family
reasons.body: With no MRTA, the loans fall on the family rather than being cleared if the borrower dies. Sean says the point of property investing is to help the family, so every loan should come with mortgage cover such as MRTA or MLTA.

actions: List every unit with its outstanding loan, current market price, instalment plus maintenance, and rent, and update the list every quarter.
Sell the units whose loan is close to their selling price, and hold those whose rent already covers the instalment.
Refinance a fully owned home for an overdraft rather than selling it. On a RM1 million house at 60%, that is about RM600,000 of standby credit, charged daily only on what you use.
Rent out any unit you own outright and live with family for now; Sean estimates RM1,000 to RM2,000 a month to put towards the shortfall.
Give each unit to an agent who specialises in that area, instead of one company for all of them, which may sit on the listings.
articles.caveat: The sell-or-hold rules assume the family can keep paying while they wait; if no one can cover the shortfall, losses have to be taken sooner. Sean also points out that the parents' own savings, which the message doesn't mention, could change the picture.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #296. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in September 2025; his rough estimate of the portfolio's total debt is left out.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #296 | GETTING OUT OF MULTIPLE SUBMISSION MESS?

articles.title: How do you know a project is not overpriced?
articles.excerpt: Projects borrow the name of a famous neighbourhood to charge its prices. Sean walks through the research that shows what an address is really worth.

question.context: Most buyers research a property by scrolling a listings portal. Developers know it, and borrow the name of a famous neighbourhood: projects next to Mont Kiara or Dutamas market themselves as part of it. Buyers end up paying the famous address's price without getting its tenants or its rents.
question.text: What research do you need to do to know whether a project is priced right?

answer.quote: We got to know the location inside out.
answer.summary: Go beyond the listing. Work out where the real neighbourhood ends, which tier of tenant it attracts, and compare the project only against like-for-like transacted prices: new against new, old against old, in the same tier.

reasons.title: A borrowed name does not bring borrowed rents
reasons.body: In June 2024, older projects in the Dutamas area averaged RM538 per sq ft outside Dutamas proper against RM818 inside it, and newer ones about RM641 against roughly RM1,070. Five minutes apart, the tenants and the premiums they will pay are completely different.

reasons.title: Know which tier you are buying into
reasons.body: Tier 1 areas such as Mont Kiara, Dutamas, KLCC and Bangsar South draw expatriates and have no real ceiling on rent. Tier 2 areas such as TTDI and Kota Damansara attract well-off locals; prices per sq ft can be similar, but rents hit a ceiling. Tier 3 is further out, with landed homes under RM500,000.

reasons.title: Compare new with new and old with old
reasons.body: At the same rent, about 95% of tenants will choose the newer unit, so buying new at an old unit's price is close to a sure win. For older Dutamas projects, the session suggested not paying above RM700 per sq ft, or RM550 in the surrounding areas.

reasons.title: Make sure two rental plans break even
reasons.body: Whole-unit leases, short stays and room-by-room rental each suit different tiers. Sean's one-plus-one in Mont Kiara earns RM5,000 from a single tenant but would make about RM4,000 by the room. Short-stay occupancy data showed demand only in Dutamas and Mont Kiara proper.

actions: Walk the area and map where the real neighbourhood ends, whatever the project calls itself.
Pull recent transacted prices, not asking prices, and find the median for your tier, split into new and old.
Aim to buy below that median. Sean bought in Mont Kiara at about RM900 per sq ft, roughly 20% below completed transactions near RM1,100.
Before buying, confirm at least two ways of renting the unit that would each cover the instalment.
Visit the site: a portal cannot show you access roads, traffic or what is being built next door.
articles.caveat: The tier system and price ceilings come from research by FAR Capital, the deal-sourcing company Sean buys through as a paying member, presented in a June 2024 live session. They are a snapshot of one area; repeat the work for your own location rather than reusing the numbers.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this episode, which recaps a live research session with FAR Capital. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Price data is as of June 2024. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

video.title: RESEARCH WORK REQUIRED BEFORE BUYING A PROPERTY

articles.title: Which taxes do I pay when I own and sell property?
articles.excerpt: Beyond the price, owners pay stamp duty, assessment, quit rent and RPGT, and income tax decides whether you can borrow at all. Sean goes through the five.

question.context: Investors often work out their profit as the selling price minus the buying price. Sean says that leaves out five taxes that change what a property really costs and earns, and that young investors should understand them before buying.
question.text: Which taxes should a property buyer in Malaysia budget for?

answer.quote: You need proof that you have money to buy.
answer.summary: Five: stamp duty when you buy, assessment and quit rent every year you own it, RPGT when you sell at a gain, and income tax. For a young buyer, income tax matters first, because a declared income is the proof a bank lends on.

reasons.title: Declared income is what banks lend on
reasons.body: Under-declaring income saves tax but blocks loans; Sean has seen hawkers forced to borrow other people's names and payslips. Someone declaring RM36,000 a year won't get a loan for a RM500,000 house, and paying a large sum in cash instead can draw questions from the Inland Revenue Board.

reasons.title: Stamp duty comes twice, in cash
reasons.body: Buyers pay stamp duty on the transfer and again on the loan agreement, in cash, which surprises many first-time buyers. The transfer scale rises in bands from 1%; Sean uses about 2.5% of the price as a quick estimate.

reasons.title: Two taxes recur every year
reasons.body: Assessment tax (cukai pintu) goes to the local council for street lights, drains and rubbish collection, charged as a percentage of the rent the council sets, which varies by council and property type. Quit rent (cukai tanah) goes to the state, and strata owners pay it too.

reasons.title: Selling has its own rules
reasons.body: RPGT is charged on your gain when you sell, at rates the government changes to cool or warm the market, and foreigners pay more. Legal fees, agent fees and improvements can be deducted. Sell many properties quickly and the Inland Revenue Board may treat it as a business and tax the gain as income, which Sean puts at up to 24%.

actions: Declare your full income and pay tax on it, so you can prove to a bank what you earn.
Budget for stamp duty on both the transfer and the loan agreement as cash, on top of the down payment.
Include assessment and quit rent in your yearly holding costs.
Keep receipts for legal fees, agent fees and improvements to reduce RPGT when you sell; you can file it yourself rather than rely on the lawyer's figure.
If you trade several properties, space out your sales; Sean says some investors sell no more than one a year.
articles.caveat: The rates Sean mentions date from late 2019 and RPGT and stamp duty rules have changed since, so check the current ones. An owner who keeps one home for the long term may never face RPGT or the business-income rules.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this December 2019 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included, and tax rates have changed since 2019.

video.title: 5 TAXES TO PAY IN PROPERTY INVESTMENT

articles.title: If my rental loses RM400 a month, isn't a fixed deposit better?
articles.excerpt: A viewer works out that a zero-down condo yielding 5% still costs RM400 a month after maintenance, and asks why not use fixed deposits or EPF instead. Sean explains why leverage changes the sum.

question.asker: From George, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: George's example: a RM480,000 Klang Valley condo bought with a full loan and nothing down, an instalment of about RM2,100, rent of RM2,000 fully furnished and maintenance of RM300. That leaves a shortfall of about RM400 a month, nearly RM10,000 a year for two such units, before wear and tear. Fixed deposits pay about 3.5% and EPF about 5.5%, and Klang Valley condo prices have been flat for a decade.
question.text: Why is property still a good investment against fixed deposits or EPF, is the shortfall just forced saving, and who can manage repairs and tenants for an investor with several units?

answer.quote: if it's without leverage it wouldn't be interesting at all
answer.summary: Compared without a loan, fixed deposits and EPF would win. But property is bought with the bank's money: with nothing or little down, the tenant pays RM24,000 a year into your loan while you cover a few thousand, and that rent also counts as income for the next loan. Just don't buy a unit whose known rent can't cover the instalment.

reasons.title: Measure return on your own cash
reasons.body: A RM500,000 subsale needs about RM100,000 in cash. At a 5% yield it earns about RM25,000 a year, a 25% return on that cash, against about RM3,500 if the same RM100,000 sat in a fixed deposit.

reasons.title: Look at what the tenant pays
reasons.body: In George's example, two units collect about RM48,000 a year in rent that pays down the loans, against a shortfall of about RM10,000. Over a 35-year loan, a RM500,000 unit costs about RM945,000 in total, most of it paid by tenants.

reasons.title: Rents are easy to check before buying
reasons.body: Portals show what neighbours rent for, so in an established area there is little excuse for buying where rent falls short. Rent of 5.4% or more covers a 4% loan; for an own-stay home, Sean's 85% rule is the minimum.

reasons.title: Prices are moving where you look
reasons.body: Sean sees strong launches in Johor and rising demand in Desa ParkCity, Mont Kiara and Cheras, even if some areas stay flat. Median prices have risen about 4% a year, and building costs jumped 28% to 32% in a year.

actions: Check the rents of neighbouring units on property portals before you buy.
Compare your yield with your own cash invested, not the full price.
Park spare cash in a flexi loan account rather than a fixed deposit when the loan rate is higher.
Declare rental income so it supports your next loan application.
Use a pay-per-job property manager rather than one taking 10% of rent on a new unit.
articles.caveat: Leverage cuts both ways: a wrong calculation or a purchase made out of fear of missing out takes years to recover from. Sean is not a licensed financial adviser.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #265. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in November 2024. Sean recommends The Makeover Guys and its management arm Cozy Homes, whose product he helped develop, and says he had just applied for a loan on a purchase through FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club he is a member of.

articles.title: Out of bankruptcy at 41. Should I take a loan to rebuild my credit?
articles.excerpt: Made bankrupt by a business loan taken in his name 20 years ago, a 41-year-old has just been discharged. A bank suggests a 20% personal loan to build his credit score. Sean says wait, and fix the monthly gap first.

question.asker: From Ed, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Twenty years ago, Ed's father took a RM675,000 business loan in Ed's name; the business failed and Ed was made bankrupt. He was discharged in July 2024 and was told the system would take about 12 months to clear him. He is 41 and takes home RM4,700; after a car loan in his wife's name, RM1,200 rent, bills and the minimum payment on about RM30,000 of her credit card debt, the couple ends each month in the red, with no savings.
question.text: How can he rebuild his credit score, should he take a 20,000 ringgit personal loan at 20% to do it, or a 30,000 ringgit loan to clear his wife's cards, and how does he start over?

answer.quote: just wait for 12 months
answer.summary: Don't take the personal loan. Wait the 12 months, apply for a credit card when he can and use it responsibly, and meanwhile close the monthly gap by earning more and spending less. Borrowing at 20% to clear 18% card debt only moves the debt from one name to another.

reasons.title: 20% is a terrible rate
reasons.body: Housing loans cost about 4% and fixed deposits pay about 3.8%. A seven-year personal loan at 20% costs more than the credit card debt it would replace. Personal loans are easy to get because they are the most lucrative product for banks.

reasons.title: Credit is rebuilt by waiting
reasons.body: Keep the release documents from the insolvency department safe. Once the record clears, a credit card approval is the sign that banks trust you again; that is the time to start building a score.

reasons.title: Every expense is negotiable
reasons.body: Sean asks whether a cheaper room, an older car, ride-hailing in spare hours or a job for his wife could each add a few hundred ringgit, with every saving going to the card debt. When Sean was in trouble, he dropped his insurance and relied on public healthcare for a time.

reasons.title: Never lend your name
reasons.body: Don't take out a loan or stand guarantor for anyone, even family. Property investors should also carry life cover, such as MLTA or MRTA, so their loans don't pass to their heirs.

actions: Wait out the 12 months rather than borrowing to build a score.
Pay more than the minimum on the card debt with every ringgit saved or earned.
Look at a cheaper room, a cheaper car or extra work to close the monthly gap.
Consider AKPK for the card debt if payments become impossible, knowing it freezes the cards.
Ask for a promotion or a better-paid job once your record is clear.
articles.caveat: Sean is not a licensed financial planner and speaks from his own experience of debt; he asked qualified viewers to offer help. Buying a home can wait until the debt is under control.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #266. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in November 2024. The viewer wrote that the stress had left him thinking of ending his life; if you are struggling, Befrienders Kuala Lumpur offers free, confidential support on 03-7627 2929. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #266 | JUST GOT OUT OF BANKRUPTCY

articles.title: Should I refinance or sell my rental unit to clear RM70,000 of debts?
articles.excerpt: A 35-year-old's first unit rents for well above its instalment, but the owner also owes RM70,000 on credit cards and personal loans. Sean compares refinancing, selling and other loan routes, and why bad debt is the real problem.

question.asker: From James, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: James is 35 and has held a first property for more than eight years. It is worth about RM430,000, with about RM270,000 left on the loan and an instalment of RM1,330, and rents for RM2,100 a month. James also owns a second property, and over the years has run up about RM70,000 in credit card and personal loan debt, without ever paying late.
question.text: Should James refinance the unit to clear the debts, or sell it to clear them and free a 90% loan slot for another purchase?

answer.quote: personally I prefer refinancing
answer.summary: Refinancing is better than selling a unit that pays its way every month, but under the newer cash-out rules a conventional refinance may release only about RM30,000, and the existing debts may also hold back approval. So check every route, and settle the high-interest debt quickly even if that means selling.

reasons.title: The debts cost four times the mortgage
reasons.body: Credit cards charge about 15% to 18% a year and personal loans roughly 5% to 10%, against about 4% for a housing loan. Swapping one for the other saves a lot, which is why refinancing appeals.

reasons.title: Refinancing now releases less
reasons.body: Banks lend up to 80% of value, here about RM344,000, which once meant roughly RM74,000 in cash. Now the cash-out portion is assessed over 10 years rather than 35, so only about a third, around RM30,000, may be available; the existing debts also weigh on the debt service ratio.

reasons.title: Selling gives up a good asset
reasons.body: A quick sale at about RM400,000 would leave about RM130,000 after the loan, enough to clear the debts with RM60,000 to spare. But the unit has risen about 35% in eight years and the tenant pays more than the instalment.

reasons.title: This is good debt against bad
reasons.body: Housing loans are hard to get because they buy assets; cards and personal loans are easy because banks profit from them, and they are the leading cause of bankruptcy among young Malaysians.

actions: Look up current rates for credit cards, personal loans, fixed deposits and housing loans.
Ask your bank how much a refinance would actually release under the new cash-out rules.
Compare a mortgage refinance from an insurer-linked lender, which may assess income more leniently but costs more.
Settle the card and personal loan debts first, even by selling if no refinance works.
Find out what caused the debts before buying another property.
articles.caveat: The rules Sean describes are as of late 2024 and he expects them to tighten. Buyers who keep their 90% loan slots full can still buy through bulk purchase, commercial titles or larger down payments.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #270. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2024. Sean refers the viewer to a friend who arranges insurer-linked home loans. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #270 | SELLING PROPERTY TO SETTLE PERSONAL DEBTS

articles.title: When does refinancing my housing loan make sense?
articles.excerpt: Refinancing can lower your rate, release equity, win back a 90% loan or clear expensive debt. Rena Choong explains each use, and the valuation and income tests that decide whether yours works.

question.context: Once owners have a loan or two running, many start asking about refinancing: moving their housing loan to a new bank, or topping it up with the same one. In this episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong what refinancing can do, and when it can't.
question.text: What can refinancing a housing loan achieve, and how do you know whether yours qualifies?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: It's really no brainer for you to do so.
answer.summary: Refinance only with a clear purpose: a lower rate, cash from equity you have built, a 90% loan quota back, or clearing high-interest debt. Whether it works depends on the bank's valuation and your income today. If you pay around 4.5% and a bank covers the switching costs, Rena calls it a no-brainer.

reasons.title: Refinancing lends 80%, not 90%
reasons.body: Most banks refinance up to 80% to 85% of the bank's valuation; only two offer 90%. A RM500,000 unit with RM450,000 still owed after ten years and valued at RM550,000 allows at most RM440,000, so there is nothing to cash out. Equity usually builds only after five to eight years, sooner on landed homes and units bought without a mark-up.

reasons.title: Cashing out has its own income test
reasons.body: Banks don't count rent toward a refinance, and they test the cash-out portion as if it were repaid over ten years, though it actually runs over the full tenure. If your income has fallen since you bought, cashing out will be hard.

reasons.title: A small rate cut adds up
reasons.body: Owners who borrowed years ago may still pay around 4.5% when new loans start at about 3.85% to 4.1%, and over 35 years even 0.1% matters. Switching banks normally costs legal fees, valuation and 0.5% stamp duty on the loan, about RM10,000 on RM500,000, but in 2023 one bank was covering all three for loans up to RM3.5 million.

reasons.title: Consolidate bad debt, never restructure
reasons.body: Debt consolidation moves personal loans (12% to 15% for most borrowers), credit card balances (18%) and hire purchase into a housing-backed loan at about 4.5% to 5%, even when your DSR is over the limit, provided the valuation covers it. Restructuring or rescheduling a loan instead leaves a mark in CCRIS that stops banks lending to you.

actions: Decide first why you are refinancing: a lower rate, cash out, a 90% quota back, or clearing debt.
Ask for the property's current valuation and your redemption sum; 80% of the valuation minus what you owe is roughly the most you can take out.
Compare banks on rate, valuation and switching costs, including any that pay the legal fees, valuation and stamp duty for you.
If you and a spouse, sibling, parent or child keep buying, consider refinancing one property into the higher earner's name so the other regains a 90% loan.
Avoid cashing out for a car or other spending; use it for assets or to clear expensive debt.
articles.caveat: A refinance is a new loan, not free money, and you must qualify for it again. If an overspending habit caused the debt, consolidation only resets it. Refinancing into an insurance company's fixed-rate term loan keeps it out of CCRIS, so banks still offer 90% on your next purchase, but the rate is above the market and you must buy MLTA and other policies.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for an August 2023 episode of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage. The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Rates, margins and bank offers are as stated in 2023 and differ between banks. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: What renovation mistakes should I avoid when I get my keys?
articles.excerpt: Sean watches a Singapore couple's list of renovation regrets and adds what he has learnt fitting out units. Cracks, lights, switches, power points, aircon piping and tile lines are the usual culprits.

question.context: With many viewers getting their keys around New Year, Sean reviews a video in which a Singapore couple list their renovation regrets, and adds his own experience from architecture and from furnishing investment units in Malaysia.
question.text: Which renovation details do new owners most often get wrong, and how can they be avoided?

answer.quote: two-way switch is very very useful
answer.summary: Plan the details that are expensive to undo: where lights hang over furniture, where switches and power points go, how aircon piping runs, and how tiles line up. Most regrets come from fixing these before the furniture and daily routine are known.

reasons.title: Different materials crack where they meet
reasons.body: Joints between timber, brick, concrete, steel and glass crack as buildings move slightly. Wire mesh under the plaster helps; otherwise expect hairline cracks to return after repainting. A crack in a beam is a different and serious matter.

reasons.title: Measure furniture before fixing lights
reasons.body: A pendant fixed over the planned dining spot ends up off-centre once a sideboard arrives. Allow about 90 cm of walking clearance, and measure large pieces before buying.

reasons.title: Switches and sockets by where you use them
reasons.body: Two-way switches, or a bedside lamp, save getting up to switch off the light. A master bedroom needs three or four power points in the right places, plus one near a mirror for a hair dryer.

reasons.title: Ready aircon points save trouble
reasons.body: Adding aircon later means boxing up piping and running new wiring, often across bathrooms or ceilings. Units handed over with aircon points and trunking save money and mess.

actions: Decide your furniture layout before fixing lighting points.
Add two-way switches or bedside lighting in bedrooms.
Place power points where you will use devices, rather than adding more.
Agree the aircon piping route with the installer before work starts.
Ask the tiler to start from the floor trap and align grout lines between walls and floors.
articles.caveat: The regrets come from a Singapore flat, so some details differ in Malaysian units. If budget allows, an interior designer can coordinate separate contractors so finishes match.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this December 2022 video, in which he reacts to a Singapore couple's renovation video; the regrets listed are theirs, and the advice is Sean's commentary. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he mentions.

articles.title: My father needs a lift. Should I rent a home, or buy one now?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old engineer earning RM5,000 lives with his parents in a Penang walk-up, and his father now needs a wheelchair. Sean says rent a place with a lift now, and that his goal of three properties can wait.

question.asker: From Sam, a viewer from Penang who wrote in by email
question.context: Sam is 27, an engineer earning RM5,000 a month, and lives with his parents in a walk-up public housing flat in Penang. His father's health has worsened and he now needs a wheelchair. Renting a home with a lift would cost RM1,000 to RM1,500 a month; buying would mean about RM400,000 or more on Penang Island, using up his loan eligibility. He had set himself Sean's goal of three properties.
question.text: Should he rent a place with a lift, or buy one and give up his goal of owning three properties?

answer.quote: I think you should rent first
answer.summary: Rent a place with a lift now, since his father cannot wait for a purchase to complete, and rent out the walk-up to offset it. Put property investment aside until he has an emergency fund, insurance and more income; the three properties are meant to come about one a decade, not now.

reasons.title: Buying can't solve it quickly
reasons.body: A subsale takes five to six months and about 18% of the price in cash, around RM72,000 on RM400,000, plus RM20,000 to RM30,000 for renovation. A new launch takes three to four years. Renting works almost at once.

reasons.title: Three properties over 20 years
reasons.body: Sean's goal is one at about 28, one at 38 and one at 48, as income grows. Judging the future by today's salary undersells what a career can earn.

reasons.title: Investing needs three things first
reasons.body: Six months of expenses saved, covering the parents who depend on him; insurance for himself as the breadwinner; and a clear career path. Property is not a guaranteed win.

reasons.title: RM5,000 is not a low income
reasons.body: Sean says Sam earns about the average and should stop calling himself low-income. The better question is how to add RM500 or RM1,000 a month.

actions: Rent a unit with a lift for your father now.
Rent out the walk-up flat to cover part of the new rent.
Build six months of family expenses in savings and get insurance for yourself.
Find ways to earn an extra RM500 to RM1,000 a month from your professional skills.
Revisit buying once you have about RM100,000 set aside and a higher income.
articles.caveat: If he already had about RM100,000 in savings, buying an affordable subsale with a lift could make sense; Sean would not count a family home bought out of need as wasted loan eligibility.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #258. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in August 2024.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #258 | SHOULD I GIVE UP IF I HAVE LOW INCOME?

articles.title: Can a rent-to-rent deal help me build a portfolio fast?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old earning about RM3,000 plans to use an agency's rent-to-rent guarantee to buy two units within a year. Sean explains why the plan, not the property, is the problem.

question.asker: From a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: He is 26, works in logistics and takes home about RM3,000 a month, with no commitments besides a credit card. He plans to buy a four-bedroom freehold unit due in 2028 with RM20,000 down and about RM1,900 a month in instalment and maintenance. An agency has offered a rent-to-rent contract: it would rent the unit from him for three, five or ten years at 10% below the market rate, and he could not use the unit in that time.
question.text: Should he use the rent-to-rent guarantee on a completed unit now, so its rent helps him buy a second property within six to 12 months?

answer.quote: Don't buy this. Not because of the property, not because of the deal.
answer.summary: No. Sean's problem is not the project or the scheme but the rush: on a RM3,000 income he is not ready to carry one property, let alone two, and a guarantee does not make an investment safe.

reasons.title: Guarantees sell to fear and laziness
reasons.body: Like the guaranteed rental return schemes before it, rent-to-rent answers buyers' fear of not finding a tenant and their wish to avoid the hassle. Sean says that if those two things worry you, property investment is not for you, and FD, EPF or a money market fund would suit you better.

reasons.title: The contract decides everything
reasons.body: Is the guaranteed rent gross or net of management costs? Who signs: the developer, a company set up for the purpose, or an agency? An agency a few years old promising rent for ten years, a market rate nobody has defined and no terms for delays, defects or a market fall are all warning signs.

reasons.title: One unit already takes half his income
reasons.body: At about RM1,900 a month, a single unit takes more than half of a RM3,000 income. If he lost his job and his tenant in the same month, a second unit would leave him asking his parents to pay the mortgage.

reasons.title: The guarantee is priced in
reasons.body: Sean says such agencies make their money by taking units from the developer in bulk and pricing them up, so the rent they pay you is often built into what you paid. You also give away the unit's best rental years, roughly years three to ten, and get back an older unit when the contract ends.

actions: Don't sign yet; first ask yourself why you are in such a hurry to build a portfolio.
Before buying, set aside RM50,000 to furnish the unit plus six months of instalments, Sean's test of whether you can afford it.
Research the rents and prices of surrounding projects yourself instead of relying on a guarantee.
Read any rent-to-rent or guaranteed-rent contract for who signs, gross versus net rent, the start date, and what happens if the project is late or the market falls.
Compare deals across all four channels, new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase, before buying at retail price.
articles.caveat: Sean says a buyer earning around RM30,000 a month can afford this kind of risk; at RM3,000 the margin for mistakes is too small. And a packaged deal is not bad in itself: when the package still comes at or below the standard market price, it can be worth taking.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #319. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in September 2026. Sean mentions that in an earlier role he promoted guaranteed-rental schemes himself.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #319 | THIS A NEW GRR SCHEME IN TOWN?

articles.title: Should I rent or buy? Why not rent my home and buy to invest?
articles.excerpt: Young people argue over whether to rent or buy. Sean says do both: rent where you want to live for flexibility, and buy elsewhere as an investment that earns rent.

question.context: Young people often debate whether renting is wasted money or buying ties them down. In 2018 condos were oversupplied, so owners competed for tenants, while buying was still seen as a hedge against inflation and, among some Chinese families, a sign a man is ready for marriage.
question.text: Is it better to rent or to buy a home?

answer.quote: why not do both
answer.summary: Do both. Rent the home you live in for flexibility and value, and buy property as an investment that earns rent. Your home need not be the property you own; there is no rush to buy a home, but there is a rush to start investing.

reasons.title: Renting keeps you flexible
reasons.body: Early in a career you may move between Johor, Seremban and Kuala Lumpur. Renting lets you live near work without tying up capital in one place.

reasons.title: Tenants have the upper hand
reasons.body: With oversupply, owners struggling with instalments will negotiate and add furnishing such as aircon and water heaters. About RM3,000 can rent a home worth RM2 million that would cost about RM10,000 a month to own.

reasons.title: Buying protects against inflation
reasons.body: Money buys less each year, while property tends to rise with demand, depending on location and the economy. An investment property works for you through other people's money and time.

reasons.title: Investors often rent their own homes
reasons.body: Many investors Sean knows own several units that earn rent, yet rent a luxurious apartment for themselves at a fraction of its ownership cost.

actions: Rent close to your work while your career is still settling.
Negotiate rent and furnishing at each renewal.
Start learning how rental investment works, including the hidden costs.
Buy an investment unit whose rent covers its costs, separate from where you live.
Compare today's prices with those of five years ago to judge the cost of waiting.
articles.caveat: Owning brings costs and paperwork renting doesn't: maintenance, assessment tax, quit rent, and the effort of buying and selling. In Germany and much of Europe, renting long-term is the norm and tenants are better protected.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this October 2018 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: BUY OR RENT?! WHY NOT BOTH??

articles.title: I sold my business at 40. Live on rent, or buy more properties?
articles.excerpt: A 40-year-old sold his nursing homes to escape the stress and parked the proceeds in his flexi loans. His eight properties leave RM11,700 a month after instalments. Sean says live on it, and don't buy more.

question.asker: From Mr Tan, a viewer from Penang who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Tan is 40, a Chinese physician who ran three nursing homes until the round-the-clock emergencies left him close to depression; he has now sold them. He owns eight properties, one to live in and seven rented out, with RM3.2 million in loans running to age 70, all semi-flexi. He has put the sale proceeds into the loan accounts to save interest. Rent exceeds instalments by about RM11,700 a month, and his family of four, including his 72-year-old mother and five-year-old son, spends RM5,000 to RM6,000.
question.text: Should he live on the rental surplus, or withdraw from his flexi loans to buy more properties before he loses his business income for loan applications?

answer.quote: personally my choice will be option one
answer.summary: Live on the surplus and don't buy more. Eight properties already pay him more than his family spends, the loans are being paid down by tenants, and the priority now is his health and time with his son.

reasons.title: The portfolio already works three ways
reasons.body: Malaysian property has averaged about 4% a year in price growth, the RM11,700 surplus is a top-20% income on its own, and every month's rent pays down the loans to build equity.

reasons.title: Parking cash in a flexi loan was right
reasons.body: With a semi-flexi loan, interest is charged only on the balance after his deposits, yet the money can still be withdrawn in an emergency for a small fee.

reasons.title: He can sell one when he needs cash
reasons.body: Selling one unit every five years would fund him for decades. Sean suggests setting about RM1 million aside for his son, and still has more than enough left.

reasons.title: Investing early bought the choice
reasons.body: Had the business income gone on luxuries instead of property, he could not have walked away. Money's purpose is health, freedom and peace.

actions: Live on the rental surplus and keep the flexi-loan cash as a buffer.
See a specialist about the low mood, and rebuild physical health with exercise.
Spend the years before your child starts school with him.
If you want to run the portfolio as a business later, consider an investment holding company.
Ignore criticism from people who don't live the life you want.
articles.caveat: Sean notes that banks now lend investment holding companies only about 60%, so a company structure suits running the portfolio rather than raising more loans.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #267. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in November 2024. The episode is sponsored by Versa, a savings app.
