articles.title: We'll retire with six properties. What should we sell, and when?
articles.excerpt: A couple of 50 and 54 plan to retire in 2032, sell their shop lot and landed home, pay off two apartments and buy a small unit near the MRT. Sean says the plan works, but decide what retirement means first.

question.asker: From Madam Y, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Madam Y is 50 and her husband 54; they plan to retire in 2032 with about RM1 million in EPF. They own a three-storey shop lot worth about RM2.1 million whose rent falls short of its instalment, the cluster home they live in, worth about RM1 million, and two rented apartments. They also paid the renovation on below-market apartments for each of their two daughters, who pay the instalments, which the rent would cover. At retirement they want to downsize to an apartment near the MRT, close to their daughters.
question.text: Should they sell the shop lot and cluster home, pay off the two apartments and buy a small unit in cash, or keep some properties for rent?

answer.quote: Plans should be drawn on sand instead of carved in stones.
answer.summary: The plan is sound and would leave them debt-free with about RM3,300 a month in rent. But first decide what retirement means: stopping completely or slowing down. If they keep some income, there is no need to sell much, and with seven years to go they can sell gradually, when the market is good.

reasons.title: Stopping work changes the whole plan
reasons.body: At 61, Sean would slow down rather than stop. Half an income means the properties that pay for themselves can stay; zero income means selling more. Many people who retire early find themselves bored and restless.

reasons.title: Know what the money is for
reasons.body: Property is a tool for reaching goals, such as travelling while you are still fit or helping family. Without a goal, RM3,300 a month and RM500,000 in cash is comfortable but not life-changing, so it is worth deciding what you want before you sell.

reasons.title: Timing the sale can add value
reasons.body: Sean expects lower interest rates and new rail lines to lift the market in the next few years. A shop lot worth RM2.1 million today might fetch RM2.5 million by 2032, and if rents rise to cover its instalment, they might prefer to keep it.

reasons.title: Their daughters' homes are a good lesson
reasons.body: Buying below market value let them borrow the full amount and spend cash on furnishing, so the units can be rented for more than the instalment. Sean's only worry is that the commitment may tie a daughter down before she has seen the world.

actions: Agree with your spouse whether retirement means stopping completely or slowing down.
List what you want the money to do in retirement, such as travel, family or health.
Sell progressively, starting with the asset that costs you money each month, and watch the market as rates fall.
Before buying the downsizing apartment, test the car park ramps, the walk from lift to unit, the refuse area and where the MRT line actually takes you.
Build hobbies, friends and fitness before you stop work.
articles.caveat: If they need a large sum for something specific, such as a long trip, selling is fine. As for the Sunway project near the MRT, Sean thinks it is a reasonable own-stay choice from a reputable developer in a mature area, though not one to expect big profits from.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #292. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Values and rents are the viewer's own estimates, and Sean's 2032 figures are guesses. Figures are as stated in August 2025.

articles.title: Moving home to retire: keep, sell or refinance our two houses here?
articles.excerpt: A family returning after 20 years abroad owns a landed house in Desa ParkCity and a stagnant leasehold townhouse in PJ. Sean says keep the first, sell the second, and choose a home by the life they want back.

question.asker: From Z, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Z's family has worked overseas for about 20 years and plans to retire in Malaysia, selling their overseas home first. They own a freehold landed house in Desa ParkCity, which has risen a lot and earns rent, and a leasehold townhouse in Petaling Jaya whose value has been flat for four or five years; both still have loans. As non-residents they pay a 30% flat tax on rent.
question.text: Should they sell or refinance the townhouse to buy a condo for rent and appreciation, or a landed home to retire in, and does a landed house in Desa ParkCity still have room to grow?

answer.quote: if I'm in your shoes I will sell the townhouse
answer.summary: Keep the Desa ParkCity house: its rent already covers the loan, it costs nothing to hold, and gated landed homes there remain in demand. Sell the flat-priced leasehold townhouse while it can still fetch its value, then decide whether that money builds more investments or buys the home they want to retire in.

reasons.title: Don't sell what costs nothing to hold
reasons.body: Selling only makes sense if they need the cash or a loan slot, which they don't. Cash loses about 5% a year to inflation, while the property preserves its value; if they ever sell, Sean would wait three to five years for the upturn.

reasons.title: Gated landed homes hold value better
reasons.body: Older, open landed areas suffer from public through-traffic, parking problems and break-ins, which caps prices at RM1.2 million to RM1.6 million. Gated, strata-titled townships like Desa ParkCity charge maintenance but offer the security buyers now expect.

reasons.title: Refinancing releases less than it used to
reasons.body: In Sean's example, a RM800,000 townhouse with RM300,000 owing could once release about RM340,000 at 80% of value. Under the newer cash-out calculation over a 10-year tenure, perhaps a third of that, a little over RM100,000, is usable.

reasons.title: Choose the home by the life you want
reasons.body: Retirees without school-age children can rent anywhere; a home of your own buys certainty and pride. Gated townships in the northern and southern Klang Valley, such as around Elmina, have risen 50% to 80% from launch prices.

actions: Keep the Desa ParkCity house, possibly refinancing only so the instalment stays close to the rent.
Get an agent's view on the townhouse's market and bank valuation, then sell.
Talk as a family about how you will live in retirement before buying a home.
Rent first after you return, and look around before committing.
If you want more income instead, buy a smaller city condo whose rent covers the instalment.
articles.caveat: Sean had no figures for the townhouse; if its value has stalled for a temporary reason, refinancing to keep it may suit a family that still wants to grow the portfolio.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #272. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2025. Sean offers to refer the family to the agent who handles his own rentals.

articles.title: Is buying a second property within a year too aggressive?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old working abroad wants a RM500,000 furnished Cheras subsale a year after buying her first unit, and worries falling birth rates will hurt property. Sean walks through the subsale steps and his long-term view.

question.asker: From CK, a viewer from Kota Kinabalu who wrote in by email
question.context: CK is 32, single and working overseas, earning about RM30,000 a month net and saving about RM20,000 of it, with savings and investments well over RM1 million in total. Last year she bought a RM850,000 dual-key unit in Kota Kinabalu, due in 2026. She is now eyeing a fully furnished low-floor subsale unit in Cheras listed at RM500,000, which her siblings have viewed, for positive cash flow. Her parents worry about the market.
question.text: Is a second purchase this soon too aggressive, what happens in a subsale after she says yes, and will falling birth rates leave Malaysia with China-style oversupply?

answer.quote: I do think the subsale unit is okay.
answer.summary: Not too aggressive for her income and finances, and the building rents well. But as a member of a bulk-purchase club she should also weigh completed unsold units, which offer a subsale's certainty with a developer's discounts. Demographics will hurt outlying areas and big houses, not city units with job-driven demand.

reasons.title: A subsale takes about 18% in cash
reasons.body: She pays a 3% earnest deposit, RM15,000, and has about 30 days to get a loan; the remaining 7%, RM35,000, is due at the SPA, followed by stamp duty, valuation and legal fees. Budget about RM90,000 for a RM500,000 unit. Transfer takes five to six months for freehold and seven to eight for leasehold, which needs state consent.

reasons.title: One lawyer is cheaper and faster
reasons.body: Separate lawyers for buyer and seller are safest, but sharing one, usually paid by the buyer, saves money and back-and-forth. Using the agent's recommended bankers and lawyers is fine, because loan terms depend on your profile.

reasons.title: Completed unsold units combine both
reasons.body: Like a subsale, you can see the building, neighbours and tenants; like a new launch, you get the developer's package and often a one-time defect repair. With building costs up from about RM300 to RM380 to RM400 per sq ft, older completed projects can also have better finishes than new launches.

reasons.title: Fewer families means smaller city units
reasons.body: Ageing countries still have unaffordable city homes, as in Tokyo, Beijing and Shanghai. Sean expects less demand for mansions and far-flung houses, and more for compact units near jobs, from singles spending on what they want rather than what a family needs.

actions: Check rents for the building on property portals, including room-by-room rates.
Reserve about 18% of the price in cash before committing to a subsale.
Plan how you will sign documents if you are abroad, since a subsale involves several separate payments and papers.
Compare the subsale with completed unsold units available through your club.
Buy in urban areas where rental demand is driven by jobs.
articles.caveat: Sean is openly bullish on Malaysian property, expecting interest rate cuts and new rail lines to lift prices, but stresses that not every purchase makes money; each still needs your own research.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #290. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in July 2025. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club CK has joined, not its owner, and he bought a completed unsold unit in Johor Bahru through it.

articles.title: Should I buy a second property, or keep it simple?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old government officer already owns a Klang Valley unit and invests in global equities. He asks whether two new projects with rebates are really good deals, or just sales tactics.

question.asker: From Mr. J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr. J is 32, in government service on a pensionable career path, and already owns a 973 sq ft unit in the Klang Valley. He invests in global equities, Malaysian stocks, Singapore, gold and cash. He is weighing two purchases: M Aspira in Taman Desa, a Type B unit of 855 sq ft at about RM682,000 after rebates, with kitchen cabinet, air-conditioners, SPA legal fees and loan stamp duty covered but MOT not covered; and Residency Padang at roughly RM600,000 with discounts and incentives.
question.text: Are these genuinely good investments or do the rebates make the numbers look better than they are, and with equities already in place, is another leveraged property worthwhile?

answer.quote: Property investment is not to make us rich but to keep us rich.
answer.summary: The rebates are retail-price sales tactics that everybody gets, and a newer project only wins when the entry price makes sense. Let the existing unit run, use your second 90% loan slot only when you can afford it, and keep the capital a third property would need in global equities.

reasons.title: Newer wins only if the price makes sense
reasons.body: In a growing area, older buildings' rents move little while new ones command more, because tenants now compare specifications. But if the new project is 20% or 25% more expensive than the old one, Sean says you have to think about it. His own Oak 163 unit in Jalan Mont Kiara was the latest project on that street, and he got it almost cheaper than the project next door.

reasons.title: Rebates are given to everybody
reasons.body: M Aspira and Residency Padang are RRP retail prices, so everyone who walks into the sales gallery qualifies for the same package and the same discount. Sean's own filter is rent that covers the instalment plus a RM500 surplus, roughly 7% to 8% ROI in the Klang Valley, and he says such deals are hard to find among new launches.

reasons.title: The exit depends on rent, not age
reasons.body: A 15-year-old unit with RM1,000 positive cash flow a month is not hard to sell, because every RM500 of surplus supports about RM100,000 more in price — every RM100,000 of loan at 4% over 35 years costs about RM450 to RM500 a month. The doomsday case is a 700 sq ft three-bedroom unit clashing with brand new affordable homes of the same size almost in the same location.

reasons.title: Cash in property is the worst deal
reasons.body: Malaysians get two 90% loan slots, so Sean would use them and let tenants carry the instalments while he keeps DCA-ing into global equities. On a third property only 70% financing is available, which means RM300,000 down on a RM1 million unit; he puts equities at a safe estimate of 8% to 10% a year, while property might go south.

actions: Set aside RM50,000 for renovation plus six months of instalments before you collect the keys — RM68,000 for a RM600,000 unit at RM3,000 a month.
Set your own filter at rent covering the instalment plus a RM500 surplus, or a 7% to 8% ROI in the Klang Valley.
Let your existing unit run and revisit a second purchase about six months after your tenant moves in.
Compare all four buying channels — new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase — before paying retail price at a sales gallery.
Keep DCA-ing into global equities with the capital you would otherwise put into a third property.
articles.caveat: The rent-covers-instalment benchmark only works if you can still qualify for a 30 to 35 year loan; on a shorter loan, Sean says to compare yield against fixed deposit at 2.8%, EPF at about 6% and REITs at 5.5%. And if you have no access to below-market deals, he says to stick to what you are good at, because property investment is not for everybody.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #323. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2026.

articles.title: How do we get the best price for the family home we must sell?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old plans to sell his overspending father's JB corner semi-D for RM2.2 million within two years to fund his parents' retirement. Sean explains how pricing, valuation and agents decide how fast it sells.

question.asker: From Mr K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr K is 34, works in asset management and is getting married this year. His father, 73, still earns about RM7,000 a month but overspends, with an old business overdraft and maxed-out credit cards. Five years ago the family refinanced their fully paid corner semi-D in Taman Pelangi, JB, adding Mr K's name for a 35-year tenure; his father pays about RM2,000 a month and has drawn RM100,000 of a RM250,000 overdraft facility. Similar houses sold for RM1.4 million to RM1.8 million, and Mr K wants RM2.2 million, with the proceeds handed to him to manage.
question.text: Is two years long enough to sell at RM2.2 million, how does he get the best price, how does he pick an agent, and are there tax issues in the transfer?

answer.quote: If you sell at market rate, you will sell at market time.
answer.summary: Two years is plenty, and JB's market is strong, but price sets the speed. Get bank valuations first: asking well above what a bank will lend means buyers must find a large cash gap, so it will sit unsold. Pick one committed agent, and expect no RPGT on a home held this long.

reasons.title: Valuation decides what a buyer can borrow
reasons.body: If a bank values the house at RM2 million, a buyer can borrow at most RM1.8 million. At RM2.2 million they need RM400,000 in cash; at RM2 million, RM200,000. Sell below the valuation and the buyer may need almost nothing down, so it sells at once.

reasons.title: Test the price, then lower it
reasons.body: Sean lists his rental units high and lowers the price every week or two until viewings and offers come. The same works for a sale if you can wait: start at RM2.2 million, and if nobody calls, the price, not the agent, is the problem.

reasons.title: One committed agent beats five
reasons.body: Multiple agents end up chasing the same buyer and undercutting one another. Sean prefers an exclusive agent who invests in their own marketing, such as an area specialist with several listings nearby, who reports viewings and offers honestly.

reasons.title: Protect the family first
reasons.body: No RPGT is due on a home held over five years, and family transfers need no special tax planning. The harder part is his father's spending: give his parents a fixed monthly budget, secure his mother's share first and keep talking openly about money.

actions: Ask several banks for a market valuation, since they use different valuers.
Set your price from the valuations, not from your hopes or the peak of the market.
Start slightly high and lower the price at set intervals until you get offers.
Give one experienced area agent an exclusive listing and agree how often they report.
Once sold, give your parents a fixed monthly budget from the proceeds.
articles.caveat: An old corner house will be renovated by its next owner, so spending on repairs before selling won't raise the price much. If he needs the money urgently, pricing at or below the valuation is the way to sell quickly.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #291. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and tax rules are as stated in July 2025; check RPGT with a tax adviser before selling.

articles.title: I own 10 fully paid condos at 59. Should I sell before I retire?
articles.excerpt: A viewer about to retire owns ten debt-free condos in Penang and Singapore. Sean agrees with selling the Penang units, but warns that selling too many too fast can be taxed as a business.

question.asker: From KB, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: KB is 59, a Malaysian who has worked in Singapore for about 35 years and holds Singapore PR. KB owns ten fully paid condos, three in Singapore and seven in Penang, and plans to retire to Penang in two to three years. The Penang units have doubled or tripled in value but yield only 3 to 4%, many are over 20 years old, and good tenants are getting harder to find.
question.text: Should KB sell some or all of the properties before retiring, move the money into fixed deposits and other assets, and stop dealing with tenants?

answer.quote: So, don't suddenly sell all, pace yourself in selling.
answer.summary: Selling the Penang units makes sense, perhaps keeping one, but slowly, so the sales aren't taxed as a property business. The three Singapore units are worth keeping for income.

reasons.title: Selling fast can be taxed as business
reasons.body: RPGT applies to sales within five years of the SPA date, and the rates change with each Budget. The bigger risk is that many sales in a short time can lead the Inland Revenue Board to treat you as trading, and tax the gains as business income.

reasons.title: Singapore rent alone can fund retirement
reasons.body: Sean estimates about S$1,000 a month per room, so three units, assuming three bedrooms each, bring in roughly S$8,000 to S$9,000, about RM24,000 to RM25,000, which is more than enough to live very comfortably in Penang.

reasons.title: Penang's LRT decides what to sell first
reasons.body: Units near an upcoming station may rent and sell better once the line opens, so Sean would hold those until it is completed and sell the others first. Distance from transport isn't always a drawback; some people, Sean included, pay more for quiet.

reasons.title: Refinancing is no longer the easy exit
reasons.body: Sean's own plan was never to sell but to draw out equity by refinancing every few years. New rules now cap the cash you can take out at RM100,000, or a sum based on a 10-year tenure, which makes selling a more realistic exit.

actions: Sell the Penang units gradually, about one every two years; Sean calls this an unwritten rule among investors, not a law.
Check the RPGT due on each sale against the current Budget rates before listing it.
Overlay the planned Penang LRT route on your units, and sell those far from future stations first.
Refresh the interiors of older units before concluding that tenants won't come.
Keep the proceeds in low-risk places such as fixed deposits and blue chips, and steer clear of new business ventures and joint ventures with friends or relatives.
articles.caveat: If you want to pass the properties to children, selling isn't the only route: Sean is exploring holding property in a company and passing on shares, though he hasn't settled on how. And for anyone still building a portfolio, his own approach is to refinance and keep, not to sell.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #315. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in July 2026; tax and refinancing rules change, so check the current ones before selling.

articles.title: Should You Settle Your Housing Loan Early?
articles.excerpt: A reader with three mortgages dreams of being debt-free. Sean explains why he would keep the loans running, and what to do with the spare cash instead.

question.asker: From Miss N, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss N is in her early 30s, single, and earns about RM15,000 a month. She has three mortgages: a rented unit, a commercial lot and a landed home under renovation. Her other savings sit in low-risk investments, and her dream is to be mortgage-free and simply collect rent.
question.text: Should she pay the loans off as fast as possible to save on interest, or let them run the full term?

answer.quote: I will definitely not settle the loan.
answer.summary: Keep the loans running. At around 4%, a housing loan is the cheapest money you can get, below the rate of inflation, so spare cash should go where it earns more than the loan costs.

reasons.title: Settling early can raise your tax bill
reasons.body: Rent counts as taxable income, but the interest on a rental property loan is a deductible expense. On a 35-year loan, Sean estimates about 85% of an early instalment is interest: roughly RM2,550 of a RM3,000 payment. Clear the loan and that deduction disappears, so part of the interest you save comes back as tax. Meanwhile the bank still counts the full rent as income when you apply for more financing.

reasons.title: Your cash can earn more elsewhere
reasons.body: EPF has paid around 5.5 to 6% in recent years, while paying down the loan saves at most about 4%. Sean adds that if interest rates fall as expected, even fixed deposits could end up paying less than the mortgage costs.

reasons.title: Her loans already pay for themselves
reasons.body: Over a million ringgit of property needed only 10 to 15% of her own money upfront. The rented unit brings in RM2,800 against a RM2,100 instalment, and the commercial lot clears about RM1,000 a month. Only the new landed home is a real cost, and her income covers it easily.

reasons.title: Her age favours more borrowing, not less
reasons.body: In her early 30s, with no family commitments yet and an income likely to keep rising until around 40, she is a strong candidate for credit. The loans will be largely paid off by her mid-50s anyway. Sean would rather she spent the energy on her health, skills and career.

actions: Leave loans alone on units whose rent already covers the instalment.
Keep a buffer of about six months of instalments for every unit, for vacancies, repairs and difficult tenants. Sean recently spent about RM15,000 refitting one unit after eight years.
Put the remaining cash into investments that beat the loan rate and suit your risk appetite.
Read up on how rental income is taxed and which expenses are deductible before deciding.
Pay a good agent or management company well. Sean pays 1.25 to 1.5 months of rent instead of one, so they serve him first.
articles.caveat: If owing the bank keeps you up at night, settling is a legitimate choice. Sean treats it as a question of peace of mind rather than maths, and says a conservative, debt-free approach makes more sense in your 60s than in your 30s.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #283. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in the episode. EPF dividends, loan rates and tax rules change, so check current ones for your own situation.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #283 | SETTLE THE LOAN EARLY TO SAVE ON INTEREST?

articles.title: I work in Singapore. Can I get a housing loan in Malaysia?
articles.excerpt: Singapore income converts well, so qualifying is rarely the problem. Rena Choong explains what Malaysian banks check for Malaysians working in Singapore, and what changes if you take up citizenship.

question.context: Many Malaysians working in Singapore want to buy back home but aren't sure how banks treat Singapore income, or how a Malaysian property affects an HDB flat. After both had met Malaysians working there, Sean and Rena Choong cover the loan rules in the sixth episode of his mortgage series.
question.text: How do Malaysian banks treat Singapore income, and what should Malaysians working in Singapore prepare before applying?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: It's more to the compliance that you need to fulfill rather than your income.
answer.summary: Converted to ringgit, Singapore income usually qualifies easily; paperwork is what trips people up. Have at least a year of steady employment, clear savings records and your Singapore documents ready, and decide first whether you plan to settle there.

reasons.title: Income converts generously
reasons.body: Banks convert Singapore dollars at about three ringgit, or their own rate, and count 80% to 100% of a fixed salary and 50% to 70% of commission. S$4,000 a month is about RM12,000, and many banks set a minimum income of S$2,000 to S$3,000.

reasons.title: Malaysians keep Malaysian margins
reasons.body: While you hold a Malaysian IC, including as a Singapore PR, the usual margins apply: 90% on your first two residential loans, then 70%. Banks read your Singapore CBS credit report alongside CCRIS, so a Singapore property or loan counts too.

reasons.title: Citizenship changes the terms
reasons.body: Once you become a Singapore citizen, you buy in Malaysia as a foreigner: margins of about 80% to 85%, a maximum tenure of around 30 years, and the minimum prices set for foreign buyers.

reasons.title: Savings and history reassure the bank
reasons.body: Without EPF contributions to show, banks lean on savings proof such as CPF, EPF, fixed deposits, ASB or account balances. Weak savings or less than a year in the job can mean a margin cut from 90% to 80%, or a rejection.

actions: Wait until you have at least a year of employment history in Singapore, and don't apply while on probation.
Prepare three months of payslips and bank statements, your CPF statement, an employment confirmation letter, your CBS report and, if you are a PR, your Notice of Assessment.
Get any payslip that isn't in English translated and certified.
Build visible savings before you apply.
Plan at least one trip back to Malaysia to sign and open the loan account.
articles.caveat: If you want an HDB flat, settle that first: Rena says HDB buyers can't own property overseas, and the rules change, so check HDB's current terms before buying in Malaysia. Converting money back to Singapore dollars also carries exchange-rate risk.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 6 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (June 2023). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Bank rules are as described in 2023 and differ between banks. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

video.title: DILEMMA OF MALAYSIANS WORKING IN SINGAPORE

articles.title: Now settled in Singapore, what should I do with my new KL unit?
articles.excerpt: A young engineer bought a Bukit Jalil unit, then got Singapore PR. Sean explains why he would rent out the whole unit, how to furnish it for the right tenant, and why there is no rush to come home.

question.asker: From Mr Y, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Y is 28, a structural engineer in Singapore earning about S$5,000 a month, and has just received Singapore PR. Last year he bought a Bukit Jalil unit for about RM625,000; the developer covered 8% of the price, so he paid only 2%, about RM12,000, which is refunded at handover around July 2026. He may not return for five or six years, worries that Malaysian engineering pay would make the loan a burden, and already has a six-figure ringgit portfolio in stocks and bonds.
question.text: Should he rent out the whole unit, rent it room by room and keep one room for visits, or let family stay, and how much should he spend getting it ready for tenants?

answer.quote: Rent the whole thing out, and you focus on your career in Singapore.
answer.summary: Rent out the whole unit and run it like a business, furnished for the tenants most likely to live there. Keeping a room for monthly visits or lending it to family wastes it, and there is no hurry to move back.

reasons.title: A spare room costs more than a hotel
reasons.body: Keeping a room empty for a monthly trip home costs more than staying in a hotel, and his family already have their own home. Sean is against holiday homes unless you can pay for them in cash.

reasons.title: The tenant decides the fit-out
reasons.body: Ask who will rent there: families, professionals or students. Families want a practical kitchen and a calm design; students need rooms with separate locks and single beds. Renting by the room is not always better: in Mont Kiara whole units do better, while in mixed areas rooms can earn more.

reasons.title: Have more than one way to cover the loan
reasons.body: A loan of about RM600,000 means an instalment of about RM2,700. If the whole unit rents for only RM1,800, three rooms at RM600, RM800 and RM1,000 would bring in RM2,400. Family-oriented projects often ban Airbnb, but medium-term stays for visiting professionals are another option.

reasons.title: RM12,000 won't furnish a rental
reasons.body: Workmanship has become expensive and RM20,000 no longer goes far; Sean's rough guess for a quote here is RM35,000 to RM38,000. Doing it yourself saves about 20% but needs time on site, which is hard from Singapore. Spend where tenants notice, such as a large smart TV and a washer-dryer, not marble floors or plaster ceilings.

actions: Check what similar units nearby rent for, and compare it with your instalment.
Get an itemised furnishing quotation from an established company to use as a benchmark, and ask where any much cheaper quote cuts costs.
Furnish for the most likely tenant, aiming for the lowest cost with the most visual impact.
If you may buy public housing in Singapore later, check how owning a Malaysian property affects your eligibility.
Keep building your career and savings in Singapore, and revisit moving back once your portfolio reaches six figures in Singapore dollars.
articles.caveat: If you can pay cash and money is no constraint, keeping a room or a holiday home is your choice. Sean adds that returning makes more sense for someone planning to start their own firm.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #317. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in July 2026. Sean recommends The Makeover Guys, who furnish his own investment units, and his channel carries a discount code for them.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #317 | CHOOSING THE RIGHT PROPERTY IS HALF THE EQUATION

articles.title: We own six properties that pay for themselves. Hold or start selling?
articles.excerpt: A couple in their 40s own a home and five rented units, all with positive cash flow. Sean explains how to decide whether to sell, hold or keep buying, starting with what the cash is for.

question.asker: From LL, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: LL and their spouse are in their 40s with a combined net salary of about RM20,000 a month. They own their home in Puchong and five rented high-rise units in the Klang Valley, a portfolio Sean values at about RM4.75 million, with each rented unit bringing in between RM200 and RM2,000 a month more than it costs, with a seventh unit due in 2030. They have about RM250,000 in cash, about RM800,000 in EPF and insurance on every loan, but worry that their leasehold units will lose value and that the economy or politics could hurt prices.
question.text: Should they sell one property and keep the cash, and if so which one, or hold everything?

answer.quote: Why do you need the cash?
answer.summary: Decide what the money is for before selling anything. If they do sell, Sean would start with the small, low-yielding Shah Alam unit; otherwise they can hold, since every unit pays its way, and agree as a couple on how much is enough.

reasons.title: Their buffer is already solid
reasons.body: Sean asks how long you could last if every unit lost its tenant at once; his own buffer is six months. RM250,000 is solid for this portfolio, kept liquid in fixed deposits, a money market fund or against a mortgage, where it can still be withdrawn.

reasons.title: Cash loses value faster than it seems
reasons.body: Sean puts his own inflation at 10 to 11% a year once family costs are counted, so RM350,000 held as cash loses about RM35,000 of buying power a year. Property prices and rents tend to adjust with the market instead.

reasons.title: Leasehold renewal has precedents
reasons.body: Petaling Jaya has announced lease extensions back to 99 years for RM5,000, on condition the property passes only within the family, and Sean knows of projects in PJ and TTDI converted to freehold for RM1,000 to RM2,000 per owner. Their own leasehold units have about 90 years left.

reasons.title: The smallest unit uses a full loan slot
reasons.body: The Shah Alam unit earns only about RM200 a month and is worth about RM350,000, yet it takes one of their two 90% loan slots in a portfolio of nearly RM5 million. That is why Sean would sell it first.

actions: Write down what the cash would be for, such as education, a business or simply peace of mind, before selling anything.
Work out your own inflation rate from what your household really spends, not the official figure.
If you sell, start with the unit that earns the least while still taking up a 90% loan slot.
Ask your tax adviser whether holding the properties in a company would suit you better, especially for passing them on.
Agree as a couple how much is enough, and once you sell, don't look back.
articles.caveat: Sean's own answer would be to keep buying, since income usually peaks between 45 and 50, though with residential loans now needing 30% down he would look at commercial property, which carries different risks. If they want to stop working altogether, selling the best performers and putting about RM1 million in EPF could pay roughly RM5,000 a month.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #320. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in September 2026; the viewer's unit-by-unit figures are summarised rather than listed.

articles.title: I lost my booking fee on a SOHO. Should I give up on property?
articles.excerpt: A young investor expected an 85% loan on a SOHO unit, got 70% and walked away from the booking. Sean explains the title mix-up and how he buys a third property and beyond.

question.asker: From J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: J is 27 and already owns two residential properties. He booked a 750 sq ft SOHO duplex in Damansara for RM210,000, expecting an 85% loan because he thought it was a commercial unit, with rent of RM1,200 to RM1,400 against an instalment of about RM900. The bank treated the SOHO as a home, so as his third residential loan it was capped at 70%, and he gave up the booking and lost a RM500 fee.
question.text: How should he book a subsale unit without risking the booking fee, how does Sean buy a third property and beyond, and is property even worth it when 30% upfront cash makes the returns worse than EPF?

answer.quote: I think you're being a little bit too harsh on yourself.
answer.summary: Don't give up over a misunderstanding of the title: anything called SOHO is financed as a home, so a third one gets 70%. Beyond two properties, Sean buys through developer deals that need little cash, finances them on credit and keeps his own capital for stocks and other assets.

reasons.title: 'Home' in the name means a home loan
reasons.body: SOHO stands for small office home office, and banks treat anything with 'home' in its type as residential, so a third residential loan is capped at 70%. SOFO, SOVO and office suites are commercial titles, which can get up to 85%.

reasons.title: Subsale and auction need the most cash
reasons.body: A subsale needs about 18% of the price upfront: a 3% earnest deposit, 7% at the SPA and the fees. At auction you put down 10% by bank draft and lose it if the loan isn't secured within 90 days, so Sean doesn't advise auctions for first-timers. Only deals struck directly with developers can avoid large deposits.

reasons.title: Use credit for property, cash for the rest
reasons.body: Bought in cash, property nets about 6%, no better than EPF, as J says. Financed, with rent covering the instalment, tenants build the equity. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought at a 20% discount, now rents for RM6,000 against an instalment of about RM4,200, and at a 6% gross yield is worth about RM1.2 million against roughly RM900,000 paid.

reasons.title: Declared rent works for you
reasons.body: Agent fees, repairs and even loan interest can be deducted from declared rental income, and banks count that income when you apply for the next loan.

actions: Check whether a unit has a residential or commercial title before booking; anything labelled SOHO counts as a home.
Count your residential loans: from the third, the margin drops to 70%.
Budget about 18% of the price in cash for a subsale, and avoid auctions until you are experienced.
Buy only where the rent covers the instalment, and keep your spare cash for other investments.
Declare your rental income and claim the costs, since banks count it for your next loan.
articles.caveat: Sean's third-property approach relies on large developer discounts through a bulk-purchase group. Without deals like that, putting 30% down can make a third property hard to justify, as J found.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #312. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in May 2026. Sean is a client of the bulk-purchase group FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: Should I buy a Cheras condo on a staff loan before starting a family?
articles.excerpt: A 31-year-old who commutes three hours a day has booked a condo near an MRT station on a cheap staff loan. Sean's advice takes a turn: keep the cash and sort out the commute and family plans first.

question.asker: From Miss M, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss M is 31, married, and plans to have a baby next year. She lives in her husband's condo in Semenyih and spends 1.5 to 2 hours each way commuting to central KL. She has booked a freehold 960 sq ft, three-bedroom condo near Taman Connaught MRT station in Cheras for RM564,000 after rebates. Her employer's staff loan, at 2% over 25 years, is capped at RM500,000, so she would pay RM64,000 in cash and about RM2,200 a month, against about RM2,300 rent for a similar unit nearby.
question.text: Is she doing the right thing for a first home bought to rent out now and live in later, should she look at subsale investments instead, and what else should she consider before starting a family?

answer.quote: Why put yourself in that situation from day one?
answer.summary: Sean would hold off. The RM64,000 is worth more as a buffer while she starts a family, and the real problem, a three-hour daily commute, may be better solved by a job or a rental closer to home. If she does buy, it should be a pure investment that works on rent, which a subsale nearby may do better.

reasons.title: Mixed intentions need the 85% rule
reasons.body: When you buy to rent out first and live in later, today's rent should cover at least 85% of the instalment, so you aren't buying on feelings alone. Here the RM2,300 rent for a similar unit already covers the RM2,200 staff-loan instalment.

reasons.title: The cash may be worth more than the cheap rate
reasons.body: The 2% staff loan is attractive, but its RM500,000 cap takes RM64,000 of her cash. A 90% ordinary loan at 4% over 35 years would cost about RM2,600 a month, around RM3,000 with maintenance, but would keep the cash free for renovation and emergencies. Check what the staff loan requires if she leaves the job.

reasons.title: With cash, a subsale may beat a new launch
reasons.body: New launches are priced for future costs as wars and inflation push construction up, and Sean says same-size units next door sell for about RM500,000. With RM64,000, a subsale bought with a loan could have positive cash flow straight away.

reasons.title: A buffer buys choices
reasons.body: At about RM4,000 a month in spending, RM64,000 covers roughly a year and a half. That could fund a break, a move to a job near Semenyih or Kajang, or renting in Cheras for about RM2,500 a month if staying in KL makes more sense.

actions: Before buying for both investment and own stay, check that today's rent for similar units covers at least 85% of the instalment.
Read your staff loan's terms on what happens if you leave your employer.
Compare same-size subsale units nearby before committing to the new launch.
Keep a cash buffer while you start a family, rather than tying it up in a property you don't yet need.
If the commute is the real problem, consider renting closer to work or finding a job nearer home before buying.
articles.caveat: If the unit were certain to make money, Sean says it would be a different story. He also notes that the developer is an established brand, so construction risk is lower than with smaller developers.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #310. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2026. Sean mentions that he gets his own investment deals as a client of the bulk-purchase group FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: My project has stalled. Will it be abandoned?
articles.excerpt: A buyer sees construction slowing and fears the project will be abandoned. Sean, a buyer in the same project, explains the difference between ailing and abandoned, and the real options for getting out or staying in.

question.asker: From A viewer who wrote in about Solasta
question.context: A viewer and their family bought into Solasta, a high-rise in the Dutamas area of KL. Sean bought a unit there too. Driving past the site, they notice construction has slowed, and it looks unlikely to finish by the promised fourth quarter. Owners' chat groups are full of talk that the project will die.
question.text: Is the project in trouble, and what can a buyer actually do if it ends up abandoned?

answer.quote: Is this the worst-case scenario? No.
answer.summary: An ailing project is not an abandoned one. Check its official status, then choose between staying in for delay compensation or walking away at a cost. A full refund is very hard to get.

reasons.title: Ailing is not the same as abandoned
reasons.body: The housing ministry's PERDA portal lists "projek sakit" (ailing projects) separately from "projek terbengkalai" (abandoned ones). A project is ailing if it falls 30% behind schedule or passes its completion date. Developers take it seriously: one ailing project can freeze the advertising permits and licences for their other projects.

reasons.title: The developer is selling assets to fix it
reasons.body: This developer has a cash flow problem but is raising money: it sold its Mont Kiara mall to Sunway and a KL land plot to Chin Hin for about half a billion ringgit. Sales like that are slow, because a seller seen as desperate gets lowballed.

reasons.title: Walking away costs money; a full refund is rare
reasons.body: Cancelling the sale agreement usually means forfeiting your 10% deposit. A full refund under section 8A of the Housing Development Act needs six months with no work at all (one worker on site counts as work), your bank's consent, and certification by the housing ministry.

reasons.title: Staying in can still pay off
reasons.body: Buyers who stay are owed compensation for every day of delay, usually paid at handover. Early buyers paid around RM700 to RM800 per sq ft, while completed units nearby trade near RM1,100 and new launches ask RM1,500 to RM1,600. The true worst case is outright abandonment, where you keep paying interest on whatever the bank has already released.

actions: Look the project up on the housing ministry's PERDA site ("carian projek sakit") instead of relying on chat-group rumours.
Follow the developer's announcements: asset sales and new funding are signs it intends to finish.
Decide honestly whether you can carry the interest until handover. If not, losing the deposit may beat months of stress.
Keep a buffer of about six months of instalments for every property, so a delay or vacancy never forces your hand.
Do not treat "publicly listed developer" as a guarantee; check its track record and finances.
articles.caveat: If this is your first and only home and the delay threatens your finances, joining other owners to press the developer, or to seek release without penalty, makes sense. Sean is calmer partly because he holds other properties and keeps cash buffers.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #316. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean is a buyer in the same project with no link to the developer. Prices and the project's status are as described in July 2026.

articles.title: Strata landed or individual title: which kind of landed home to buy?
articles.excerpt: At a talk in Batu Kawan, Sean explains the difference between gated landed strata homes and traditional individual-title houses, from security and maintenance to who will buy at RM1.8 million.

question.context: Landed homes in Malaysia come in two main forms: traditional individual-title houses on public roads, and newer landed strata developments with a guardhouse, shared landscaping and a management body. Sean answered this question at a talk in a landed strata township in Batu Kawan, Penang, drawing on a strata home he bought in Johor Bahru eight years earlier.
question.text: What is the difference between landed strata and individual-title homes, and which holds its value better?

answer.quote: the least I expect from a house is actually security
answer.summary: Landed strata costs more up front and comes with rules and maintenance fees, but gives security, planned infrastructure and a say over the neighbourhood. Sean expects most future landed homes to be strata, and individual-title prices to hit a ceiling because buyers at that level expect security.

reasons.title: You pay for planning
reasons.body: The developer has to plan landscaping, facilities, roads, drains and metering up front, so strata homes cost more. Individual-title houses are quicker and simpler to build, which is why developers once preferred them.

reasons.title: Rules limit renovation
reasons.body: When Sean bought his strata home for about RM1.8 million, he found he couldn't change the facade or colours freely. Managements have since become more flexible about kitchen extensions and other changes.

reasons.title: Individual titles hide their upkeep
reasons.body: Owners of traditional houses often defer repairs to water tanks, gates and paint until a buyer complains. In strata, a management team maintains the estate, and owners can vote on uses such as a neighbour's house becoming a temple.

reasons.title: Who buys at RM1.8 million?
reasons.body: A household needs about RM24,000 a month to afford an RM1.8 million house. Buyers at that level expect layered security, which an open street can't give; some wealthy owners are downsizing into secure apartments instead.

actions: Ask what renovations and facade changes the management allows.
Budget for maintenance fees, and compare them with the hidden upkeep of an older house.
Check what infrastructure surrounds the plot, such as sewage plants or substations.
Compare commute times; landed homes are often far from city jobs.
For an own-stay home, check that local rents cover about 85% of the instalment.
articles.caveat: In Penang, land scarcity on the island means Sean would put a larger budget into commercial or industrial property rather than more high-rise. His views on individual-title prices are, by his own account, unpopular.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from the first part of Sean's English captions for this 1 hour 51 minute question-and-answer session, held at a developer's landed strata project in Batu Kawan; later questions on other topics are not covered. Sean says he owns units in other projects by the same developer. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Is a student-rental unit near Sunway a good investment?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old is eyeing a USJ 1 project built for room-by-room student rentals, linked by BRT to the Sunway universities. Sean thinks it can work, but warns that only another investor will ever buy it from you.

question.asker: From J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: J is 30, married, earns RM7,000 a month and owns his own home in PJ, with only a RM700 car loan. He is looking at a new project in USJ 1, due in late 2028, designed for students reaching the Sunway-area universities by BRT. A 689 sq ft two-bedroom-plus-study unit of about RM480,000 to RM516,000, split into four rooms, is projected to rent for about RM4,800 a month against an instalment of about RM2,200.
question.text: Are student investment properties around Sunway sound, what are the risks, does furnishing matter, and should he pay a company to manage the rooms?

answer.quote: In conclusion, I think this is fine.
answer.summary: It can work. Sunway's universities and schools aren't likely to move, which removes the biggest risk, and the agent's figures aren't unrealistic. The real risk is the exit: a unit built only for students can be sold only to investors, and only while its numbers still add up.

reasons.title: A campus moving out is the main risk
reasons.body: Student areas suffer when a college relocates, as happened around one Cheras campus and to some extent SS15. In Bandar Sunway the university, schools and Taylor's lakeside campus are fixtures, and rents depend on how wealthy the students are, so results differ from one university town to another.

reasons.title: Only investors will buy it from you
reasons.body: Own-stay areas rise because people pay more to live there. A student or short-stay unit is bought only on its rent, so once wear and tear drags rents below the instalment, nobody will pay you more for it. The first five years feel great; by year seven, decide whether to exit.

reasons.title: Students wear buildings out
reasons.body: Young tenants use the lifts and facilities hard and care less than owners. Sean expects maintenance to slip after the first few years unless owners stay active in the joint management body or management corporation.

reasons.title: Furnishing is expected, and costs more
reasons.body: Students won't buy their own beds or fridges, so each room needs a bed, wardrobe, desk, curtains, air-conditioning and its own lock. Four bedroom sets cost more than a normal layout; furnishing a unit now costs RM38,000 to RM50,000, so freebies like air-conditioners and a kitchen cabinet are worth RM12,000 to RM15,000.

actions: Check the agent's projected room rents yourself on co-living and rental sites.
Visit nearby student areas to see how such buildings look after a few years.
Weigh the furnishing package in the sale, since it is covered by the loan.
Pay a management company 5% to 10% of the rent if your time is worth more than handling repairs and tenants yourself.
Plan when to exit while the rent still clearly covers the instalment.
articles.caveat: Sean once said he would only invest in a unit he would live in himself, but he has dropped that rule: data on what tenants actually pay matters more than his own taste. Tighter student visa policies abroad and at home could still change demand.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #294. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rents and prices are the agent's projections as Sean read them in August 2025. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company he mentions in the episode, and says he is not selling this project.

articles.title: I'm 20 and earn RM3,500. How should I prepare for property?
articles.excerpt: A 20-year-old accounting student running his own social media agency wants to start investing after graduating. Sean says to hold off and build the business first.

question.asker: From V, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: V is 20, a full-time second-year accounting student who runs a social media agency and does freelance videography, earning about RM3,500 a month. He has been learning about property since school. By graduating in mid-2027 he aims to earn RM5,000 a month from the agency and have at least RM10,000 in savings to start with.
question.text: What should he do over the next few years to prepare for his first property?

answer.quote: I would suggest to not prioritize property investment first.
answer.summary: Don't make property the priority yet. While the business is young, flexibility and active income come first; property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich, so scale the agency and diversify once it earns well.

reasons.title: The business will out-earn any investment
reasons.body: Sean expects a media business to make more over the next ten years than any investment. Once V pays himself about RM5,000 a month and the company makes RM50,000 to RM100,000 a year, he can start diversifying.

reasons.title: Property ties up money
reasons.body: Property cannot be sold quickly when you need cash, the opposite of the flexibility a young business owner needs.

reasons.title: RM10,000 is not enough
reasons.body: Sean's test is to have, when you collect the keys, RM50,000 to furnish the unit plus six months of instalments, about RM63,500 for a RM500,000 unit, besides a six-month emergency fund, a medical card and a clear career path. At 22 he put all RM30,000 of his savings into a down payment, then found a subsale purchase needs about 17% to 18% in cash.

reasons.title: Expecting fast money is the classic mistake
reasons.body: Audit anyone giving advice by whether they live the life you want. Fake gurus work on ignorance and greed, and genuine investors rarely broadcast their wins, so physical community events are the place to meet them.

actions: Put your energy into scaling the agency: decide between sole proprietorship and Sdn Bhd, plan your hiring and use AI.
Keep your lifestyle well below your income as it grows.
Build savings towards a six-month emergency fund, then RM50,000 plus six months of instalments for your first unit.
Get medical insurance so you never become a burden on your family.
Join physical investor events to find a community, and judge advisers by the lives they lead.
articles.caveat: Sean bought young because his corporate career was in property development, where it fitted his path. Once the business is established and pays V a stable income, property becomes the natural next step.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #302. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in November 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #302 | PROPERTY INVESTMENT SHOULDN’T BE YOUR PRIORITY

articles.title: I own two properties at 25. How do I reach RM10 million?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old second-generation business owner holds two KL properties bought below market and wants RM10 million in property within ten years. Sean says to pause and grow elsewhere.

question.asker: From JT, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JT is 25, married to a foreign wife, lives with his parents and works in his family's business. He bought a 1,098 sq ft Bangsar unit at auction for RM870,000, now rented with positive cash flow and about RM500,000 below the median value, and an 800 sq ft Damansara Heights unit for about RM1.1 million, 20% below market, still awaiting keys. His loan margins are used up.
question.text: How should he grow towards RM10 million in property in ten years: commercial property, a purchase using his wife's foreigner quota, or more residential?

answer.quote: The critical path is your income journey.
answer.summary: For now, don't grow it. He already has the two or three properties Sean encourages over a lifetime, so the next step is to settle the second unit, put his own money into other, uncorrelated assets, and grow his income and business knowledge, because property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich.

reasons.title: A third property is expensive
reasons.body: Beyond two 90% loans, financing drops to 70%, so a RM1 million unit needs about RM300,000 down, or RM350,000 to RM380,000 with legal fees. Sean asks whether that money would do more in other assets than in a property growing marginally each year.

reasons.title: Commercial property is playing with fire
reasons.body: The successful commercial investors Sean knows buy subsale shop lots that already rent at 5% to 6%, rather than new launches that can take eight to 12 years to come alive. Businesses often buy commercial and industrial property mainly to hedge against inflation.

reasons.title: Diversify into uncorrelated assets
reasons.body: Sean uses his credit for Malaysian property, the game he understands, and his own money for other assets. Property cannot be dollar-cost averaged, so one bad purchase at the top of a cycle can ruin your credit and your confidence; he made that mistake himself after three successful deals.

reasons.title: Judge success by cash flow, not asset value
reasons.body: RM10 million can be reached with a single penthouse, so the number means little. Sean's first level of success is a portfolio that breaks even; the second is a surplus that also pays for your own home.

actions: Settle, furnish and rent out the second unit before looking for another.
Put your own savings into other assets, such as Malaysian or US stocks, and learn how they work.
If you buy commercial, choose a subsale unit that already rents at 5% to 6%.
If you use a foreign spouse's quota, buy a family home where RM1 million is the area's normal price, with a larger down payment, rather than an investment.
Before any purchase, run Sean's four basic steps: intent, affordability, 20 properties compared, then an informed decision.
articles.caveat: This is advice for someone already well ahead at 25, with family backing. Sean's worry is the opposite of most viewers': that the backing tempts him into risks beyond his means. For most buyers, his usual aim of two or three properties over a lifetime still applies.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #307. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2026. Sean buys through FAR Capital's bulk purchases as a member, not its owner.

articles.title: I want 10 properties in 10 years on RM5,500 a month. Too aggressive?
articles.excerpt: A 29-year-old with RM50,000 saved wants positive cash flow and ten properties within 15 years. Sean explains cash back against cash flow, how rent drives a high-rise's value, and why to go slowly.

question.asker: From YK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: YK is 29, works in a helping profession and earns about RM5,500 a month, with a six-month emergency fund, RM50,000 in savings and comprehensive insurance, and recently joined a bulk-purchase club. YK wants positive cash flow and early retirement, and is weighing a completed unit with high cash back but a monthly shortfall, then two more units soon after.
question.text: Should YK take high cash back with negative cash flow, how is capital growth judged, is buying three units in quick succession overcommitting, and should spare cash go into a flexi loan?

answer.quote: So, my suggestion is to go slow.
answer.summary: Take positive cash flow over cash back where possible, buy one unit at a time and get each one rented before the next, and build up salary first. Ten properties in ten years on RM5,500 a month is a target nobody else has set.

reasons.title: Cash back is borrowed money
reasons.body: It suits someone using it to clear credit card debt at about 18% or a personal loan at about 8%, or a business owner using a flexi loan as cheap working capital. Without that need, a smaller loan with rent above the instalment is better; buyers who spent their cash back are the ones who ended up in auctions.

reasons.title: Rent sets a high-rise's value
reasons.body: Each RM450 a month of surplus rent supports about RM100,000 more loan over 35 years at 4%. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM950,000, rents for about RM1,500 above its instalment, so the next investor could pay about RM1.25 million and still break even. That surplus mostly happens in tier one locations.

reasons.title: Studios suit only expensive land
reasons.body: Studios work where land is too costly for bigger units, such as Mont Kiara, Bangsar South and KLCC. In outlying areas they are a mismatch, however cheap they look.

reasons.title: Active income drives the portfolio
reasons.body: Investors who build portfolios fast usually earn RM30,000 or more. On RM5,500, a RM20,000 repair can hurt. Property keeps you rich; growing income is what makes you rich, and rental income replacing a salary is a goal for 55 or 60, not 35.

actions: Choose a lower loan with positive cash flow over cash back you don't need.
Rent each unit out before committing to the next.
Pick one route, subsale, auction or bulk purchase, and execute it rather than joining several courses.
Put spare cash in a flexi loan unless you can reliably earn more than the loan's 3.8% to 4%.
Set a goal by monthly cash flow or total value, not a number of units by a deadline.
articles.caveat: For someone with expensive debts to clear, a high cash back unit with a small monthly shortfall can make sense, provided the cash back is kept as a buffer and not spent.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #284. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in May 2025. Sean is a client of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club YK has joined, not its owner; he says he bought his last four properties through it at members' prices. He leaves the specific project YK is considering to the club's advisers.

articles.title: My tenant has stopped paying rent. What can I legally do?
articles.excerpt: A tenant who stops paying but won't leave is every landlord's nightmare. Lawyer Tea explains the legal route Sean's viewers can take: a letter of demand, then a court distress order.

question.context: Sean counts a tenant who stops paying but won't leave among a landlord's two worst cases. Many owners don't know the legal steps, so they wait months or even years, or try cutting off the water or changing the locks. Sean puts the problem to Lawyer Tea, who handles distress proceedings for landlords.
question.text: When a tenant stops paying rent and won't leave, what is the legal way to get your money and your property back?

by.name: Lawyer Tea
by.role: a lawyer who acts for landlords against non-paying tenants

answer.quote: So yeah, the best way I would say it will be the distress orders.
answer.summary: Act on the first missed month: send a letter of demand, and if the tenant hasn't paid within 14 days, apply to court for a distress order. The order lets you seize and auction the tenant's belongings and take the unit back, in two to three months at best.

reasons.title: Start while the deposit still covers you
reasons.body: Landlords usually hold two months' deposit. Sending the letter of demand after the first missed month means the court order can be ready by about the third month, before the losses run far beyond the deposit.

reasons.title: A distress order moves quickly
reasons.body: The landlord applies alone, without the tenant appearing in court, which is why it can take as little as two to three months. The tenant is normally given 14 days to leave, and anything left in the unit is presumed theirs and sold at a court auction.

reasons.title: Doing it yourself can backfire
reasons.body: A tenancy agreement normally promises the tenant quiet enjoyment of the unit. Cutting off water or electricity, or locking them out, can let them sue you for their losses or for belongings they say went missing.

reasons.title: Paperwork decides what you recover
reasons.body: An agreement has to be stamped to be admissible in court, which costs only a few hundred ringgit, and an expired agreement still counts. Without one you can apply for a writ of possession to get the unit back, but recovering money is hard; rent paid by bank transfer, not cash, helps prove the tenancy.

actions: Use a proper, stamped tenancy agreement that sets out each side's rights and what happens if rent isn't paid, not an agent's copied template.
Collect rent by bank transfer, and put the electricity account in the tenant's name.
Run a CTOS check on prospective tenants. Sean also treats an offer of a year's rent in cash, or a rush to move in the next day, as warning signs.
Send a letter of demand after the first missed month, and apply for a distress order if 14 days pass without payment.
Budget about RM10,000 in legal fees for the letter and the order, and let the court bailiff and the police carry out the eviction.
articles.caveat: Against squatters, or with no agreement or payment record, you can usually recover only the property, not the rent. If you suspect illegal activity in the unit, report it to the police at once; an owner who knew and said nothing can be held responsible.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2026 conversation with Lawyer Tea, who acts for landlords in distress proceedings. The quoted answer is Lawyer Tea's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Fees are as quoted in the episode. This is general information, not legal advice for your case.

articles.title: My tenant wants to pay six months upfront. Will it hurt my next loan?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old in Kota Kinabalu bought a subsale condo below market value and rented it out the day renovation finished. Sean explains what he did right, and why rent paid six months at a time can cost him his next loan.

question.asker: From Mr J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr J is 26, self-employed in Kota Kinabalu and earns about RM10,000 a month net. His mother spotted a listing in the condo where he lives: RM520,000, partly furnished, with a market value of about RM580,000. The owner wanted a quick sale, so he negotiated it to RM500,000, and the bank valued it at RM650,000. He handled the paperwork himself, did minor renovations and rented it out for about RM200 a month more than his instalment. The tenant now offers to pay RM12,600 every six months for two years.
question.text: Will rent paid every six months, rather than monthly, affect his income assessment when he applies for a second property?

answer.quote: Luck is when opportunity meets preparation.
answer.summary: Yes, it will. Banks look at rental income month by month in your bank statements, so lump sums or uneven amounts may not be counted, and that can cost him the next property. Ask the tenant to pay the same amount every month instead.

reasons.title: Banks want steady monthly credits
reasons.body: When you apply for a loan, the banker reads your statements month by month. Rent that arrives every six months, or varies because repairs were deducted from it, looks inconsistent and may not be recognised as income.

reasons.title: Keep repairs separate from rent
reasons.body: Letting a tenant fix things and deduct the cost is common, but it breaks the pattern. Sean has repairs fixed and paid separately, while the full rent is still paid to him each month.

reasons.title: Subsale lets you negotiate
reasons.body: With a subsale or bulk purchase you can counter the asking price; a developer's retail price is fixed. Knowing his own building let Mr J judge a below-market listing and act quickly.

reasons.title: Stay ready for the deal
reasons.body: Sean checks his own CCRIS and loan eligibility regularly, because good-value listings go to whoever can commit first. A subsale needs about 18% of the price in cash, so savings must be in place before the chance appears.

actions: Decline lump-sum rent if you plan to apply for another loan soon.
Offer the tenant an auto-debit, or 12 post-dated cheques to bank in each month.
Pay for repairs separately rather than deducting them from the rent.
Keep your loan eligibility and CCRIS checked, so you can move when a below-market listing appears.
Ask for a better price or rate at every step, from the seller to the lawyer and the bank.
articles.caveat: If you don't need the rent counted for a loan in the next year or two, advance payment matters less; the issue is only how a bank reads your statements.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #281. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2025. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean says furnishes and manages most of his investment units; it does not bear on this answer.

articles.title: Should my third property be subsale, auction, new or bulk purchase?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old with two landed homes and RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash weighs subsale, auction, new and bulk purchase for her third. Sean says to keep her cash and let the deal decide.

question.asker: From YX, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: YX is 30 and single, earns about RM8,000 net from her job and declares about RM5,000 a month from her own marketing business. She shares the loan on a landed own-stay home with her sister and bought a second landed house at auction for RM560,000, financed by an insurer whose loans don't appear in CCRIS, so she still has one 90% loan left. She has RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash and is a member of a property investment club.
question.text: For her third property, should she use cash on a subsale or auction unit with 10% down, or buy new or through bulk purchase, and save her cash?

answer.quote: Use as little of our money as possible.
answer.summary: Keep the cash and use credit. Sean has no favourite channel; he buys wherever the best deal is, but with her aim of letting the property pay for itself, new launches and bulk purchases fit better than subsale or auction, and her savings are worth more as runway for her business.

reasons.title: Less cash in means more options later
reasons.body: A subsale bought with a bigger down payment may give RM500 a month of positive cash flow, while a new unit with a larger loan may only break even. Sean still picks the one that ties up less money, and spends the difference on furnishing the unit so it stands out to the best tenants.

reasons.title: A bigger discount beats a standard one
reasons.body: Developers give everyone the same standard 10% or so. A bulk purchase with a 20% to 30% discount lets you own the unit, furnish it and still leave your savings untouched; any spare cash can sit in the loan to cut interest while staying available.

reasons.title: Auctions carry hidden problems
reasons.body: She was lucky with a landed auction house. Of ten auction units Sean has heard about, one or two had problems, and high-rise ones bring questions about arrears, whether the developer still exists and whether the strata title has been issued.

reasons.title: Her business may out-earn her job
reasons.body: If her side business grows from RM5,000 to RM15,000 a month, it may be time to focus on it. With living costs of about RM4,000, RM400,000 in savings would let her quit and build the business on her terms rather than take every job just to survive.

actions: Make sure the property itself makes sense before choosing how to buy it.
Compare the same project across all four channels when they overlap, such as just after completion when unsold, subsale and auction units all exist.
If you have paid for an investment club, use its research and advisers before comparing deals yourself.
Keep your savings as an emergency fund and business runway rather than spending them on down payments.
If you are a first-time buyer, stay away from auction high-rises until you understand their risks.
articles.caveat: If you dislike owing the bank a lot, Sean says it is fine to stop at two properties using both 90% loans. And financing from an insurer costs more: the rate is fixed and usually higher, and you must buy insurance from them.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #306. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in January 2026. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, the property investment club YX belongs to, not its owner, and he says he is biased towards its bulk-purchase deals. He also recommends a contact for insurer financing in the video.

articles.title: Three transit-linked condos, same cash flow. How do I choose?
articles.excerpt: A 40-year-old civil servant in Johor Bahru has shortlisted three new transit-linked serviced apartments in the Klang Valley for cash flow. Sean explains what to compare after cash flow, and why she must visit in person.

question.asker: From KD, a viewer from Johor Bahru who wrote in by email
question.context: KD is 40, single, a government servant earning RM9,100 a month net, with a car loan of RM944. She lives with her mother in a house transferred to her, and invests in shares, fixed deposits and money market funds, reaching half of her RM5,000-a-month passive income goal. For her first investment property she wants monthly cash flow and has shortlisted three new transit-oriented serviced apartments, in Kajang, Cheras and Petaling Jaya, buying new because she lives far away.
question.text: If all three give similar cash flow, what should decide it, how much does walkable convenience matter, why are some Mont Kiara subsales so cheap, and how should she judge bulk-purchase units near KLCC with cash back?

answer.quote: we should always look at pricing first then location then only timing
answer.summary: After cash flow, compare each project's price with the median of past transactions around it, and the cash each needs up front. Walkable shops and transit genuinely justify higher rent. And living in Johor is no reason to buy new: visit the sites, and consider subsales and bulk-purchase deals too.

reasons.title: Below-median prices leave room to grow
reasons.body: A unit that rents well but is priced above its neighbours has limited capital appreciation. A unit bought below the area's median that still covers its instalment is the better buy.

reasons.title: Upfront cash differs by deal
reasons.body: One project may need RM50,000 to own, another nothing, and some even pay cash back while still covering the instalment. Through his investment club, Sean buys units with positive cash flow and no money down.

reasons.title: Older units are cheap for a reason
reasons.body: Older Mont Kiara blocks sell at about RM600 per sq ft against about RM1,000 for new ones, because of lower ceilings and layouts, such as toilets along the facade, that cannot be changed.

reasons.title: Prime location is not enough
reasons.body: Units near KLCC with good shops still lose money if priced above market. A premium is fine when you know why you are paying it, such as a proven retail operator.

actions: Pull the past transacted prices for each project and its neighbours.
Compare how much cash each deal needs up front, not only the monthly cash flow.
Take a week to visit Klang Valley properties in person, about 20 if you can.
Check whether shops, transit, schools and clinics are within walking distance.
Consider subsale and bulk-purchase options alongside new launches.
articles.caveat: Rental income is not entirely passive; tenants and repairs still need managing unless you pay a management company. Buying new from a developer that sells only direct can be the best channel when early phases are priced low.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #256. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2024. The episode is sponsored by PropertyGuru's Brickz transaction reports, which Sean recommends for checking prices. He is a VIP member of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner, and his units are managed by Cozy Homes.
