articles.title: Is a condo linked to a train station a better buy?
articles.excerpt: Every new project near an MRT or LRT station now calls itself a TOD. Sean explains what transit-oriented development means, who it suits, and the trade-off between convenience and security.

question.context: With new MRT lines opening, developers market almost any project near a station as a transit-oriented development, or TOD. Mixed developments now combine homes, offices, serviced apartments, hotels and malls on one site, linked to rail.
question.text: What is a transit-oriented development, and is a home in one a better buy?

answer.quote: convenience doesn't really come with security
answer.summary: A TOD is built around public transport, so residents can live, work and shop without relying on a car. That makes it strong for rental to young workers, but the same accessibility brings crowds, noise and weaker security, so it suits investors and singles better than families who want privacy.

reasons.title: Young tenants want the link
reasons.body: Workers in their first few years of employment can barely make ends meet, and a direct rail link saves them time and the cost of a car. That demand supports rents.

reasons.title: Easy access cuts both ways
reasons.body: When a station's commuters pass through a development, privacy suffers. High-end residents have even objected to stations near them, which is why expensive projects tend to be less accessible.

reasons.title: Someone pays for the walkways
reasons.body: Public link bridges and walkways need lighting, cleaning and guards. In some projects, residents' maintenance fees cover areas used by every commuter.

reasons.title: Compartmentalisation matters
reasons.body: In a mixed development, the residential part should be well separated from the mall, offices and station, or residents share their lifts and lobbies with the public.

actions: Ask whether the project actually connects to a station, or is merely near one.
Ask who maintains and secures the public walkways, and whether your fees pay for them.
Check how the residential block is separated from retail and transit areas.
Match the project to its tenants: TODs suit young workers who commute by rail.
Choose a more private development if security for a family comes first.
articles.caveat: Some projects are both rail-linked and highly secure, but they command a premium. Sean also questions whether buyers of RM1.6 million units, who seldom commute by train, need a rail link at all.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this May 2018 video. The captions are of poor quality, so only points that are clear are included. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Unsold units near completion: warning sign or better deal?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor sees plenty of units still for sale in a project close to handover. Sean explains why developers end up with unsold stock, and when that works in a buyer's favour.

question.asker: From JJ, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JJ is under 30, married with no children, and has no property or loans yet but a good credit score. Most of his money is in stocks, and he had avoided property because of the upfront cash it needs. He is looking at a bulk-purchase listing in Dutamas, near Mont Kiara, that is close to vacant possession but still has many units available, is already late enough for late-delivery damages to apply, and includes dual-key and tri-key layouts.
question.text: Do the unsold units signal a problem, does the delay matter to a buyer like him, and are dual-key and tri-key units worth it?

answer.quote: So, to me it's not a concern at all.
answer.summary: Not in this case. Few Malaysians can borrow for a unit above RM1 million, so slow sales near completion are expected, and a developer that keeps building through a delay is a financially strong one. Judge the unit on location, rent and long-term value, and treat any discount as a bonus.

reasons.title: Developers clear stock quietly
reasons.body: Banks pay developers stage by stage as the building goes up, so a developer still holding units near completion wants the cash. Open discounts would upset the first buyers, so stock is often cleared through bulk-purchase clubs, at prices kept confidential.

reasons.title: Price limits who can buy
reasons.body: To borrow RM1 million you need an income of about RM12,000 to RM15,000 a month, which Sean puts at roughly the top 20% of Malaysians. A unit above a million will naturally sell more slowly.

reasons.title: Delay hurts families more than investors
reasons.body: Late-delivery damages run from your own SPA date, so a later buyer's clock starts later than the first buyers'. For an investor the main cost of a delay is renovation: Sean says furnishing a unit that once cost RM28,000 now costs RM48,000 to RM50,000. A family waiting to move in loses far more.

reasons.title: Dual-key units stretch one loan slot
reasons.body: A single 90% residential loan can buy a dual-key or tri-key unit that rents as two or three, where buying separate studios would push the third onto a 70% loan. Sean says the format suits dense urban areas, and tri-key rooms can rent for less than a studio while giving more privacy than a shared flat.

actions: Visit the site before you buy: land cleared and foundations under way before launch are signs of a well-funded developer.
Check the late-delivery terms against your own SPA date, not the project's launch.
Compare the expected rent with the instalment at your discounted price, not the list price.
Consider completed unsold units: you see the finished building, the view and the neighbours before you pay, and still get the developer's packages.
Spend any cash back on renovation and buffers first, then put what remains towards the loan.
articles.caveat: This assumes a prime location and a developer able to finish; Sean says prime projects are rarely abandoned, but it can happen. If you bought early in such a project, unsold stock cuts the other way: buyers will compare your subsale unit with the developer's discounted ones.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #313. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in June 2026. Sean says he is a client of the bulk-purchase club FAR Capital, not its owner, and has bought a unit in the project discussed.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #313 | ARE UNSOLD UNITS GOOD OR BAD?

articles.title: How do I know a location suits me before buying a home?
articles.excerpt: Viewers often ask Sean whether a home is worth buying. He can't know their lives, so he offers two tests to run first: affordability, then a weekday and a weekend in the new location.

question.context: The question Sean finds hardest is whether someone should buy a particular home to live in, because he can't know their needs. So he devised a test buyers can run themselves before booking.
question.text: How can you tell whether a home and its location will suit your life before you commit?

answer.quote: Imagine yourself living an entire weekday in the house.
answer.summary: Run two tests. First, can you carry the instalment for 30 to 35 years? Only then picture an ordinary weekday and weekend from that address, from the commute to school runs and errands, and see whether it still works.

reasons.title: The instalment shapes your whole life
reasons.body: A RM1 million home costs about RM4,500 to RM5,000 a month for 30 to 35 years. On a RM10,000 to RM12,000 salary that is half your income, or one partner working the whole month just for the house, and it can stop you joining a business opportunity later.

reasons.title: Weekdays are most of your life
reasons.body: Walk through a working day: where you work and how you get there, where you eat and buy groceries, and how far the daycare, school and tuition centres are. Newer, cheaper areas often come without schools and shops ready yet.

reasons.title: Don't buy for a once-a-month view
reasons.body: A golf course view you enjoy once a month may not be worth a traffic jam every weekday. Weigh weekend routines too, such as children's activities, a place of worship or your favourite brunch spot.

reasons.title: Bigger isn't always better
reasons.body: A 4,000 sq ft house means more to clean and maintain. Sean, who values time above all, would rather have a smaller home that serves him than become a slave to a big one.

actions: Work out the monthly instalment and what share of your income it takes.
If you are buying with a partner, talk honestly about whether you can afford it and whether you need to buy now.
Map a typical weekday from the new address: work, meals, groceries, and every drop-off and pick-up.
Map a typical weekend: activities, worship, family and friends.
Picture your life when you get the keys, possibly years away: marriage, children or a new job.
articles.caveat: These tests are for a home you will live in, not an investment. The answer is personal: if a trade-off, such as a longer drive for a view you love, is worth it to you, it can still be the right choice.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this July 2020 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in 2020.

articles.title: What should I actually check in my sale and purchase agreement?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers initial every page of their SPA without reading it. Sean goes through his own landed strata agreement and points out the clauses that protect a buyer of a new property.

question.context: Buyers of new properties sign and initial every page of the sale and purchase agreement, but few know what is in it. When there is a dispute, the agreement is what the developer and the housing tribunal go by, and developers know it inside out.
question.text: Which parts of a sale and purchase agreement should a buyer actually read and understand?

answer.quote: go and read through the entire agreement
answer.summary: Read the whole agreement, and know the clauses that give you leverage: the stated price, the payment schedule, the schedule of finishes, the conditions for vacant possession, area adjustments and the defect liability period.

reasons.title: Taxes follow the stated price and date
reasons.body: Stamp duty, legal fees and real property gains tax are based on the price in the SPA, not on what you pay after cash back. The date sets your holding period; in 2019, selling after five years cut the gains tax on residential property to 5%.

reasons.title: The payment schedule is fixed for homes
reasons.body: For residential titles, the law fixes how much a developer can claim at each construction stage, with the last 2.5% held for the defect period. Commercial titles have no such protection, so a developer can claim, say, 40% early and you pay interest on it for years.

reasons.title: Finishes are described, not branded
reasons.body: The schedule of finishes lists materials room by room, such as tiles or laminated timber, usually without grade or brand. It is still the only description of what you are owed.

reasons.title: Keys need a certificate, and facilities too
reasons.body: A developer can only hand over once a certificate of completion and compliance is issued. In strata projects, common facilities must be finished at the same time, or late-delivery damages run at 10% a year of the price.

actions: Check the stamping date and the stated purchase price.
Confirm whether your title is residential or commercial, and read the payment schedule.
Compare your plot or unit area with the plan; differences above 2% adjust the price.
Note restrictions on changing your facade or colours in a strata development.
Report defects within the 24-month defect liability period; if the developer doesn't fix them in 30 working days, a registered contractor's cost can be deducted from the 2.5% retention.
articles.caveat: Subsale and commercial agreements can differ from the standard form for new homes, and the tax rates mentioned date from 2019; check current rules with your lawyer.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this 2019 video, in which he goes through his own SPA for a landed strata home. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Some figures in the captions were unclear and are left out.

video.title: WHAT'S IN YOUR SPA ?!

articles.title: Is it a good time to buy? What ten years of data says
articles.excerpt: Why did some Malaysians lose money on property over the past decade? Sean reads ten years of official data and swaps timing for a test you can actually apply.

question.context: Many Malaysians say they lost money on property over the past ten years, and with shares, crypto and other assets competing for their savings, people keep asking whether now is the moment to buy. Most decide on gut feel.
question.text: Why did some buyers lose money over the last decade, and how do you tell whether it is a good time to buy?

answer.quote: I don't encourage gut feel first.
answer.summary: Nobody can time the market, so stop trying. If your finances are ready, buy only below the location's past transacted median, with rent that gives a healthy yield. That limits the damage even if you happen to buy at a peak.

reasons.title: When you bought decided who lost
reasons.body: In 2015, GST and a rule limiting buyers to two 90% loans cooled demand sharply. People who bought in 2018 and 2019, near what should have been a peak, are behind if they sell today; those who bought amid the gloom of 2016 and 2020 are ahead. During COVID, door frames cost about six times more and labour three times more, so launches stayed low until 2023.

reasons.title: Property does not double every ten years
reasons.body: According to the official house price index, landed homes rose about 25% from 2015 to 2024, or 2 to 3% a year, while high-rise rose about 9 to 10% over the whole decade, through two crashes. Expecting prices to double is why so many owners feel they lost.

reasons.title: Nobody can call the bottom
reasons.body: Buying when everyone was pessimistic worked in 2016 and 2020, but nobody knows in advance whether prices will fall further. What does protect you is paying below the local median and having rent that carries the unit.

reasons.title: The outlook is positive, but supply is rising
reasons.body: The share of launched units sold rose from about 31% to 34% in 2024, and launches are back at 2017 levels. A rate cut from the 2.75% OPR or a build-then-sell rule could lift demand further. More launches also means more choice, so selection matters more than timing.

actions: Decide whether you are ready first: your finances, not the calendar, set the timing.
Compare against past transacted prices for the area, not the latest launch. A nearby launch at RM2,800 per sq ft does not make RM2,000 a bargain where sales have sat near RM1,600 for years.
Check the rental yield; Sean treats 6 to 7% as healthy, or rent covering the instalment on a 35-year loan.
Use as little of your own money as possible: borrow for property and invest your capital where you are confident.
Watch policy: interest rates, gains tax and launch rules all move demand.
articles.caveat: These are national averages from official statistics; a single project can do far better or worse. Landed homes have been the steadiest performer, and Sean says that with enough money, buying corner lots in established townships is hard to get wrong.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this September 2025 episode, which draws on NAPIC data from 2015 to 2024. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Market figures are as presented in the episode.

video.title: WHY SOME MALAYSIANS LOSE MONEY IN PROPERTY FOR THE PAST 10 YEARS? ALSO IS 2025 A GOOD TIME TO BUY?

articles.title: What happens to my properties when I die?
articles.excerpt: Property owners spend decades building a portfolio but rarely plan how it passes on. Two succession lawyers explain what happens with and without a will, and how to prepare one.

question.context: Property investors spend decades building a portfolio but rarely plan how it will pass on. After visiting several retirement homes, Sean puts his own questions to Gary and Xin Hui, two succession lawyers. Their answers cover non-Muslim estates; Muslims follow Syariah principles.
question.text: What happens to your properties if you die, with or without a will, and how should a property owner prepare?

answer.quote: For me I think there must be some objective you want to achieve.
answer.summary: Without a will, the Distribution Act decides who inherits, and your family must go to court before anyone can act. A will lets you name an executor and decide who gets what, and the lawyers treat it as a plan for your family, not just a list of assets.

reasons.title: Without a will, the law picks your heirs
reasons.body: For non-Muslims, a spouse and parents with no children split the estate equally; with children, half goes to the children and a quarter each to the spouse and parents. Partners, friends and charities receive nothing unless a will names them.

reasons.title: Your family needs a court order first
reasons.body: No one can sign for a deceased owner. With a will, the named executor acts; without one, a family member must apply to court and be found fit to administer the estate. The lawyers describe one family whose dispute over an estate with no will dragged on for two years.

reasons.title: Loans don't fall due at once
reasons.body: If a property has no MRTA or MLTA, the executor can keep paying the instalments, and the bank won't recall the loan while they are paid. On a joint loan where each owner is insured for half, the insurer pays only the deceased's half; the survivor carries the rest, though banks may agree to restructure.

reasons.title: Executors must trace assets and debts first
reasons.body: Executors have a year to locate the assets and confirm the debts before distributing, and should file the deceased's final tax return with LHDN. An executor who pays out and then meets an unpaid debt can be held liable for it.

actions: Start with three questions: what you have, who should get it, and how, guided by the picture you want for your family ten years from now.
Keep an up-to-date list of assets and loans, including land titles and quit rent bills, so your executor isn't left on a treasure hunt.
Expect a simple will to cost from about RM300, with most between RM300 and RM1,500; complex estates can reach RM5,000 to RM10,000.
Review your will every year, and revisit what your children will need at least every five years.
Explain any unequal split in a letter kept with the will, and consider a trust protector to supervise the executor.
articles.caveat: This applies to non-Muslim estates; Muslims follow Syariah principles. Passing properties through a family company or a trust raises tax and control questions of its own, so take advice on your own situation.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2026 conversation with succession lawyers Gary and Xin Hui. The quote is one lawyer's own words; the captions don't show which of the two is speaking, so it is credited to both. Everything else is paraphrased, and fees are as quoted in the episode. This is general information, not legal advice for your situation.

articles.title: What mistakes do young buyers make in a slow market?
articles.excerpt: In 2019, with sales slow and developers offering ever more rebates, Sean's inbox filled with young buyers in trouble. He lists four: abandoned projects, signing before the loan, buying with a partner, and overgearing.

question.context: In 2019 property sales were weak, smaller developers were short of cash, and agents and speakers pushed generous promotions. Young buyers, anxious that prices would leave them behind, rushed in, and many wrote to Sean after things went wrong.
question.text: What are the most common mistakes young buyers make, and how can they be avoided?

answer.quote: don't buy things that you cannot afford
answer.summary: Four keep recurring: buying from developers who may abandon the project, signing the SPA before the loan is approved, buying with a boyfriend or girlfriend, and spending the cash back from heavily discounted deals. Be patient, check your loan eligibility first, and buy only what you can afford.

reasons.title: Abandoned projects still cost you
reasons.body: If a developer goes under after the structure is built, the bank has already paid out, say, 20% of a RM500,000 price, and you keep paying interest on RM100,000 for an unfinished building. Residential projects under the Housing Development Act have more protection; commercial ones don't.

reasons.title: Never sign the SPA before the loan
reasons.body: A booking fee is usually refundable, but once the SPA is signed you are bound. Developers offer an extra 1% to sign quickly; if the loan is then rejected, you can lose your deposit.

reasons.title: Don't buy with a partner
reasons.body: Sean gets many emails about properties shared with an ex. Share a purchase with siblings, parents or business-minded investors, not a boyfriend or girlfriend.

reasons.title: Cash back tempts overspending
reasons.body: Using cash back to cover the monthly shortfall is a valid strategy. The danger is the sudden sum in the bank going on a car or holidays, leaving nothing when the instalments bite.

actions: Check the developer's company records, track record and any blacklist before booking.
Find out how much you can borrow before you visit sales galleries.
Sign the SPA only after your loan is approved.
Keep cash back in a separate account for the property.
Take time to research rather than rushing out of fear of missing out.
articles.caveat: Some of the rebates Sean describes were expected to tighten after 2019. Buyers who understand the numbers can still use discounted deals, provided they can carry the commitment.

articles.title: We're 26 and earn RM20,000 together. Is an RM800,000 home too much?
articles.excerpt: A debt-free couple of 26 with RM300,000 in savings want a new launch of RM700,000 to RM900,000 to start a family in. Sean says they can afford it, with two conditions, and how to judge a building before it exists.

question.asker: From Howard, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Howard and his fiancée are 26, earn about RM20,000 a month gross between them and have about RM300,000 in liquid assets, with no debts. They live rent-free in a relative's apartment in Seri Kembangan, likely until 2027. They want a new launch of 1,100 sq ft or more at RM700,000 to RM900,000, an instalment of about RM3,500, to raise a family in. His fiancée does not want to rent, or to buy a worn subsale.
question.text: Is that price too high for their income, can he borrow in his name alone, should they buy new now or subsale later, and how can they judge a building's common areas before it is built?

answer.quote: I think it's a green light to go
answer.summary: They can afford it, and his RM10,000 income alone roughly qualifies at three times the instalment. Two conditions: don't pay much above the area's median price, and check that rent for similar units nearby covers about 85% of the instalment, so the home can be rented out when the family outgrows it.

reasons.title: The 85% rule protects the upgrade
reasons.body: With an instalment of RM3,500, nearby rents of about RM3,000 show demand for the space. Five to seven years on, with children and perhaps a helper, they will likely want more room and can rent out or sell without a loss.

reasons.title: Don't overpay for romance
reasons.body: Paying perhaps 10% above the median for a setting they truly value is fine as an informed choice; paying well above it simply because they love a concept is not.

reasons.title: Banks judge today's income
reasons.body: Banks lend on current income, not future raises. Interest during construction can be avoided with schemes such as HouseKEY, which has fewer developer rebates.

reasons.title: Learn to read a floor plate
reasons.body: Dimensions are fixed once approved, but finishes are not. Visit completed projects, walk from the car park through the lift lobby and corridor to a unit, and compare dark lobbies and corridors with ones that have voids or daylight.

actions: Compare the project's price per sq ft with the area's median.
Check rents for similar nearby units against 85% of your instalment.
Ask developers about completed, unsold units, which offer certainty with some launch perks.
Visit existing projects, not just sales galleries, and each list three likes and three dislikes.
Invest some of the RM300,000 rather than leaving it idle.
articles.caveat: In a project that sold well, buying early can pay off: Sean bought his own Bukit Jalil home's first phase at about RM700 per sq ft, and later phases sold above RM1,000. In a slow-selling project, waiting for completion carries less risk.
